articles.title: Tribal Narratives on Screen: A Study of Stereotypical Semiotics in Tamil Films Viduthalai Part 1 & 2
articles.authors: Divakar P; Abdullah Alfazeena
articles.abstract:
This paper considers the way in which modern Tamil cinema portrays tribal communities, with reference to
Viduthalai Part 1 and Part 2. It pays attention to the signs and symbols which filmmakers make to get a perception
of tribal identity, oppression, and marginalization. Indian cinema seldom allows tribal communities a fair and correct
representation, and this is an issue that has been raised by critics over the years. This study excavates the particular
signs and symbols that these films operate with to narrate the lives, struggles, and identities of the indigenous people.
Historically, tribal groups in India have been driven to the periphery, where they experience a social and economic
pressure. That reality is common in movies, but there are occasions when, rather than the reflective power of a
culture and its capabilities, movies merely reiterate the wide-worn-out clichés of tribes as pathetic victims or exotic
outsiders. Viduthalai is one that is working that line; the movie foreshadows oppression and resistance by the tribes,
but it also demonstrates that it is not an easy task to depict disenfranchised individuals in a cinematic world
realistically. The unique thing is that it is a tendency: such movies tend to reveal the tale of tribal suffering and
resistance in the form of victimization and sacrifice without any stories of strength and endurance. With the help of
the works of film studies and studies about the problems of cultural representation, this paper locates these
presentations within the overall context of how the Indian society and film industry tend to treat the tribal populations.
Semiotics assists in decomposing all this. Using the analysis of the pictures, symbols, and the types of characters
used in these movies, it can be said what indeed is getting through. Viduthalai relies on stereotypes of old, with its
main focus placed on oppression and the lack of more empowering points of view. Such a narrative confines tribal
identities to a very small trap and casts genuine questions with regard to authenticity and morality. The article brings
the discussion to the next level, denouncing the risks of these stereotypes and asking filmmakers to make much more
individual and deep films on tribal life in India. Such signs and signals are not only essential to study, but also, it is
about cultural awareness, social justice, and responsible storytelling. This study urges an improving way: telling
stories that not only repeat tired clichés but also actually glorify the variety and richness of tribal cultures. Film is a
need that affects people within the way of thinking, policy formulation, and even brings a change in the real treatment
of a tribe to the rest of the world. Ultimately, this study is not only a critique but also a form of call to reconsider the
way in which cinema can be culturally ethical and truthful in terms of its qualities to depict any identity.

articles.title: The use of big social data for audience segmentation: A rapid literature review
articles.authors: Claudia Abreu Lopes
articles.abstract: This paper discusses approaches for applying big data analytics for the segmentation of digital audiences to tailoring content to different sub-groups and evaluating the impact of that strategy. Segmentation of audiences requires theoretical and analytical models to identify characteristics of content such as themes or topics, online and offline behaviours, values or other users’ characteristics. Based on a rapid literature review, we selected 15 papers that applied different data science approaches and presented case studies for their application related to health areas. It becomes clear that the objectives of big social data analysis often revolve around demonstrations of analytical techniques and or use of innovative data rather than exploring the value of the analysis for applications in the real world - for programming or policy. Big social data analysis needs more discussion on the meaning of the insights that produce and the validity of generalisations to other online or offline contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Book of Abstracts- Media Metamorphosis & AI: Unveiling the Future of Content
articles_hidden.authors: Abdullah Alfazeena; Manikkam K; Jone Antony Raja. J
articles_hidden.abstract: The Book of Abstracts for the International Conference 2025 on “Media Metamorphosis & AI: Unveiling the Future of Content”, organized by the Department of Visual Communication, Hindusthan College of Arts & Science, Coimbatore, is a compilation of scholarly contributions presented during the conference held on 30th October, 2025. This volume showcases a diverse collection of research abstracts from academicians, scholars, and professionals exploring the dynamic relationship between media, artificial intelligence, and digital transformation. The works featured in this book highlight the changing contours of media practices, ethical challenges, creative innovations, and the transformative potential of AI in shaping the future of communication and content creation. It encapsulates multidisciplinary perspectives on how technology continues to redefine the media ecosystem. It serves as a valuable resource for researchers, educators, and practitioners seeking to understand and contribute to the evolving media landscape.

articles.title: An item bank of reporting items and concepts in evidence synthesis reporting guidelines
articles.authors: Kyle Morrison; Edward R. Ivimey-Cook; Malgorzata Lagisz; Ayumi Mizuno; Manuela Santos Santana; Eduardo S. A. Santos; Alfredo Sánchez-Tójar; Zachary P. Simpson; Matthew James Grainger; Biljana Macura
articles.abstract: Evidence synthesis integrates findings from multiple research studies, and its value for decision making depends on complete, transparent reporting. Authors often rely on reporting guidelines, checklists, flow diagrams, or structured text guiding manuscript reporting, but they still struggle to implement what counts as clear, complete reporting. A central issue is that many guidelines address the same underlying concepts using different wording, making it unclear whether differences between guidelines are meaningful or merely semantic. To address this, we compiled an item bank of 2,249 reporting items from 59 unique evidence synthesis reporting guidelines (from 83 studies, 68 checklists), using a six-step process: literature searching and screening, item collation, readability analysis, concept extraction, and overlap assessment. Compiled items were relatively verbose (mean words/item = 19.9) and linguistically complex (Moving-Average Type-Token Ratio = 0.959), indicating limited reuse of consistent wording—likely making items harder to interpret and compare. Because items can contain multiple concepts, and concepts can recur across items and guidelines, we identified 403 unique reporting concepts. Guidelines also showed modest conceptual overlap (Jaccard Similarity Index = 0.166, n = 1,830 pairwise comparisons), suggesting some concepts were widely shared across reporting guidelines for different methodologies and disciplines, pointing to clear potential to harmonise reporting guidance and reduce duplicated effort. We provide all reporting items and concepts in the supplementary files. We further discuss trends and gaps in item use and wording across guidelines, outline applications of the collated item bank, and note limitations that point to future research. Together, our findings offer much-needed direction for developing and harmonising future reporting guidelines, an essential step toward more consistent and transparent reporting across evidence synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: The NF Data Portal: A Community-Driven Resource to Accelerate Neurofibromatosis and Schwannomatosis Research and Drug Development
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Quaid; Belinda B. Garana; Chang In Moon; Aditya Nath; Christina Parry; Efren Munoz; Jineta Banerjee; Alexandra J. Scott; Milen Nikolov; Sang Y. Lee
articles_hidden.abstract:
The NF Data Portal (nf.synapse.org) is a free, open-science platform that centralizes data and resources related to neurofibromatosis (NF) and schwannomatosis (SWN), a group of rare genetic tumor predisposition syndromes. The portal hosts a growing collection of NF and SWN multimodal datasets including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and imaging with links to resources such as patient-derived tumor tissue collections, cell lines and preclinical models. The goal of the portal is to provide the broader academic and commercial research community with well-annotated, trusted datasets that can be used in a variety of ways, including asking new scientific questions, benchmarking new methods or tools, and combining datasets across studies. Ultimately, our mission is to accelerate the discovery of treatments and cures for NF and SWN through maximizing the global usability of high-quality data. . 
The NF Data Portal has a cross-institutional backbone of supporters composed of funding organizations, a data coordination center, and a community of clinicians and scientists. Together, this community has developed reusable building blocks for open science, including shared infrastructure, governance frameworks, metadata standards, and a structured data contribution lifecycle. In this publication, we reflect on over a decade of effort to support the data contributor and data user journeys. We share recent platform features and integrations and highlight newly available datasets. 
Whether longtime NF scientists or those encountering this resource for the first time, the NF Data Portal provides access to one of the largest NF datasets available to advance academic research, industry-driven discovery and therapeutic development. For industry users, the portal serves as a strategic translational research asset that supports target validation, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and data-driven decision making, helping to de-risk development programs and inform clinical strategy. As AI-driven analytical methods transform biomedical research, richly annotated, disease-specific datasets like those housed in the NF Data Portal, will be essential raw material for developing and validating new tools and novel treatments.

articles_hidden.title: How Much Replication Is Enough? Balancing Novelty and Replication in a Truth-Driven Evolutionary Simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Kaitlyn Harper; Felix D. Schönbrodt
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific progress relies on a balance of original research, which furthers the boundaries of knowledge, and replication, which assures the quality of existing knowledge. In recent years, calls for increased replication have gained momentum, but replication requires resources that could otherwise support novel research. Here, we take a cultural-evolutionary approach to answer the question: what share of limited scientific resources should be allocated to original versus replication studies? We simulated a scientific ecosystem with a “utopian” selection criterion: whether research moves beliefs closer to the truth. Within this ecosystem, researchers differ in their tendency to pursue original or replication work, and more successful strategies (i.e., those which contribute most to truthful Bayesian information gain) are selected for over time. Under broadly realistic parameter assumptions, the model suggests an optimal replicator share of 5-32%, with 7-21% of published studies being replications, and replication success rates of 20-30% (all replications) and 72-88% (only published replications). Stronger publication bias, greater base null rates, and smaller original study sample sizes all increase the optimal replicator share. Our model may underestimate the optimal replicator share, because the model omits biases such as p-hacking that additional replication could help correct, or overestimate, because our model’s simplistic choice of replication targets may be less efficient than more strategic ones. Ultimately, our simulations suggest that replication primarily evolves as a compensatory mechanism in response to distorted research environments, and that overall scientific progress is maximised when underlying issues such as publication bias are resolved, which would largely eliminate the need for replications.

articles_hidden.title: Time for Journals to Claim a Sustainable Future in Scientific Publishing
articles_hidden.authors: yong sik ok
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific publishing depends on trust, fairness, and transparency. This article argues that publishers should take greater responsibility for how research integrity concerns, investigations, and retractions are handled. It calls for clearer procedures, fair opportunities for authors to respond, stronger editorial involvement, and proportionate decisions based on scientific judgment. Greater accountability and cooperation among publishers, editors, researchers, and institutions are essential for building a more trustworthy and sustainable scientific publishing system.

articles.title: Refbank: an open repository of iterated reference game data
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Jess Mankewitz; Fiona Feng; Benji Fernandez; Ryder Fried; Michael C. Frank; Robert Hawkins
articles.abstract: Language users flexibly produce and interpret language in context, and over time modulate their language use to convey meanings with greater accuracy and efficiency. Adaptive language use is often studied using iterated reference games, which represent a controlled way of studying how people communicate in the absence of codified labels, and how conventionalised labels form over repeated reference to the same targets. While iterated reference games are a common paradigm, the research questions, pre-processing, and analytic approaches differ across papers so their results are challenging to synthesise using meta-analysis. Here, we present Refbank, a harmonised repository of iterated reference game data from 20 different papers, enabling quantitative synthesis in novel and larger-scale analyses. We conduct five mega-analyses that shed light on the robustness and variability of convention formation under different experimental settings. Refbank also has potential future uses for targeted experiment design, computational modelling, and language model evaluation. These directions demonstrate the utility of reusing data from iterated reference games, and we invite contributions of additional datasets to Refbank.

articles.title: Bounding Causal Effects in Pretest-Posttest Designs with a Control Group
articles.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles.abstract: With data from a pretest-posttest design with a nonequivalent control group, researchers have two main options for identifying the causal impact of a treatment: covariate adjustment (CA) or difference-in-differences (DID). Each strategy rests on strong assumptions: the adjustment criterion (unconfoundedness) for CA and the common trend assumption for DID. In practice, neither of these assumptions is typically fully satisfied, resulting in biased effect estimates. To address uncertainty about potential assumption violations, we propose reliability-based bounds for the average treatment effect (ATE) that rely on a linear structural causal model and the reliability of the outcome's pretest measure with respect to an unobserved confounder. Unlike existing bracketing approaches, the reliability-based bounds do not require the stationarity assumption and remain valid even when the pretest and posttest measures are on different scales. Using simulated data, we demonstrate that the proposed bounds outperform existing methods by covering the true ATE even when stationarity is violated, while often producing narrower bounds when stationarity holds. The bounds also remain informative under moderate violations of linearity and the single-unobserved-confounder assumption. An empirical example illustrates how the bounds are established based on subject-matter knowledge and that they tend to cover the benchmark effect estimate from a corresponding randomized experiment.

articles.title: Tests of measurement invariance for nine relationship relevant scales across straight, gay/lesbian, and bisexual individuals
articles.authors: Hannah S Elizabeth; Margaret Clark
articles.abstract: Utilizing a data set including roughly equal numbers of straight, gay/lesbian, and bisexual individuals, we tested the measurement invariance of nine relationship relevant measures—relationship quality (Fletcher et al., 2000), sexual satisfaction (Park & MacDonald, 2022), social comparison orientation (Gibbons & Buunk, 1999), social support (Mitchell et al., 2003 and Cutrona & Russell, 1987), homophily (McCroskey et al, 1975), attachment (Fraley et al., 2000), relationship status satisfaction (Lehmann et al., 2015) and self-expansion (Hughes et al., 2020). When justified based on the measurement invariance results, we conducted tests for latent mean differences. Our results lead us to recommend researchers studying varying sexual orientations utilize Fletcher et al. (2000), Park & MacDonald (2022), Mitchell et al. (2003) and Lehmann et al. (2015). Two others—McCroskey et al., 2011 and Fraley et al., 2000—required modifications before attaining scalar invariance. Gibbons & Buunk, 1999 showed evidence of good fit with the original model, but only partial invariance across sexuality groups. We urge caution with this measure. We do not recommend use of the final two measures: Cutrona & Russell and Hughes et al, 2020. Given the exploratory nature of the work, our results should be both used with caution and replicated.

articles.title: Ensemble feature distribution representations support visual stability
articles.authors: Vladislav Khvostov; Julie Golomb
articles.abstract: Visual stability refers to people’s subjective experience of a stable visual environment despite incomplete or disruptive retinal input, e.g., due to blinks and frequent saccadic eye movements. Known stability mechanisms involve updating individual objects’ positions before and after saccades. This is infeasible in real-world scenes, which contain dozens of important items. Here we present evidence supporting an Ensemble Feature Distribution hypothesis: that visual stability relies strongly on ensemble feature representations of groups of objects. In three preregistered experiments (N=51, university students), observers were sequentially shown two sets of colored disks and reported the number of disks that changed their colors. We found that if the ensemble color distribution was altered between the two displays, observers easily noticed changes, even when they occurred during saccades. Yet observers perceived the environment as stable and almost completely missed equivalent changes when the ensemble feature distribution stayed the same but individual colors swapped positions.

articles.title: Self-Esteem and Self-Reported Personality Traits: When Attitudes Toward Traits Make a Difference
articles.authors: Sergei Shchebetenko; Giorgio De Marchis
articles.abstract: Personality questionnaires do not directly record recurring conduct. Rather, they elicit task-bounded reports of personality attributions: how respondents characterise themselves using personality-descriptive content. From this perspective, established associations between self-esteem and self-reported personality may depend on the evaluative meaning attached to that content. We tested whether attitudes toward the Big Five traits moderated associations between self-esteem and corresponding personality reports in a baseline sample of Russian university students assessed in 2013 (N = 1,029) and in a dependent 2021 follow-up comprising 245 participants with linked observations. Holm-corrected analyses (Holm, 1979) supported positive interactions for Extraversion and Emotional Stability in 2013, and for Emotional Stability in 2021. The 2021 Extraversion interaction remained positive but did not survive correction. Adjusting for an internally derived normative-desirability index retained the 2013 Extraversion and Emotional-Stability interactions and the 2021 Emotional-Stability interaction. Thus, the association between self-esteem and personality reports depends partly on how respondents evaluate the trait content. The reappearance of the Emotional-Stability interaction at follow-up provides evidence of recurrence within one cohort rather than an independent replication; it does not identify a between-assessment process, and the analyses cannot determine whether evaluations shape personality attributions or develop from them.

articles.title: A moderated nonlinear factor analysis workflow for detecting and estimating multiple sources of differential item functioning and evaluating their impact on scale scores
articles.authors: Reihaneh Farzinnia; Louise Black; Joao Garcez Aurelio dos Santos; Neil Humphrey
articles.abstract:
Measurement invariance is essential for valid psychological comparisons, yet the most widely used approaches consider one source of non-invariance at a time. This risks oversimplifying measurement heterogeneity and potentially biasing comparisons when item functioning is associated with multiple correlated continuous and categorical characteristics. Moderated nonlinear factor analysis (MNLFA) can model multiple sources simultaneously, including covariate effects on latent traits (impact) and differential item functioning (DIF).

We present an open-source regularised MNLFA workflow in R for DIF detection, unpenalised model re-estimation, and expected a posteriori (EAP) score generation for creating scale scores. The workflow uses regDIF to identify candidate DIF effects and OpenMx to re-estimate the selected model, avoiding regularisation-induced shrinkage in estimates, before evaluating whether DIF adjustment changes latent trait estimates. We demonstrate the workflow using the Short Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale in an integrative data analysis (IDA) framework, pooling six UK adolescent studies comprising 155,360 participants and 221,418 observations. 

Across three calibration samples, regularised selection identified a largely consistent set of item-level DIF effects related to age, sex, and study membership. Covariate-effect estimates remained stable across model specifications, and impact-plus-DIF and impact-only EAP scores showed near-perfect agreement (all r ≈ .99; root-mean-square differences = .008 – .016). Thus, adjustment for the detected DIF had negligible influence on latent wellbeing estimates. These findings show why item-level DIF should be distinguished from practically meaningful test-level bias. More broadly, the workflow provides a route for evaluating measurement invariance, harmonising measures, and generating comparable latent scores in heterogeneous or integrated datasets.

articles.title: The Future of Educational Psychology: Between Vision and Dystopia
articles.authors: Julia Moeller; Carla Geiger; Henrik Saalbach
articles.abstract:
This study examined trends in the future development of educational psychology using a mixed-methods approach. First, a scoping review identified articles containing explicit statements about the future of educational psychology, from which categories of anticipated developments were derived. Second, experts in educational psychology completed an online survey with open-ended questions on expectations, hopes, and best- and worst-case scenarios for the field’s future, and rated 84 statements—derived from the scoping review—on their perceived probability of occurring. ChatGPT completed the same survey. Articles from the scoping review and experts’ open-ended responses were analyzed using natural language processing techniques (e.g., sentiment analysis, word clouds) alongside qualitative categorization.
The findings revealed a wide range of predictions, spanning from utopian to dystopian scenarios. Utopian visions emphasized interdisciplinary, multimethod, and evidence-based research with strong societal and political impact, leveraging advanced technologies to support personalized learning as well as mental health and social-emotional development. Dystopian scenarios expressed concern that educational psychology and quality education could become marginalized, politically constrained, inaccessible to many learners, or replaced by automated systems. Experts also identified concrete action points aimed at fostering desirable developments and preventing unfavorable futures.

articles.title: Social Media as a Context of Narrative Identity Development: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis Study
articles.authors: Irena Stojković; Marijana Veselinović; Božidar Filipović
articles.abstract: In the present study, we aimed to understand how emerging adults experience their social media engagement and how these experiences may be relevant to narrative identity construction from the perspective of the process model of narrative identity development (McLean et al., 2007). Individual semi-structured interviews with 27 emerging adults (19 females, 8 males) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes were developed: Social media as a space for meaningful communication, Online identity as a selective presentation of self, and Curating the social media profile through self-reflection. The first theme captures self-expression, exchange of perspectives, and social recognition through social media. The second refers to perceptions of online self-presentation as selective and providing a partial, and at times misleading, representation of the person. The third describes the process of editing one’s profile through evaluating whether posts accurately reflect one’s current identity. Taken together, these themes suggest that social media can provide a context for situated storytelling and narrative identity construction, offering opportunities for meaningful communication while also potentially constraining self-expression and autobiographical reasoning, depending on how individuals engage with these platforms.

articles.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity
articles.authors: Kali Trzesniewski; Sarah J Gripshover; Allison Master
articles.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning. This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students’ choices. We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users. We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.

articles.title: Alternative interpretations of the association between interparental conflict and adolescent online flaming: A reanalysis of Zeng et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Zeng et al., we reassess the evidence supporting their proposed mediation model linking interparental conflict to adolescent online flaming. We demonstrate that the observed relationships can be reproduced with high precision by an alternative latent variable model that does not require the sequence of influence suggested in the original article. In this alternative account, adolescent-reported interparental conflict, psychological stress, online disinhibition, and online flaming are viewed as manifestations of broader underlying tendencies related to general disinhibition. The findings illustrate the problem of model underdetermination in observational research, whereby distinct theoretical explanations may fit the same empirical data. We therefore recommend greater attention to competing model specifications and caution when interpreting correlational findings as evidence for specific influencing mechanisms.

articles.title: Designing for Human Flourishing: A Sociotechnical Framework for AI Chatbots
articles.authors: Louis Tay; Karina Vold; Gloria Liou; Harsh Kumar; Daniel Harris; Ashton Anderson
articles.abstract: The rapid adoption of AI chatbots - ranging from purpose-built systems to general-purpose large language models (LLMs) - for supporting human well-being and broader human flourishing requires an integrative interdisciplinary framework. In this article, we advance a sociotechnical framework for designing AI chatbots that support human flourishing, synthesizing four essential disciplinary perspectives (philosophical, behavioral, interactional, and technical) and articulating how their interplay shapes both the promises and risks of AI-based support. Central to our framework is the identification of two fundamental tensions that structure the design and evaluation of such systems: the temporal (i.e., immediate vs. longer-term benefits) and self-community (i.e., individual vs. collective outcomes) tensions. By making these tensions explicit, the framework offers an integrative lens for organizing disparate literatures on AI and human flourishing, generating novel hypotheses about system design and its effects on individual users and society more broadly.  The framework guides both developers seeking to align AI system objectives with human values and policymakers governing the deployment of AI in mental health, education, and social welfare. We advance the field by equipping researchers, practitioners, and policymakers with a roadmap for the responsible design and regulation of AI chatbots that enable, rather than diminish, human flourishing.

articles.title: Preparing the University for Generation Alpha: A Research Agenda for the Digital Transformation of Higher Education
articles.authors: Sandra Grinschgl; Malte Elson; Tina Hascher; Andre Klostermann; Etna Rosa Krakenberger; Adrian Ritz; Thomas Christian Sauter; Amanda Zurkirchen; Michael Schulte-Mecklenbeck
articles.abstract: Generation Alpha, a cohort growing up with smartphones and generative AI as ordinary features of everyday life, will soon enter a higher education system that is itself undergoing profound digital transformation. We argue that the central challenge of this transformation is not technological alone but human and that it is shaped by three fundamental tensions: upskilling vs. deskilling, autonomy vs. dependence, and individualization vs. collaboration. Developed by an interdisciplinary Community of Practice at the University of Bern (UniBE), we introduce the BRIDGE model, which conceptualizes the university as an ecosystem of three interdependent groups: students, academic (researchers and lecturers) and organizational support staff whose psycho-social, health, well-being, and performance competencies must be understood across the trajectory from school to working life. Building on this model, we propose a two-phase research agenda: systematic identification of competencies, expectations, and institutional processes through a multi-year, longitudinal research program spanning all three groups, followed by collaborative transformation of higher education through empirically evaluated interventions. This agenda provides what digital transformation in higher education currently lacks: an empirical basis for deciding where digital tools strengthen learning, work, and well-being--and where they undermine them--and tested interventions to shift that balance. It thereby operationalizes UniBE's Digitalization Strategy 2030 and responds to national as well as international calls for evidence-based, human-centered digital transformation.

articles.title: A mathematical and computational formalization of the affect regulation hypothesis of alcohol use
articles.authors: Jonas Dora; Kevin Michael King
articles.abstract: One of the most enduring ideas in alcohol research is that people drink to regulate negative affect and the stress that causes it. Despite decades of investment the field cannot say when, why, or for whom this occurs. An empirical contradiction illustrates the problem: experimentally induced stress reliably raises both the urge to drink and drinking in the laboratory, but in daily life negative affect predicts the urge without predicting drinking, while positive affect predicts drinking instead. We argue that this impasse is not a failure of data but of theory: the major affect regulation accounts are verbal, too loosely specified to generate testable predictions or to be revised when evidence contradicts them. We address this by formalizing the affect regulation hypothesis as a system of equations and implementing it as a computational model. In the model, affect reaches behavior through the urge to drink, a proximal motivational state; stress raises the value of alcohol, biasing choice; and context gates the path from urge to drink, discounting alcohol's value and, as the situation becomes less permissive for drinking, blocking the drink itself. Through simulation, we show that a single causal architecture reproduces both the laboratory and the daily-life pattern, rendering the contradiction an expected consequence rather than an anomaly. From the model we derive novel, falsifiable predictions and describe the empirical designs that would test or refute them. Most importantly, formalization makes the predictions checkable and revisable. We offer it as a falsifiable starting point for iterative theory development.

articles.title: The locus coeruleus – norepinephrine system as a regulator of social perception
articles.authors: Maryam Ziaei; Camilla Bay Panduro Jensen; Hazim Hussein; Claire O'Callaghan; Valerio Zerbi; Heidi I. L. Jacobs
articles.abstract: Social perception allows us to rapidly interpret others' emotions, intentions, and actions, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we propose a framework linking neuromodulatory function to large-scale networks involved in social perception. The framework centers on the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC–NE) system as an orchestrator of cortical networks. We argue that social perception is optimized when moderate tonic LC activity is paired with strong phasic responses to social-emotional cues, enabling selective attention, flexible updating of expectations, and accurate interpretation of social information. By contrast, both reduced and excessive LC activity are predicted to impair social perception. LC hypoactivity limits engagement with socially relevant cues, whereas hyperactivity produces diffuse arousal, distractibility, and hypervigilance, reducing discrimination of relevant from irrelevant social signals. We further propose that social perception emerges through modulation of local cortical gain, large-scale brain networks, and perceptual evidence accumulation, providing a mechanistic bridge between cellular processes and social behavior. Finally, we outline testable predictions and consider how disrupted LC function may contribute to social cognitive deficits in aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and neuropsychiatric disorders. By placing the LC–NE system as orchestrator of adaptive social perception, this framework offers a unifying account of how neuromodulation shapes social behavior.

articles.title: Positive Affect is Associated with Interactive Social Media Use: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Evelyn Alice Halliday Murray; Daniel Shaw; Jisun Kim; Andrew Jones; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington
articles.abstract: Research examining associations between social media usage (SMU) and adolescent psychological wellbeing has relied on cross-sectional self-report data, limiting understanding of specific social media behaviours and within-person variability. To address these limitations, the present study combined an objective experimental task with Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) to investigate associations between adolescents’ SMU styles, momentary affect, and trait depressive symptoms. 229 older adolescents (110 females; Mage = 22.60, 18-25 years old) completed the Social Networking Site Behaviour Task, which classifies SMU along a passive to interactive continuum, across three days (573 datapoints). Trait depressive symptoms were assessed on Day 1 using the Maryland Trait and State Depression Scale, while momentary affect was measured on each day using the International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Linear mixed-effects models revealed between-person variability in SMU style. Positive affect was significantly associated with more interactive SMU (liking and commenting relative to scrolling), whereas negative affect and trait depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with SMU style. Our findings suggest that SMU styles reflect both stable individual differences and dynamic within-person variation associated with positive affective states. This demonstrates the value of combining objective behavioural measures with longitudinal EMA design to advance understanding SMU and psychological wellbeing.

articles.title: So much variety, so much to eat : The neuro-cognitive bases of visual food categorization in infancy
articles.authors: Camille Rioux; Pia Rämä; Elodie Farineaux; Lionel Granjon; Olivier Mascaro; Stefanie Peykarjou
articles.abstract: Food is fundamental to life. Yet, detecting members of the food category raises a substantial cognitive challenge as different foods do not have any apparent common visual features. Moreover, what is deemed edible and appropriate to eat also varies greatly across social groups. While the neuro-cognitive bases of visual food category representations are well documented in adults, their early ontogenetic origins remain unknown. The current study investigated the emergence of visual food categorization abilities in infants’ brains, using the fast periodic visual stimulation paradigm (FPVS) coupled with electroencephalography (EEG). In FPVS paradigms, images from a target category are periodically inserted into a rapid stream of base images from other categories. If the brain treats the target images as a distinct category relative to the base images, a distinct EEG response appears at the frequency of presentation of the target images. In our study, French-speaking adults, 12- and 6-month-old infants (n = 25 per age group) were presented with target food stimuli inserted into sequences of base stimuli from various non-food categories (e.g., man-made objects, plants). Results show that, similarly to adults, 12-month-old infants distinguished images of food from those of other categories. In contrast, 6-month-old infants showed no detectable categorization response for food images. The current study is the first to investigate the developmental course of visual food categorization in the human brain and showed that, by their first birthday, infants already group perceptually diverse foods into a single category.

articles.title: Yuck is in the eye of the beholder: Disgust, but not anger, guides 14-month-old infants' person-specific expectations about food preferences
articles.authors: Camille Rioux; Olivier Mascaro
articles.abstract: We investigated whether infants use emotional expressions — a ubiquitous social signal — to learn about food and food preferences. Across two experiments, 14-month-olds completed a combination of Violation-of-Expectancy (VoE) and manual forced-choice tasks. In Experiment 1, an adult reacted to one novel food with disgust and to another neutrally. Subsequently, infants looked significantly longer when she ate the disgusted food than the other one. Thus, infants expected the adult to avoid foods she had found disgusting. This expectation was disgust-specific. When anger replaced disgust in a contrastive condition, infants did not look significantly longer when an adult ate food she had been angry at than food she had reacted neutrally towards. In Experiment 2, infants showed no violation-of-expectancy effect when an individual ate the food a different person had reacted to with disgust. This pattern held irrespective of whether the emoter used ostensive communicative cues or not. These results suggest that infants processed disgust as conveying person-specific subjective preferences.  Moreover, in both experiments, when infants were given an opportunity to choose between the two foods, the adult’s past emotional expressions did not influence their choices. Together, these findings show that infants selectively use negative emotional information about food. Specifically, infants link disgust (but not anger) to food avoidance. Moreover, they treat disgust expressions as conveying person-specific subjective preferences rather than information that generalizes across individuals. This selective use of disgust may reflect an early-emerging understanding that food preferences, unlike many other properties, can vary idiosyncratically across individuals.

articles.title: Plans and the Development of Speech Acts
articles.authors: Kim Plunkett
articles.abstract:
Children's behaviour, both linguistic and non-linguistic, is limited by the
  kinds of plans which they are able to formulate. Two different types of plan,
  simple and complex, are identified as underlying the abilities to make
  requests and ask questions, respectively. A cross-sectional, experimental
  study is described. Its results indicate a child’s ability to make requests
  develops at the same time as his ability to perform a non-linguistic task (the
  ‘buzzer game’) which requires the same planning capacity. Similarly, the
  ability to ask questions emerges together with the ability to play the ‘light
  game’. It is thus argued that the development of plans is the essential change
  that enables a child to act in an adult-like manner.

articles.title: Measurement Matters: A Revised Scoring System for the Infant Behavior Questionnaire – Revised Short Form (IBQ-R SF) and Age Noninvariance
articles.authors: Yvonne Chen-Yih Kuo; Carol Lee Wilkinson; Michelle Bosquet Enlow; Samuel P. Putnam; Maria A. Gartstein; Caitlin C Clements
articles.abstract: Researchers frequently rely on the Infant Behavior Questionnaire–Revised Short Form (IBQ-R SF) to assess caregiver-reported infant temperament. However, understanding infant temperament depends on the validity of the measures used to assess it. This study examined the validity of the IBQ-R SF factor structure, which underlies its scoring system that uses 14 dimension scores to generate three factor scores (Surgency/Extraversion, Negative Affectivity, and Orienting/Regulation). In a sample of 979 infants aged 3, 5, 7, 10 or 12 months, results suggested that the original and several subsequently published factor structures showed inadequate fit. After testing in discovery and replication datasets, we propose an alternative factor model with four factors that adds a Sustained Engagement factor consisting of the Duration of Orienting and Low Intensity Pleasure scales. The corresponding alternative scoring system is provided. Additional measurement invariance analyses assessed whether the IBQ-R SF measures temperament similarly at each age. Configural and metric invariance were achieved, indicating comparable relationships between IBQ-R SF dimension and factor scores across ages and rank-order stability. Failed scalar invariance may reflect age-related changes in the expression of temperament; we recommend using age as a covariate in IBQ-R SF analyses, as scores are not directly comparable across ages.

articles.title: Have I Seen This Story Before? Multiple indices of memory after one year
articles.authors: Lily Steele; Samantha Syd Cohen; Kate Hilmeyer; Ingrid R. Olson; Nora Newcombe
articles.abstract: Children’s memory improves markedly during early childhood. However, few studies track long-term retention for verifiable stimuli using multiple indicators. In this study, we followed 58 children (ages 5-8 years, M = 7.05) who had viewed six short, silent cartoons, narrated each story, and were tested for memory after one week (Hill et al., 2025). One year later, they viewed three repeated (“old”) and three novel (“new”) cartoons, judged whether each had been seen before, narrated each, and returned one week later for free and cued recall. Recognition of “old” versus “new” cartoons increased sharply with age: older children were nearly four times more likely to discriminate between old and new cartoons. In addition, narrative quality and free recall were higher for old cartoons, equally across age, indicating savings in relearning. To examine the basis of memory savings, we examined its relations with recognition of repetition, and enhanced narrative quality for old cartoons. Neither could explain age-invariant savings. Thus, young children retain complex, dynamic events after a one-year delay, as indexed by savings, while showing steady age-related change in free recall, and a qualitative age-related shift in conscious recognition of previous experience. Multiple indices of memory development are required for a complete portrait of the developmental trajectory.

articles.title: From app open to app close: Function and well-being across TikTok sessions
articles.authors: Sabrina Fay Norwood; Tamás Andrei Földes; Nick Ballou; David Joachim Grüning; Malte Elson; Andrew K Przybylski
articles.abstract: Social media use is often measured in aggregate or characterised by a single motivation, despite individual sessions being temporally bound and potentially dynamic. We used experience sampling to capture behavioural function (entertainment, access, social attention, escape/avoidance) and momentary well-being at both the onset and offset of naturally occurring TikTok sessions. Across seven consecutive days, 161 participants produced 3,943 paired sessions. Exploratory analyses showed that 42% of sessions ended with a different function than they began, with transitions frequently ending in entertainment. In preregistered multilevel analyses, individual escape-oriented sessions were not reliably associated with lower post-session well-being within persons, whereas participants who more frequently used TikTok for escape reported lower post-session well-being under the preregistered model specification. However, the within- and between-person coefficients did not themselves differ significantly, and the between-person association was attenuated to near zero in a sensitivity analysis. Exploratory transition analyses further suggested that well-being change was more closely organised around the function reported at session close than at session onset. Together, these findings suggest that conclusions about social media use and well-being depend on both the analytical level and temporal point at which behaviour is measured, and demonstrate that within-session dynamics can be observed directly by aligning measurement with the natural boundaries of app use.

articles.title: Reimagining Social Media Literacy: A Narrative Review on The Importance of Social Contexts and Peer Relationships
articles.authors: Jolien Trekels; Chiara de Jong; J. Loes Pouwels
articles.abstract: This narrative review explores the convergence of media literacy and adolescent social media use, highlighting the essential role of understanding social context in shaping adolescent behaviors and overall well-being. As young people increasingly navigate through social media platforms, they encounter a multifaceted landscape filled with both opportunities and challenges. We argue that effective media literacy interventions must go beyond individual knowledge and critical awareness to address the social dynamics and peer influences that profoundly impact online behavior. By utilizing social network theory, we propose strategies for integrating these social dynamics into media literacy programs, focusing on the importance of leveraging peer relationships to cultivate positive digital habits. By situating media literacy within broader social contexts, this paper aims to outline an agenda for future research aimed at improving the effectiveness of social media literacy interventions.

articles.title: Liar's Dice: Eye Measures in a Social Deceptive Game
articles.authors: Valentin Foucher; Anke Huckauf
articles.abstract: Eyes have been identified as markers of deception. Yet, most existing research typically relies on instructed deception directed toward screens or confederates, limiting ecological validity. The present study introduced a novel paradigm from the Liar’s Dice game to investigate spontaneous deception in an interactive context. Two players alternated between the roles of “bidder”, who rolled dice and made truthful or deceptive bids, and “challenger”, who evaluated the bid’s veracity. The challenger could either contest, ending the round, or accept, becoming the new bidder who rolled new dice and made a higher bid. The challenger won if the contested bid was false and lost if it was true. Participants played against a computer in Experiment 1 and against another participant in Experiment 2. The study addressed three objectives: to characterise the effects of spontaneous deception, social dynamics, and veracity judgments on response times, fixations and blinks. Across experiments, lying was associated with longer response latencies, fewer and longer fixations, consistent with an increased cognitive load arising from decision complexity. Experiment 2 further showed decreased blink rate, an effect potentially amplified by the social context. Fewer fixations directed at the opponent’s face when lying suggest that deception was attentionally directed toward the social agent. Challengers exhibited longer response latencies, fewer and longer fixations, fewer blinks, but also increased attention on the bidder’s face when contesting a bid. These findings provide new insights into receivers of deception and veracity judgments, indicating that suspicion reduces eye movements but enhances attention toward the opponent.

articles.title: Disrupting social media habits: a one-week detox produces enduring reductions in use and automaticity
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Suhaavi Kochhar; Mariek Magdalena Petra Vanden Abeele; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: This randomised controlled trial examines if a one-week social media abstinence intervention can reduce social media use by lowering automaticity of and craving for social media use. Participants motivated to reduce their social media use were assigned to an immediate one-week detox (N = 50) or a waitlist control condition (N = 64). Using a combination of smartphone usage logging and weekly surveys, we found that the detox produced significant reductions in social media use (d = 0.51), automaticity (d = 1.10), and craving (d = 0.58) one week post-detox relative to the waitlist group. Exploratory mediation analyses provided suggestive evidence that automaticity partially mediated the detox's effect on social media use. Furthermore, baseline automaticity predicted self-reported vulnerability to slips of action during the detox, i.e. spontaneous attempts to open removed apps. Pooling data from both groups after each had completed the detox (N = 108), we found that the reductions persisted across the three-week follow-up and that social media use remained below baseline at a six-month follow-up in a subsample (N = 46). The detox also shifted participants' subjective relationship with social media, increasing perceived control and reducing self-reported mindlessness, without changing how much they liked it or considered it purposeful. Together, these findings suggest that for those who want to cut back, taking a short break is an effective way to disrupt social media habits and restore a sense of control.

articles.title: Human Origins and Language Origins 1: A polycentric scenario for biocultural niche expansion
articles.authors: Francesco d'Errico; Chris Sinha; Michael Arbib; Peter Gärdenfors; Bernd Heine; Tania Kuteva; rukmini bhaya nair
articles.abstract: This article presents a gradualist perspective on material and symbolic niche construction and expansion that integrates data and theories from archaeology, biology, genetics, linguistics, neuroscience, psychology, and semiotics. Empirical evidence is reviewed from the broader archaeological inventory of material culture (lithics and bone artefacts, pigments, ornaments, other material signs) and from evidence for ecological niche expansion. The evidence supports an account centred on the polycentric and asynchronous emergence of symbolic practices across diverse human populations. The complex, multi-regional nature of human origins and language origins highlights the dynamic interplay between biological and cultural evolution. We reject monocausal explanations implicating a unique speciation event for symbolization and language and any theorization of language as an “add-on” in human evolution, stressing rather how the cognitive foundations of complex technical practices and symbolic practices co-evolved with the evolution of the human developmental niche. Our findings necessitate a re-evaluation of traditional theories of language origin and cognitive evolution, proposing a more integrative and nuanced understanding of the human evolutionary trajectory, situated in an EvoDevoSocio perspective on human biocultural evolution.

articles.title: Gestures speed up responses to semantic knowledge questions in a virtual reality interactive quiz
articles.authors: Cecilia Husta; Caitlin Decuyper; JUDITH HOLLER; Eleanor Huizeling; Sharice Clough
articles.abstract: Interlocutors often gesture in conversation. Emerging evidence indicates that gestures can facilitate fast turn-taking. Corpus studies have shown that yes-no questions are answered faster when paired with gestures compared to without. This finding was confirmed in a controlled behavioral experiment in which participants responded to yes-no questions presented with and without gestures with a button press, focusing on iconic gestures in particular (i.e. gestures that depict semantic information, such as objects and actions). However, it is unclear whether iconic gestures also facilitate verbal responding in dialogic, controlled settings, and whether this effect extends to other question types. In a study using a virtual reality setup, we bridge naturalistic and experimental approaches to test whether gestures facilitate verbal responses to both yes-no and wh-questions. Sixty participants took part in this experiment using a Meta Quest 3 head-mounted display. A virtual human asked 112 semantic knowledge questions, which participants answered as quickly as possible. On half of the trials, a critical word in the question was paired with an iconic gesture, with the informative movement (gesture stroke) beginning 227 ms before word onset, informed by analyses of their natural timing. On the remaining trials, the virtual human asked questions without any accompanying gestures. Gestures sped up responses to both yes-no questions and wh-questions, showing that gestures facilitate turn-taking across question types. Thus, the presence of iconic gestures in questions might aid information uptake (e.g. based on prediction or other mechanisms) and, in turn, facilitate simultaneous speech planning processes.

articles.title: Perceptions of a Foreign Leader: Donald Trump, Democratic Identity, and the Reconfiguration of Traditional Geopolitical Alignment
articles.authors: Marie Kovářová; Martina Klicperová; Eric Shiraev
articles.abstract:
This study focuses on the relationship between attitudes to the American President, democratic identity and cultural identification. The Czech Republic served as a case study because its geography and history placed it at the intersection of Western and Eastern Europe.
A two-wave national quota panel in Czechia (N = 977 matched respondents) was used to assess attitudes toward Donald Trump before (August 2024) and after his re-election (April 2025). A four-point rating scale included positive, neutral or mixed, and negative categories, supplemented by open-ended questions. Stability and change in attitudes were examined along with relationship to democratic identity, cultural identification, perceived geopolitical threats, and religiosity.
The higher order typology based on ratings across both waves comprised six categories: Consistently Negative (n = 326), Positive Shift (n = 178), Negative Shift (n = 125), Consistently Mixed (n = 119), Consistently Positive (n = 63), and Consistently Neutral (n = 63). Negative evaluations were the most common and stable. Positive change typically reflected shifts from negative to mixed evaluations; full reversals were rare (n = 3).
Respondents Consistently Negative toward Trump identified more strongly with Western culture and democratic Europe, placed greater importance on living in a democracy, more likely perceived Russia as a threat, less likely perceived Ukrainian migrants as a threat, and reported lower religiosity. Consistently positive respondents showed a contrasting profile, including weaker identification with the West and with democratic Europe and stronger identification with Eastern civilization/Slavic culture. Respondents whose evaluations of Trump improved did not display coherent profiles, suggesting a pragmatic reconsideration. 
The findings indicate a significant relationship between attitudes toward a foreign leader and broader social identities and geopolitical worldviews. In this Central European case, they suggest a significant reconfiguration of the traditional geopolitical alignment in which an American president represented the democratic West: commitment to democracy was instead associated with negative attitudes toward Trump.

articles.title: A twin study of genetic and environmental aetiologies of associations between sensory processing sensitivity and psychotic-like experiences
articles.authors: Marloes Mak; Angelica Ronald; Corina Greven; Tessa Marije van Leeuwen
articles.abstract:
Background
Individual differences in Sensory Processing Sensitivity (SPS) indicate variation in depth of information processing, emotional and empathic reactivity, and sensitivity to subtle environmental details. Psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) are non-clinical psychotic symptoms (usually occasional, mild hallucinations and delusions). This study tested the associations between SPS and PLEs, and whether associations between PLEs and neuroticism and stressful life events are moderated by SPS.

Methods
A sample of 2888 adolescent twins, from the Twins Early Development Study, were assessed longitudinally at 16, 21 and 26 years.  The phenotypic and aetiological associations of SPS and PLEs were studied using twin model fitting. Additionally, the interaction between SPS and life events in determining PLEs was studied longitudinally. 

Results 
All tested PLEs were significantly associated with SPS. The largest point estimates were for associations between SPS and Paranoia, Hallucinations, and Cognitive Disorganization (Bs: 0.14 – 0.30). AE models with Cholesky decomposition showed that genetic influences on SPS accounted for 23%-71% of phenotypic correlations between SPS and PLEs Paranoia, Hallucinations and Cognitive Disorganisation, beyond Neuroticism. Longitudinally, SPS moderated the association between number of stressful life events and experienced PLEs (i.e., Paranoia, Hallucinations and Hedonia). 

Conclusions
This study is the first to demonstrate phenotypic and aetiological associations between SPS and PLEs. The results further indicate that the longitudinal association between stressful life events (another known PLE risk factors) and PLEs is genetically moderated by SPS.

Keywords
Sensory Processing Sensitivity; Psychotic-Like Experiences; Stressful Life Events; Twin Design; Longitudinal

articles.title: Do Youth Offending Labels Matter? The Impact of the Label “Young Serious Offender” on Public Attitudes Toward Youth Justice
articles.authors: Julia Yesberg; Clare-Ann Fortune; Hasi Kolongahapitiya
articles.abstract: Research on the impact of crime-first labels on public attitudes has focused almost exclusively on sexual offending. This pre-registered conceptual replication of Harris and Socia (2016) examined the effect of the label 'young serious offender' on support for punitive youth justice policies and beliefs about rehabilitation. Using an experimental design, 393 adult residents of New Zealand and Australia were randomly allocated to receive statements using either 'young serious offender' or the person-first alternative 'young people who have committed serious offences'. Contrary to our hypotheses, we found no evidence the label influenced attitudes relative to the person-first alternative, and no consistent moderation effects were observed. Exploratory analyses identified political orientation, ethnicity, and educational attainment as significant predictors of both punitive attitudes and belief in rehabilitation. These findings suggest crime-first labelling effects may only appear where strong stigma and well-established stereotypes already exist (e.g., sexual offending). However, this null result reflects only a single, one-off exposure in a survey context. The introduction of the Young Serious Offender designation in New Zealand embeds crime-first language into policy, with potentially cumulative effects that a one-off exposure cannot capture. Future research should use longitudinal designs to examine repeated exposure to labels over time.

articles.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation as a Digital, Individualized, and Adaptive Neurotechnology Platform
articles.authors: Anup Sharma; Manu Sharma; Hamed Ekhtiari
articles.abstract: Brain and mental health disorders are heterogeneous, dynamic, and increasingly managed through combinations of pharmacologic, psychotherapeutic, neuromodulatory, and digital interventions. Psychoeducation remains foundational though it is often delivered in static, standardized formats, in which fluctuations in cognition, affect, insight, and readiness to learn are not explicitly addressed. This chapter proposes Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) as a digital, individualized, and adaptive neurotechnology platform that reframes psychoeducation as a learning-driven intervention targeting mechanistic understanding, metacognition, and self-regulation. NIPE is conceptualized as a closed-loop learning system in which multimodal brain-behavior and contextual inputs are used to infer clinically meaningful functional states, such as arousal, fatigue, attentional stability, and affective load. These states guide responsive delivery of neuroscience-grounded explanations and skills, followed by explicit evaluation of learning-relevant responses and reinforcement processes that support consolidation and durable skill transfer beyond the platform itself. The chapter describes how adaptive personalization can be implemented through layered approaches, including rule-based logic to preserve interpretability and safety, data-driven machine learning to estimate functional learning states and optimize content delivery, and constrained generative interfaces to translate validated concepts into personalized language while maintaining clinical fidelity. Because NIPE sits at the interface of psychoeducation, digital therapeutics, and clinical decision support, trust, ethics, and equity are treated as core system requirements rather than downstream considerations, with emphasis on ongoing consent, privacy, transparency of adaptive processes, and alignment with clinical workflows. NIPE outputs are framed to support patients, clinicians, and health systems through low-burden learning summaries, interpretable clinician-facing dashboards, and group-level insights that extend beyond engagement metrics. Finally, the chapter outlines future directions for NIPE, including mechanistic studies of learning and metacognition, evaluation designs for adaptive interventions, and platform-level validation and governance. Together, NIPE is positioned as an infrastructure for brain-based learning support for patients and their stakeholders.

articles.title: Individual Patterns in the Association Between Social Media Use and Adolescent Well-being
articles.authors: Jane Shawcroft; Samantha Vigil; Drew Cingel; Sarah Coyne
articles.abstract: Research on the association between social media use and youth well-being has begun adopting an individualized paradigm by focusing on the within-person associations between social media use and well-being to provide clarity in a literature characterized by inconsistent findings. We provide a more holistic examination of the individualized nature of the effects of social media on youth well-being by using EMA data from 99 adolescents living in the United States to (1) show the between- and within-person variability in social media harms and benefits related to eight dimensions of well-being and (2) create individualized predictive models of youth well-being using fifteen features of youth’s social media experiences. Across both analyses, we found considerable nuance and variability when examining the interplay between social media use and well-being at an individual level, illustrating the challenges an individualized approach poses to researchers seeking to build a generalizable understanding of social media use and well-being.

articles.title: Knowing when to doubt: a measure of epistemic vulnerability to scientific disinformation
articles.authors: José Eduardo Rosales-Trabuco; Jesús Adrián-Ventura; Diego Avendaño; Cornelia Betsch; Lars Korn; Elvis Andy Pinedo Yzaguirre; Juan Manuel Espinoza Nuñez; Maniela Dejo-Vásquez; Carlos Moquillaza Vizarreta; Angelo Fasce
articles.abstract: Scientific disinformation poses a challenge for public understanding of science, yet the psychometric assessment of epistemic dispositions underlying vulnerability to misleading scientific claims remains underdeveloped. This study introduces and validates the Epistemic Vulnerability to Scientific Disinformation Scale across six samples from Peru, Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, and the United States (total N = 4,932). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses across samples yielded a 12-item unidimensional scale encompassing source and credibility analysis, evidence evaluation, logical reasoning, and contextualization of scientific information. The final scale showed satisfactory factorial validity, internal consistency, and configural and metric invariance across samples. Construct validity was supported by theoretically consistent associations with epistemic beliefs, attitudes toward science, fake news detection, vaccine hesitancy, climate change denial, familiarity with scientific concepts, and overclaiming. The scale provides a concise and psychometrically robust measure of epistemic vulnerability to scientific disinformation.

articles.title: Change by Compassion: Introducing moralistic versus compassionate evaluation as a bridge between do-gooder derogation, nonviolent communication, and self-compassion
articles.authors: Daniel Florian Dorji Gratzer; Jana Katharina Köhler
articles.abstract: We introduce the construct of moralistic evaluation—contrasted with compassionate evaluation—as a bridging concept linking do-gooder derogation (DGD) with frameworks of self-compassion and nonviolent communication. We further provide exploratory evidence that moralistic evaluation increases DGD, thereby reducing persuasiveness relative to compassionate evaluation. In a preregistered within-participants online experiment (N = 458 non-vegan German speakers), participants viewed two short videos of a vegan advocating a plant-based diet, presented in moralistic or compassionate evaluation. Manipulation checks confirmed higher perceived judgment in the moralistic condition. Compassionate framing increased likability (reverse DGD) and persuasiveness (r(rb) = .88 and .74, respectively). In a mediation model, likability statistically accounted for the association between framing and persuasiveness (β = 0.69); no direct path was detectable. Interpreted through the lens of self-compassion and nonviolent communication, these findings provide exploratory support for the proposed bridging construct and invite further study.

articles.title: Semantic Cognition for and from Language Models
articles.authors: Kanishka Misra
articles.abstract: The success of neural network language models (LMs) at showing semantically sophisticated behavior raises questions about the extent to which they are compatible with human conceptual knowledge, and if they can perhaps also advance our understanding of semantic cognition. This brief opinion explores this potentially bidirectional connection between LMs and semantic cognition. Specifically, I review a range of methodology used to establish the structure and the function of conceptual knowledge in LMs, primarily inspired by the semantic cognition literature. I then summarize three possible ways that future work could take to make contributions in the opposite direction, by using insights from language models to make conclusions about the language-based origin and mechanisms of human semantic cognition.

articles.title: Fast Love in Hard Times: Societal Stress Shapes Romantic Representations Across Five Decades of US Songs and Movies
articles.authors: Markus Foramitti; Daniel Reiter; Mauricio Martins
articles.abstract:
How do cultural representations of romantic relationships respond to societal adversity, and can they anticipate changes in pair-bonding behavior? Behavioral-ecological theories predict that harsh and unpredictable environments reduce investment in long-term relationships in favor of immediate attraction. To test this hypothesis, we used large language models to quantify slow love (emotional attachment and long-term partner investment) and fast love (passion and immediate attraction) across three corpora spanning five decades of US popular culture: 266,086 Billboard Hot 100 chart appearances (1973-2023), 1,180 highest-grossing US movies within 1977-2018, and 14,505 US movies produced within 1950-2018. We examined long-term historical trajectories, responses to major societal shocks, and associations with psychological distress, political instability, and pair-bonding.
Representations of romantic relationships evolved through distinct historical phases rather than continuous linear trends. Across media, romanticism declined during the decades surrounding the sexual revolution, increased throughout the late twentieth century, and subsequently diverged, with song lyrics showing a pronounced decline between 2001 and 2016, before rising again. In movies, romanticism generally increased after 2000. Across datasets, periods of greater psychological distress and political instability consistently showed a relative shift toward immediate attraction and away from long-term emotional investment. The 2008 financial crisis provided suggestive evidence of accelerating this trend in song lyrics, whereas the COVID-19 pandemic produced no comparable effect. Temporal analyses further suggested that greater cultural romanticism preceded lower future political instability and, in movie production, higher future marriage-to-divorce ratios. Conversely, psychological distress preceded a stronger focus on sexual attraction.
Together, these findings suggest that modern romantic culture is neither historically linear nor socially autonomous. Instead, it evolves through successive historical phases that systematically covary with broader psychological and societal conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with behavioral-ecological accounts proposing that societal adversity reduces the psychological romantic tendencies essential to invest in long-term pair bonding.

articles.title: Similarity or Cumulative Load? A Response Surface Analysis of Autistic Traits and Parental Stress in Mother-Child Dyads
articles.authors: Jan Łabędź; Julia; Alicja Niedźwiecka; Joanna Ludwika Beck; Ewa Pisula; Gianluca Esposito; Agnieszka Pluta
articles.abstract: Phenotypic overlap in autistic traits between parents and children may have contrasting implications for caregiving. Greater similarity may promote mutual understanding, predictability, and shared communication styles, potentially facilitating parent–child interactions. Conversely, when both parent and child show elevated autistic traits, their combined characteristics may increase caregiving demands and reduce the parent's capacity to respond effectively to the child's needs.We examined 115 mother-child dyads to determine whether congruence or mismatch in autistic trait levels was associated with maternal parenting stress. Mothers’ and children’s autistic traits were assessed using age-appropriate forms of the Social Responsiveness Scale, Second Edition (SRS-2). Response surface analysis was used to evaluate two competing hypotheses. The Congruence Hypothesis proposed that maternal parenting stress would be lower when mothers and children showed similar levels of autistic traits, whereas the Discrepancy Hypothesis proposed that parenting stress would increase as the difference in autistic trait levels between mothers and children became greater. Finally, the Directionality of Mismatch Hypothesis predicted higher parenting stress when children’s autistic trait levels exceeded those of their mothers. None of these hypotheses was supported. Instead, higher autistic trait levels in both dyad members were associated with greater maternal parenting stress, with children’s traits showing the stronger association.

articles.title: Seeking and integrating social information under uncertainty: the role of high stakes and risky others
articles.authors: Caroline J Charpentier; Xiaodi Hu
articles.abstract: When making decisions under risk and ambiguity, we often have the opportunity to know what other people did and adjust our decisions. Yet, the cognitive mechanisms underlying how people actively seek social information, and how such information is integrated into choice, remain poorly understood. We addressed this question using a new social risk-ambiguity task in which participants first made baseline decisions under risk and ambiguity, then, in a social block, actively chose whether to view the decisions of two other players before deciding again. Across two large online samples (Ndiscovery=394, Nreplication=378), we found that social information-seeking increased with reward magnitude and reward probability, but was not affected by ambiguity. Individual differences further showed that participants who were more sensitive to reward probability during baseline choice were also more driven by reward probability when seeking information. Social information influenced both risky and ambiguous choices, even though participants weighed their own prior preferences more strongly. Critically, influence was asymmetric: the risky player exerted stronger influence than the safe player, with more risk/ambiguity-averse individuals exhibiting relatively weaker influence from the risky player. Computational modelling revealed a dissociation between two key processes captured by separable parameters: egocentric discounting (weight of individual vs social information) and asymmetry between risky and safe social influence. Together, these findings provide more integrated insights into the cognitive mechanisms underlying baseline choice, social information-seeking, and social influence under uncertainty, as well as the heterogeneity linking them.

articles.title: Tracing uncertainty in mind perception: Examining the role of affirming versus denying mental capacities in robots.
articles.authors: Yasmina Giebeler; Nueud Kassaye; Basil Wahn; Eva Wiese
articles.abstract:
Mind perception, the capacity to infer others’ intentions and affective states, is central to social
cognition. Its two dimensions, agency (act and plan) and experience (sense and feel), shape
perceived responsibility and empathy, structure moral behavior, and determine perceived social
relevance. Robots are less readily perceived as “having a mind”, which can negatively impact
human-robot interaction. Although it is well established that an agent’s appearance impacts mind
perception, it remains unclear how body and face cues selectively promote perceptions of agency
and experience. Moreover, prior research strongly relies on explicit ratings, offering limited
insight into decision-making processes and potential uncertainties associated with judging a
robot’s mind. Mouse-tracking provides a promising approach capturing both explicit mind
perception judgments and associated uncertainties. As uncertainty is linked to negative affective
responses and cognitive conflict, the present study uses mouse tracking to examine whether
explicit agency and experience ratings, associated with robotic face and body features variations,
trigger uncertainty. Explicit ratings showed distinct effects of appearance: body features were
associated with variations in agency perception, whereas facial features explained variations in
both agency and experience. Mouse-tracking parameters did not differ as a function of physical
features (body vs. face) or mind perception dimensions (agency vs. experience). Interestingly
though, overall greater uncertainty was observed when participants affirmed versus denied
mental capacities, which was particularly pronounced for agency assessments. These findings
demonstrate that face and body cues reliably shape mind perception, while also being linked to
intrinsic uncertainty associated with affirming mental capacities in artificial agents.

articles.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
articles.authors: Thomas H Costello; Nathaniel Rabb; Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Gordon Pennycook; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1035) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in different conspiracies one to two months later in the wake of subsequent crisis events. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

articles.title: Social cure goes global: Socioeconomic and cultural factors shape social identifications’ effects on wellbeing across 56 countries.
