articles.authors: Radhika Butalia; Tegan Cruwys; Jolanda Jetten; Catherine Haslam; Katrien Fransen; Stef Van Puyenbroeck; Rolf van Dick; Lies Bongaerts; Filip Boen
articles.abstract: Social identification has been robustly linked to wellbeing. However, most of this evidence relies on samples from White and WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich,  Democratic) nations. In this study, we tested the association between social identification and wellbeing in a global sample (46,156 participants in 56 countries), and assessed whether socioeconomic and cultural factors could explain variation between countries. Across this sample, social identification was positively associated with wellbeing, but these benefits were not uniform. Identification with family and friends (β = 0.24) showed stronger and more consistent associations with wellbeing than national identification (β = 0.07). While associations between national identification and wellbeing were positive in 93% of countries, they were reliable (i.e., confidence intervals did not cross zero) in fewer than half. The positive association between social identification and wellbeing was stronger in settings characterised by greater wealth and inequality, and varied systematically with cultural values: in less secular and less emancipative societies, national identification was more strongly associated with wellbeing whereas identification with family and friends was less strongly associated with wellbeing. These findings show that promoting wellbeing globally requires attention to the strength and nature of people’s social identifications, and the socioeconomic and cultural conditions in which they are embedded.

articles.title: Identifying effective misperception correction messages to increase public support for biodiversity policies
articles.authors: Sandra Jeanette Geiger; Jeffrey Martin Lees; Mathew P. White
articles.abstract: People often underestimate support for pro-environmental policies. While correcting such misperceptions should, in theory, boost policy support, the evidence remains mixed. To improve message effectiveness, we develop and test a systematic process titration approach based on three stepwise, theoretically informed criteria: messages that target (1) substantial misperceptions of (2) majority positions, which are (3) conceptually close (statistically related) to policy support. Across three preregistered studies in the US (n = 21,600)—a survey, single-message experiments, and a tournament of ten corrective messages—we apply this approach to 32 perceptions of others’ beliefs, emotions, values, policy preferences, and behaviors, to increase support for the UN Convention on Biological Diversity. Criteria 1 and 2 most reliably distinguish effective from ineffective messages (δ = 0.24, 95% CrI [0.11, 0.36]). Contrary to theory and existing research practices, Criterion 3—statistical associations between misperceptions and the outcome—provides no predictive value in identifying effective interventions beyond Criteria 1 and 2. Overall, a two-step titration process approach offers a practical and effective way to identify misperception targets before large-scale implementations.

articles.title: HOW ARE INVISIBLE RELIGIOUS LONGINGS AND HOPES TRIGGERED BY SOCIAL MEDIA AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE?
articles.authors: Bojan Godina
articles.abstract:
This article examines the activation of invisible religious longings and hopes in the
modern digital media landscape. Building on research from 2003–2007, which identified
elements of transcendence in films, video games, and advertising, this study analyzes a
paradigm shift. Whereas offers of transcendence were previously conveyed sporadically
through specific media content, today their activation occurs continuously and in a
highly individualized manner through the algorithmic architecture of social media and
artificial intelligence. Using a proven three-part explanatory model – consisting of the
needs for transcendent identity, perfection, and salvation – this work illustrates how
modern recommender systems exploit human vulnerabilities to lead users into so-called
“rabbit holes.” Drawing on current phenomena such as the digital cult of beauty, the
trend of “Looksmaxxing,” extremist promises of salvation, and the perception of AI as an
omniscient authority (“GPTheology”), the study demonstrates how algorithmic processes
operationalize religious longings.
The article concludes that social media and AI should be viewed as hybrid systems
that form functional equivalents of religious structures, thereby generating a new form of
“implicit transcendence.” The findings call for greater integration of ethical issues and
human rights into the media discourse.

articles.title: Acoustic cue weighting in voice discrimination varies across words and sentences and by speaker gender
articles.authors: Tianze Xu; Xiaoming Jiang; Volker Dellwo
articles.abstract: Voice perception is often described as relying on several acoustic dimensions, but whether the relative importance of these dimensions stays stable across contexts remains an open question. This study examined how two fundamental contextual factors—the linguistic level of the speech (words vs. sentences) and speaker gender—affect the acoustic cues listeners use to discriminate between voices. We analyzed behavioral data from Mandarin-speaking listeners who judged whether pairs of speech recordings were produced by the same speaker. Interpretable machine learning classifiers, including both linear and tree-based models, were used as analytical tools to predict two types of labels from acoustic differences between speech pairs: ground-truth and perceived-identity labels (same- vs. different-speaker), with the latter based on listeners’ judgments. The models performed well when trained and tested on the same linguistic level but exhibited asymmetric declines in cross-level generalization: sentence-trained models over-classified word pairs as different-speaker, while word-trained models showed the opposite bias. Feature importance extracted from the classifiers revealed a shared acoustic scaffold (including pitch, formant structure, harmonic shape, spectral balance), alongside adaptations specific to linguistic level and speaker gender. At the sentence level, tempo cues (especially for male voices) and variability-based spectral-balance cues (especially for female voices) became more prominent in voice discrimination. These changes likely reflected greater prosodic modulation in sentences and contributed to the asymmetric cross-level generalization. Overall, our findings that cue weighting flexibly adapts to linguistic level and speaker gender highlight the dynamic and context-dependent nature of voice identity perception, extending prototype-based models in which acoustic dimensions are often treated as fixed.

articles.title: Context Matters: Within-Person Effects of Smartphone Use on Momentary Well-Being
articles.authors: Katherine Roehrick; Mahnaz Roshanaei; Serena Jimyn Soh; Sumer Sumeet Vaid; Joanne M. Chung; Joseph Bayer; Gabriella M. Harari
articles.abstract: We adopt a contextual framework to examine the within-person associations between smartphone use and subsequent momentary well-being. In a large intensive mobile sensing and experience sampling study (N = 1,003 young adult; 36,949 observations), we examined the relationship between five broad indicators of well-being (loneliness, stress, sadness, contentment, and energy level), two indicators of smartphone use (frequency and duration of use), and two contextual factors (social and spatial). We found that frequent “check-ins” had a small positive association with momentary well-being: when people unlocked their phones more often than usual, they reported feeling less lonely, less sad, more content, and more energetic. On the other hand, long sessions had a small negative association with momentary well-being: when people spent longer periods of time on their phones than usual, they reported feeling more lonely and more sad, while also feeling less content and less energetic. Moreover, we found that contextual factors were (a) a more important predictor of momentary well-being, and (b) moderated the within-person associations between smartphone use and well-being. Frequent and prolonged smartphone use was more detrimental to momentary well-being when occurring in social settings (around strong or weak ties vs. when alone) and in public or work environments (vs. at home). Overall, we find a relationship between smartphone use and momentary well-being exists, but the direction of this effect is sensitive to context—underscoring the value of a situational approach to media effects research.

articles.title: Too Much, Too Little, or Just Right? Identity Processes and Motivations Explain  Everyday Perceptions of Time Spent on Social Media
articles.authors: Gabriella M. Harari; Serena Jimyn Soh; Zhenchao Hu; Sanaz Talaifar; Alan Meca; Noah Vinoya; Rui Pei; Samantha Jo Grayson; Sumer Sumeet Vaid; Nilam Ram
articles.abstract: Emerging adults use social media—and evaluate their use—while navigating the critical task of identity development. We investigate how evaluations of time spent on social media are associated with (a) individual differences in identity development and (b) situational fluctuations in identity-relevant social media motivations. In our longitudinal field study (N = 2,251; 87,283 observations), emerging adults forming their identity tended to evaluate their social media time as balanced (i.e., the right amount), whereas those evaluating their identity tended to perceive imbalance (i.e., too much or too little time spent). Using social media to connect with others was associated with momentary perceptions of balanced use, whereas doing so to explore personal and professional goals was associated with imbalance. These findings suggest that emerging adults’ evaluations of their time spent on social media may depend on how well use aligns with identity-relevant needs. We discuss implications for psychological and digital well-being.

articles.title: Change in Adaptive Identity Processes and Well-Being Supported by  Self-Reflection and AI-Mediated Reflection in Digital Intervention
articles.authors: Serena Jimyn Soh; Subigya Nepal; Noah Vinoya; Gabriella M. Harari
articles.abstract: Young people are increasingly turning to conversational AI agents for support in figuring out what they want to do with their lives. Reflecting on career goals is characteristic of emerging adulthood (ages 18 to late twenties), a critical time for exploration and commitment to one’s personal and vocational identity. Yet it is unclear whether and how conversational AI agents benefit or hinder the development of positive and coherent identities, which has potential consequences for well-being. Our two pre-registered field experiments (Study 1: N= 165; Study 2: N = 248) tested the efficacy of digital intervention treatments designed to promote adaptive identity processes via career-focused reflection activities. Using an active-controlled RCT design, we assigned participants to either a Self-Reflection or an AI-Mediated Reflection condition. We found that both conditions promoted within-person adaptive change in daily identity exploration and commitment processes on treatment days, compared to no treatment days. However, when comparing the relative efficacy of the two treatments, we found that self-reflection may better facilitate adaptive changes (e.g., increasing identity commitment, decreasing ruminative exploration), compared to AI-mediated reflection. Exploratory analyses also showed that the intervention had positive effects on daily affect and post-intervention eudaimonic well-being, although AI-mediated reflection was less beneficial. Linguistic analysis of the reflection content suggest that the conditions may shape the cognitive and affective experience of reflection in meaningfully different ways. Our discussion contextualizes these findings within the literature on conversational AI agents as a tool for self-development and highlights future directions for research on human-AI interactions.

articles.title: Virtual Empathy Scale (VES): Development and Psychometric Validation Among Indian Young Adults
articles.authors: Aishu S Gowda; Akash Nethravathi Raju; Dhiksha J
articles.abstract:
This research was targeted at constructing and testing the virtual empathy scale (VES) that is intended to assess the empathy that is realized in the online communication between young college-going adults. It is based on multidimensional empathy models and is composed of three: empathic expression, cognitive empathy, and affective empathy. There was a generation of a pool of 49 items, and it underwent the face and content validity examination by experts reducing the pool to 41 items. Then we performed EFA on a sample of 421 college going students. This gave a 32-item scale, and good factor loading. We subsequently applied CFA to another sample of 331 students, and this supported the three-factor model, with reasonable fit statistics (CFI= .90, TLI=.899, RMSEA=.061). To conduct the reliability analysis, it was demonstrated that the results had high internal consistency (α > 0.87, ω > 0.87) in all three factors. The scale demonstrated convergent validity as demonstrated in high factor loading and composite reliability, however, the average variance extracted was a little below the optimal thresholds. And lastly, discriminant validity with some factor correlation approaching upper limits was determined with the use of HTMT. This scale has demonstrated high psychometric characteristics and is a potentially useful instrument to measure empathy in digital communication and can be used in a variety of psychological studies, online learning, and digital wellbeing intervention.
Keywords: virtual empathy, digital communication, psychometric validation, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, young adults.

articles.title: Digital media intervention research for young people across geo-cultural contexts: A critical review of bias and representation
articles.authors: I. Chaplinska; Peter Nikken; Sophie Mary; Carlo Schuengel
articles.abstract: Children's digital wellbeing develops within unequal conditions of access, skills, support, and institutional response, which shape which digital needs are recognised, evaluated, and made actionable. Evaluated digital media interventions may inform policy; yet when evaluations concentrate in particular regions, dimensions of wellbeing, and delivery settings, the evidence base offers a structurally partial view, leaving some children, contexts, and experiences outside the scope of institutional action. This paper examines what the evaluated evidence base reveals about whose digital wellbeing becomes institutionally visible and actionable across geo-cultural contexts. Drawing on 120 publications reporting 131 intervention instances across 38 countries (2006–2024), we apply the Global Kids Online risks-and-opportunities framework and treat the literature as a selective record of institutional legibility. Four findings stand out. Evaluative visibility is geographically concentrated: nearly half of all country-linked observations come from five countries, with Africa and South America minimally represented. Risk-oriented interventions consistently outnumber opportunity-focused ones, positioning children as users to be protected rather than as participants, creators, and rights-bearing subjects. Three-quarters were delivered through schools, while family, peer, community, and platform-proximate contexts remain marginal. Participant characteristics – including ethnicity (14%) and neurodivergence (4%) – are rarely specified, rendering some groups analytically invisible and digital inequalities largely unexamined. The evaluated field is thus shaped by what is institutionally feasible rather than by socially needed responses. Policy built on it, therefore, risks reproducing the same partiality. Strengthening evaluation capacity in under-represented regions, broadening opportunity-oriented agendas, and developing non-school-based models are necessary steps towards a more equitable and child-centred evidence base.

articles.title: Development and Validation of Home Factors for Critical Reading Scale
articles.authors: Jenni Ruotsalainen; Leena Paakkari; Mari Manu; Emmi Ulvinen; Jenni Salminen; Kamil Kuracki; Minna Palmu; Minna Torppa
articles.abstract: Today, children need critical reading skills from an early age, making it essential to explore how these skills can be supported in the home environment. Since no measure currently exists for examining home factors that may affect critical reading development, this study aimed to develop and validate scale for families with children aged 7–16 years. The study included three phases in Finland: 1) item generation, 2) item selection through two pilot studies (n=260; n=280), and 3) validation of the scale with two separate datasets from Finland (n=11,090; n=328). External validity was examined in a Polish sample (n=120). Initially, 178 items were generated, 82 of which were selected for piloting. Through the pilot studies, the 14 best-performing items were selected for validation. A six-factor structure was identified for the scale, referred to as the Home Factors for Critical Reading (home-CR) scale: 1) Critical reading practices, 2) Attention to child initiatives, 3) Control of media use, 4) Reading interest and expectations, 5) Valuing knowledge, and 6) Rigid thinking patterns. The consistency of the factor structure across samples and its alignment with theoretical constructs supported the construct validity of the scale. Criterion validity was examined in relation to the number of books at home, parental reading frequency, and digital parenting, and the home-CR scale was found to be related to—yet distinct from—these constructs. The confirmatory factor analysis loading structure and test–retest results supported the reliability of the scale. The iterative, validity-driven development process yielded a brief, multidimensional home-CR scale.

articles.title: The Conflict Device: A Control Theory Model of Problematic Digital Media Use
articles.authors: Warren mansell; Amy Mowle; Louis Trouchet; Mehdi Zemestani; Jason Sharbanee; Tauseef Gulrez; Danielle Einstein
articles.abstract: Digital media refers to smartphone use, social media, video-gaming and artificial intelligence among other forms, which are becoming increasingly integrated across platforms. Whilst there are widely recognised benefits, their documented harms, especially pre-adulthood, are leading to statutory restrictions across the world. For most adult users exempt from any bans, it is critical to understand the contexts and vulnerabilities within which digital media use is experienced as problematic, to inform individual, community and device-focused interventions. We critically review contemporary research and theories to develop an integrative model across digital media based on perceptual control theory. Through conceptualising digital media as a closed-loop extension of the self via hyper-efficient, dynamically adaptive and digitally amplified feedback pathways, we illustrate the mechanisms through which restricted attention utilises neural reorganisation to entrench habitual control. This entails a range of additional vicious cycles maintaining distress. As an exit from this state, we specify the factors that support the development and maintenance of a mindset of metacontrol flexibility (MCF) associated with tolerance of goal conflict and the effective use of fringe consciousness. The seeds of the MCF are the diverse opportunities to attend to, and meet, basic needs via restorative factors in the offline world.

articles.title: From TikTok Keeps Me Going to TikTok Keeps Me Unknowing: Profiling Adolescents Based on Their Online Short Video Use for Mental Health Information and Support
articles.authors: Marie Geertrude Oldeman; Bram Orobio de Castro; Melanie de Looper; Eva van Reijmersdal; Eline Suzanne Smit
articles.abstract:
Introduction: There is much debate on how online short videos (OSVs) on social media (e.g. TikToks) may interact with adolescent mental health. For example, there is concern about adolescents using these videos for mental health information and support. The goal of this study was to identify groups of adolescents based on their OSV use for mental health information and support, and to examine differences between these groups.

Methods: We conducted an online cross-sectional survey in 2024 among Dutch adolescents with and without mental health complaints (general sample: N = 1532; Mage = 14.20; 53.92% female, 44.97% male, .85% other; clinical subsample: N = 239; Mage = 15.70; 65.69% female, 34.31% male, 0.00% other). We inquired them about their OSV use, mental health, mental health literacy and attachment representations. 

Results: In both samples, we identified three profiles: Regular users, Occasional users, and Non-users. In the clinical subsample, we additionally identified two groups: Intermittent users and Support seekers. In both samples, profiles characterized by higher consumption of mental health information and/or support via OSVs experienced more severe mental health concerns, more insecure attachment representations, and greater mental health literacy. 

Conclusions: These results show that different adolescents use online short videos differently. There is a need for targeted research and interventions, as not all adolescents use OSVs equally and may thus ultimately experience different positive and negative effects.

articles.title: Effects of Shot Size on Social Impressions in Humans and Multimodal AI
articles.authors: Hua Hwang; Dahyeon Kang; Sung Park
articles.abstract: The same person can be judged differently depending on how tightly they are framed. As image- and video-based evaluations become increasingly common in settings such as hiring, screening, and interviews, this raises a practical question: does shot size change social-impression ratings in human observers and a multimodal large language model (GPT-4o)? From one master photograph of each of eight adults with neutral expressions, we created medium-shot (MS), close-up (CU), and extreme-close-up (ECU) versions while holding expression, pose, lighting, perspective, and output size constant. Sixty participants rated all eight identities in a balanced design, and a fixed GPT-4o configuration evaluated each of the 24 images in ten stateless repetitions. Both evaluators rated the same five outcomes: Trust, Competence, Likeability, Discomfort, and Approachability. In human crossed linear mixed models, tighter framing increased Discomfort and decreased the other four outcomes; all five MS–ECU contrasts remained significant after Holm correction. Discomfort showed the largest human MS–ECU change (b = +0.600), whereas Competence showed the smallest (b = −0.221) and decreased in 5 of 8 identities. GPT-4o showed the same overall direction of change across all five outcomes, and all five identity-level MS–ECU sign-flip tests remained significant after Holm correction. The predicted larger CU–ECU change was not supported in humans, and no GPT-4o outcome showed a significant transition difference. For Discomfort, the larger observed change occurred from MS to CU in humans but from CU to ECU in GPT-4o. Across both evaluators, tighter framing produced less favorable social impressions and greater Discomfort for the same neutral identities.

articles.title: A Bayesian Psychometric Item-Level Resource for Korean Early Vocabulary and Developmental Measurement
articles.authors: Jun Ho Chai; Eon-Suk Ko
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Parent-report vocabulary measures are widely used to study early language development, but CDI-based analyses typically summarize children’s responses using total vocabulary scores. This approach provides limited information about how individual words differ in developmental timing and psychometric function. This study develops a Korean item-level vocabulary resource that jointly characterizes developmental emergence, item response theory parameters, and input frequency.
Method: Using Korean Words & Gestures comprehension and Words & Sentences production data from Wordbank, we estimated Bayesian age of acquisition (AoA) at the 50% response threshold. We then examined associations between Bayesian AoA estimates, Bayesian two-parameter item response theory item difficulty and discrimination parameters, and corpus-derived Korean input frequency. The stability of Bayesian AoA and item response theory estimates was evaluated through repeated child-level resampling.
Results: Bayesian AoA and item response theory estimates were stable across repeated resampling. Words that emerged earlier also tended to be psychometrically easier, and more frequent words tended to emerge earlier and show lower latent difficulty. However, AoA and input frequency were only weakly associated with item discrimination, indicating that developmental timing and input frequency do not fully explain how informative a word is for distinguishing children along the latent vocabulary scale.
Conclusion: Early Korean vocabulary items vary along partially distinct developmental and psychometric dimensions. The resource characterizes Korean CDI words by AoA, latent difficulty, discrimination, and input frequency, providing a foundation for item-level analyses of Korean early vocabulary development to relate measurement properties to theories of lexical development.

articles.title: Beyond the empathogen label: the social-affective profile of MDMA
articles.authors: Makaela Weeda; Valeria Gazzola; Monique Smith; Josjan Zijlmans; Christian Keysers; Ákos Babiczky
articles.abstract: 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is widely described as an “empathogen”, yet empathy is not a unitary process. Here we review MDMA’s social effects by decomposing them into social perception and emotion discrimination, sociability and social reward, affective sharing, cognitive empathy and mentalizing, and prosocial behaviour. Available evidence gathered in humans and other mammals demonstrate that MDMA has distinct effects across these domains, although research coverage remains uneven across domains. We argue that MDMA is best understood not as a global empathy enhancer, but as a domain-specific modulator of social reward, threat perception, positive-valence affective sharing, and interpersonal appraisal. Moving beyond this simplified empathy enhancer concept is essential for understanding both the therapeutic promise and the interpersonal risks of MDMA.

articles.title: Measuring the effective polarity and level along the excitation patterns produced by focussed cochlear-implant stimulation
articles.authors: Robert P. Carlyon; Francois Guerit; John M. Deeks
articles.abstract:
Three experiments estimated the effective polarity and level of neural activation
produced by trains of “baseline” symmetric biphasic pulses, where the order of the phases
of each pulse was anodic-cathodic (AC) or cathodic-anodic (CA). Detection thresholds were
measured for trains of quadrupolar-mode anodic-leading pseudomonophasic probe pulses,
where each pulse was presented immediately after a baseline pulse or in quiet. Thresholds
were substantially lower in the presence than in the absence of the baseline in several
conditions, including for monopolar baselines in CA order. This unmasking was also
observed with wide-bipolar (BP+10) and wide-tripolar (TP=3, TP+5) baselines, whenever
the probe was presented to an electrode where the second phases of the baseline pulses
were anodic. Because the polarity of the baseline varied across the electrode array for BP
and TP stimuli, this allowed us to measure reversals in the effective polarity of the
baseline stimulus along its excitation pattern. The unmasking is attributed to constructive
charge interactions between the first (anodic) phase of each probe pulse with the second
phase of the preceding baseline pulse. The results are compared to voltage profiles for
each baseline measured along the electrode array, and are discussed in terms of potential
implications for the development of improved cochlear-implant stimulation methods.

articles.title: Acculturation as a Situated Transactional Process
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu
articles.abstract: Acculturation research commonly links broad preferences for heritage-culture maintenance and participation in the receiving society to psychological and sociocultural adjustment. Yet meta-analytic and longitudinal evidence shows that these associations are often weak, heterogeneous, and limited over time, suggesting that broad preferences alone cannot explain why cultural engagement leads to different outcomes across situations. This conceptual article develops a situated transactional framework within a broader complex dynamic systems account. Building on established work showing that acculturation is contextual, domain-specific, and interactional, the framework specifies how these influences come together within concrete encounters. It proposes a process in which locally relevant conditions shape appraisal, the mobilization of culturally patterned resources, response, relational and institutional reception, multidimensional outcomes, and feedback into later encounters. The article also distinguishes the adaptation process, understood as the continuing person-environment transaction, from adaptation outcomes, including psychological, sociocultural, relational, and externally observed consequences. By organizing these elements into an explicit recursive architecture, the framework generates testable predictions about context-specific responses, reception, multidimensional outcomes, learned response patterns, and structural change. It thereby provides a concrete empirical agenda for testing whether these mechanisms improve explanation and prediction beyond broad-orientation and contextual-moderation accounts.

articles.title: Reframing Acculturation:  When (and Why) Acculturation Science Warrants a Systems Explanation
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Karen Phalet
articles.abstract: Acculturation has always been understood as a process of change, and contemporary research examines that change from several complementary perspectives, including developmental trajectories, reciprocal intergroup relations, ecological contexts, situated cultural processes, and multilevel social change. The field therefore contains many elements of a systems account without a shared architecture for relating them. This article offers a selective integrative review and metatheoretical synthesis using complex dynamic systems theory (CDST). CDST provides a coordinating framework that complements existing acculturation theories and encounter-level models of adaptation. It distinguishes five explanatory questions distributed across different traditions: what form change takes, who or what influences whom, how change moves across levels of organisation, where broader conditions become relevant, and how processes unfolding at different rates become linked. We organise these questions through five dimensions: nonlinear dynamism, relational reciprocity, multilevel emergence, situated adaptation, and multiscale temporality. Together, they provide a way to examine how patterns of acculturative change depend on prior experience, relationships, local conditions, levels of organisation, and processes unfolding at different rates. For each type of systems claim, we specify a linear-additive alternative and the evidence needed to distinguish between them. Power differences and prior history are treated as conditions that can shape how the system operates and changes. The framework therefore shifts attention from average associations between acculturation variables and outcomes toward explaining how acculturative change is organised, when different processes become connected, and when a systems explanation adds value beyond conventional models.

articles.title: Interactional dynamics in online spoken conversations with people who do and do not stutter
articles.authors: Lotte Eijk; Emilia Horn; Buhan Guo; Sophie Meekings
articles.abstract:
Everyday conversation involves precise co-ordination between speakers as they take turns, a collaborative effort that is necessarily affected by motor speech difficulties such as stuttering. People who stutter (PWS) report difficulties in conversational interaction that have a significant impact on quality of life. However, relatively little research exists on turn-taking in this population.
This study examines sixty conversations between ten pairs of people who do not stutter (PWNS), and ten PWNS-PWS pairs. Conversations were analysed for turn-taking speed, utterance length, number of backchannels, interruptions and completions - factoring in speaker disfluency and the fluency of the utterance being responded to. The pitch profile of interruptions and completions was also analysed.
Across groups, talkers responded most to disfluent utterances and more disfluent speakers had conversations with longer gap durations. PWNS with a higher stuttering severity score had conversations with longer turns, and PWS with a higher stuttering severity score had conversations with more interruptions compared to more fluent speakers. Interruptions were produced with higher pitch than completions, but this difference narrowed as stuttering severity increased. Overall, results suggest that disfluency affects interactional dynamics regardless of whether talkers have a motor speech disability, but there are additional challenges in interaction for PWS.

articles.title: Using Text Embedding Models to Quantify Strategies in Multilingual Verbal Fluency: Evidence from Young and Older Adults
articles.authors: Huitian Chen; Chin Tung Wu; Zhengyuan Liu; Haoyun Zhang
articles.abstract: Verbal fluency tasks, particularly semantic fluency, assess language and executive functions, yet conventional measures may not fully capture cross-language retrieval dynamics or their cognitive correlates in multilingual speakers. We developed an automated approach that represents consecutive responses as vectors and derives Mean Semantic Distance (MSD), the average distance between adjacent responses, and the Standard Deviation of Semantic Distance (SD), reflecting variability in those distances. Experiment 1 evaluated four candidate models. BGE-M3 was selected for strong agreement with human semantic judgments, convergence with another psychologically plausible model, and less compressed distance geometry. Experiment 2 examined 45 young Cantonese, Mandarin, and English multilingual adults. Conventional fluency measures showed the strongest performance in Cantonese and the weakest in English. In contrast, MSD was highest in Mandarin and lowest in English, whereas SD was lower in English than in Cantonese and Mandarin. Proactive control was differentially associated with Mean Cluster Size across languages, while processing speed–MSD associations differed between Cantonese and Mandarin. Stroop interference showed no reliable language-specific modulation. Experiment 3 compared the young adults with 26 older Cantonese and Mandarin bilingual adults. Older adults produced fewer words, but the cross-language MSD and SD patterns were broadly similar across age groups. Proactive control showed selective age- and language-dependent associations with Total Number of Words and Mean Cluster Size, whereas processing speed showed no reliable three-way interaction with MSD. Together, these findings show that continuous semantic distance measures complement traditional fluency scores by revealing retrieval patterns and cognitive associations that conventional measures may miss.

articles.title: Care Versus Friction: Water Sustainability Attitudes, Conservation Behaviour and the Intention–Action Gap Among Young Singaporeans
articles.authors: Gemma Anne Calvert; Krishnan Menon; Steven Graham; James Breeze; Zakhran Khan; Ganesh Honnur
articles.abstract: Singapore is among the most water-stressed nations in the world, yet has engineered a resilient supply through its Four National Taps strategy and its reclaimed water programme, NEWater. That system depends not only on infrastructure but on a population willing to value, conserve and accept unconventional water. Using an artificial-intelligence powered conversational interviewing platform, we conducted 498 semi-structured interviews with Singapore residents aged 15 to 35, of which 497 were analysable, covering conservation habits, tap and recycled water attitudes, smart monitoring technology, shopping behaviour, embodied water footprints, and the ethics of transboundary water consumption. Pro-environmental belief approached saturation: 92% reported a recent water-saving action, 64% were comfortable drinking recycled water, and 77% were interested in smart water meters. What constrained further action was not indifference but the accumulation of small frictions: an unfamiliar word, an inconvenient routine, an unclear price differential, a perceived trade-off with comfort. The pattern was sharpest in the ethical domain, where 78% judged overseas water shortages unfair yet only 34% said this would definitely change their purchasing. Coding cost, environmental value and comfort independently, we find these considerations co-occur within individuals rather than distinguishing between them: 322 of 497 respondents held all three, and only 30 held one alone. Message targeting therefore cannot resolve a tension respondents hold within themselves. We further identify a sequencing effect, whereby household effort is judged negligible until larger consumers act, and a verification gap, in which willingness to credit environmental claims is limited by the absence of checkable evidence rather than by distrust. We propose that the operative tension for this cohort is care versus friction rather than care versus apathy, and derive design principles accordingly.

articles.title: Conceptual maps of social knowledge support trait generalization
articles.authors: Gavin Mullin; Leor M Hackel; Peter Mende-Siedlecki
articles.abstract: People rapidly infer traits from the social behavior of others, supporting predictions about their future behavior. How do people use this learning flexibly in novel social situations in which they have no direct experience with someone? We propose people use maps of social knowledge (representing similarity between traits) to generalize impressions and predict behavior in new domains and contexts—a prediction we tested across four experiments. In Experiment 1, participants learned about targets (either humans or non-human slot machines) whose behavior in a task revealed sociability, and later, chose which partners to engage with in new tasks associated with other traits. Trait similarity (i.e., between original and novel domains) shaped partner choice, but critically, this relationship was socially specific: participants generalized social learning based on trait similarity when interacting with other humans but not with slot machines. In Experiment 2, participants were given explicit trait labels describing potential partners. Trait similarity continued to influence generalization across an expanded set of traits and task contexts, above and beyond the mere valence similarity of traits. Next, Experiment 3 demonstrated that this similarity-based generalization occurs spontaneously: in a false recognition task, participants were more likely to misremember conceptually-similar traits as having been used to describe a person’s behavior. Experiment 4 extended these findings by demonstrating that similarity-based generalization persists even under cognitive load, suggesting it operates efficiently and with minimal cognitive resources. In sum, these findings illuminate how people flexibly navigate social contexts by efficiently drawing on structured representations of social knowledge.

articles.title: Beauty Care as a Self-Compassion Intervention for Family Caregivers of Care Recipients with Dementia: A Preliminary Community-Based Study
articles.authors: Hana Sakurai; Tomoko Wakui; Fumiko Miyamae; Riko Nakayama; Mutsuko Okamura; Kumiko Fukasawa; Chiaki Ura; Tsuyoshi Okamura
articles.abstract:
Background: Family caregivers of care recipients with dementia often experience substantial stress. Self-compassion and self-efficacy have been identified as modifiable factors that may help caregivers cope with stress more adaptively. Beauty care, which encourages self-attention, may offer a practical and accessible approach to fostering self-compassion and self-efficacy; however, empirical evidence in caregiving contexts remains limited.
Objective: This preliminary study examined the psychological effects of a community-based beauty care programme on self-compassion and caregiving self-efficacy and subjective health status among family caregivers of care recipients with dementia.
Methods: A single-group pre–post design was employed. The programme consisted of a single-session beauty care intervention, including stretching, facial massage, skin care, and makeup, delivered collaboratively by Shiseido, Urban Renaissance Agency, and Tokyo Metropolitan Institute for Geriatrics and Gerontology. Self-compassion was assessed using the Self-Kindness subscale of the Japanese version of the Self-Compassion Scale, and caregiving self-efficacy was measured using the Self-Efficacy for Obtaining Respite subscale of the Revised Scale for Caregiving Self-Efficacy. Subjective health status was measured with a single item. Pre- and post-intervention scores were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
Results: The final analysis included 8 participants. A marginally significant increase in self-kindness was observed after programme participation. No significant change was found in caregiving self-efficacy for obtaining respite and subjective health status.
Discussion: The absence of significant change in caregiving self-efficacy and subjective health status may reflect the brief, single-session nature of the programme, which may be insufficient to affect skill- or health-based outcomes. In contrast, the marginally significant increase in self-kindness suggests that emotionally oriented outcomes may be more responsive to short-term interventions. Future programmes might incorporate more targeted, skill-based components alongside beauty care to address both the emotional and practical dimensions of caregiver well-being.

articles.title: Rethinking Group Differences in Psychopathology Networks: A Slow–Fast Perspective on Context and Symptom Activation
articles.authors: Kyuri Park; Denny Borsboom; Michael Lees; Leonie Elsenburg; Gabriela Lunansky; Karien Stronks; Johan Bollen; Mary Nicolaou; Vítor V. Vasconcelos
articles.abstract:
Groups differing in social and economic circumstances often differ markedly in depressive symptom levels while their estimated symptom-network structures show few clear differences. Null results in network comparisons are interpreted as if indicating that the two groups' symptom systems are the same. However, it only indicates that no difference is detected in the interactions between symptoms. How readily symptoms become present, and how that may depend on the contextual conditions under which symptoms are observed, is rarely compared. Building on a slow--fast perspective, we conceptualize depressive symptoms as a relatively fast-changing system embedded in more persistent social, economic, psychosocial, health, and lifestyle conditions that shape symptom activation.

Using a cohort of 23,689 adults from Amsterdam, we illustrate this perspective with depressive symptoms measured by the PHQ-9 and a composite index of slow-layer contextual conditions, which we call {\em Slow Risk Load} (SRL), capturing persistent socioeconomic, psychosocial, and health-related conditions. Participants with High SRL showed substantially higher depressive symptom levels than those with Low SRL. A standard Network Comparison Test did not detect an overall difference in network structure between the groups, although global strength was modestly higher in the High SRL group.

Ising models, which separate how symptoms co-occur from how readily each becomes present, indicate that activation is higher under high SRL for eight of nine symptoms, and model comparison consistently favored group-specific activation over group-specific interactions.

The slow--fast perspective reframes group network comparisons as a problem spanning multiple time scales in which symptom-network structure, symptom activation, and contextual conditions should be considered jointly. It places symptom-focused and context-focused interventions at different layers of the same coupled system rather than in competition.

articles.title: The Reproducible Open Coding Kit: A Human and Machine Readable Standard for Coding Qualitative Data
articles.authors: Gjalt - Jorn Peters; Szilvia Zörgő
articles.abstract: The Reproducible Open Coding Kit (the ROCK) is a standard for human- and machine-readable qualitative (coded) data. It was designed to be accessible to researchers without dedicated software, while simultaneously offering enough structure to enable programmatic processing. Through this combination and a number of features tailored to these ends, the ROCK lends itself well to facilitate application of open science principles in qualitative research, to catalyse methodological innovation in qualitative research, and to progress towards machine-readability and interoperability of (coded) qualitative data, to ultimately enable truly Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) qualitative data. In this canonical reference, we lay out the ROCK standard v1.0. We hope this allows developers to implement the ROCK in existing free and open software, stimulates the development of additional applications, and ultimately, democratizes methodological innovation in qualitative research.

articles.title: Numerical resolution can exceed measurement precision in psychometric score reporting
articles.authors: Takenari Fujio; Hiromi Fujio
articles.abstract: Scores are routinely reported at a numerical resolution finer than the precision supported by the underlying measurement process. We develop a framework linking this display–measurement mismatch to the psychometric conditions required to sustain fine distinctions and to a testable behavioural account of overadaptation to uncertain evaluation metrics. Using classical test theory and item response theory, we quantify the conditions under which distinctions at the 0.01-standard-deviation scale—equivalent to 0.1 points on the Japanese hensachi scale—could be measured rather than merely printed. Under classical test theory, reliability must approach unity: about 0.9999 for the standard error of measurement to equal 0.1 hensachi points, and about 0.999993 for the full 95% interval width to fall within 0.1 points. Idealized item-response calculations require thousands of highly informative, locally targeted items, while finite-bank simulations show that 0.01-SD precision, where attained at all, is strongly ability-dependent. These results distinguish numerical resolution from psychometric precision and motivate a preregistered behavioural programme, supported by formal operating characteristics, to test whether fine display resolution inflates perceived certainty and alters decisions. The framework provides a quantitative basis both for score reporting and for studying how people adapt to uncertain scores.

articles.title: Sport for Flourishing: Challenges, Considerations, and Calls to Action
articles.authors: Richard Alastair Cameron Simpson; Richard Cowden; Constantine Psimopoulos; Tim Lomas; Matthew J. Moore; Arabella Ashfield; Tyler J. VanderWeele; Todd Barrett Kashdan; Patrick McKnight
articles.abstract: Sport has often been recognized as a microcosm of broader society. Such acknowledgement demonstrates the potential of sport to shape, and be shaped by, individuals and communities. Indeed, across its many socioecological contexts (e.g., youth, recreational, developmental, educational, organizational, elite), scholars and practitioners from a range of disciplines have shared ways in which sport can contribute to, or undermine, health and well-being. To bridge the chasm between knowledge within sport (e.g., sport psychology, sociology, philosophy) and broader flourishing scholarship, we present a dual conceptual model of sport and flourishing to help align collective efforts and to centralize attention for researchers, practitioners, decision-makers, and sport professionals. First, we discuss the empirical and conceptual challenges that are apparent within sport and why this has limited progress concerning its relations to human flourishing. We also discuss broader contentions about flourishing and how sport could help address these challenges. Second, we discuss the elements of the model pertaining to flourishing within sport (e.g., sport as a sphere for flourishing: comprising embeddedness, purview and scope of well-being, quality of the sport environment) and pertaining to sport for flourishing (e.g., sport as a conduit for flourishing: promoting individual flourishing, communal and relational flourishing, and flourishing of humanity). Third, we conclude with various implications and ‘calls to action’ for methodological (e.g., qualitative and quantitative work), applied (e.g., developing guidelines and interventions for promoting flourishing in sport), and research (e.g., Global Flourishing in Sport Study) advancement to realize a more unified sport and flourishing community.

articles.title: Cracking the Code: Grant Writing for Health Psychology Scholars
articles.authors: Tugce Varol; Thomas Gültzow; Sanne Raghoebar; Kristina Pfeffer; Patrick Stefan Höhener; Rory Coyne; James A Green; Katie Newby; Benjamin Schüz; Eline Suzanne Smit
articles.abstract: Research grants form a cornerstone for enabling research, providing researchers with the funding and support necessary to perform research, purchase tools, and form teams. Most post-PhD early- and mid-career scholars will be required to develop research grant writing as a core professional competency, and will be — at least partly — evaluated on their ability to successfully obtain research funding by employers and academic promotion committees. Drawing on insights from an EHPS EMPOWER 2025 pre-conference workshop and a subsequent webinar on the topic, this piece serves as a practical guide designed to help health psychology scholars navigate the funding landscape and write highly competitive research proposals, covering key areas such as idea generation, aligning ideas with funding opportunities and grant writing.

articles.title: Best practices for crosslinguistic masked priming: A tutorial using jsPsych
articles.authors: Kelly Kendro
articles.abstract: The masked priming paradigm (Forster & Davis, 1984) investigates whether a target item can be cued via a prime that is shown quickly to mitigate conscious awareness during processing. In the decades since the task’s inception, researchers have used this task to probe both automatic lexical retrieval processes as well as how task parameter manipulation affects priming patterns. This paper serves a dual role. First, it functions as a tutorial for implementing a masked priming task using jsPsych (De Leeuw et al., 2023), a free and open source framework for creating web-based behavioral tasks. Second, it synthesizes information from prior research about several task parameters: masking techniques, task type, outcome variables, prime–mask language directionality, stimulus-onset asynchrony, inter-stimulus intervals, prime duration, prime type, presentation duration, and visibility tests. Materials for implementing a masked priming task, including an editable .js template for use with jsPsych 8, are included in an external repository. The tutorial also demonstrates how researchers can compare expected and observed prime duration and incorporate a visibility measure to provide an additional evaluation of prime awareness. Ultimately, the goal of this paper is to help researchers make empirically informed decisions about masked priming task design and implement this task using the jsPsych ecosystem.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Learners’ beliefs about teachers’ social characteristics influence their pronunciation preferences: A replication and extension of Hayes-Harb, Barrios & Tripp (2022)
articles.authors: Shannon Barrios; Rachel Hayes-Harb
articles.abstract: Learners’ beliefs about language and language users impact the inferences they make about linguistic structure as well as their learning outcomes (Ballard & Winke 2017; Falkert 2016; Hayes-Harb, Barrios & Tripp 2022). Hayes-Harb et al. (2022) demonstrated that participants preferred speech samples exhibiting a pronunciation pattern that was associated with a “teacher” over that of a “student” in a simulated language classroom context, indicating that language learners differentially weight their input based on characteristics of the speaker. We first replicated this study with a new pronunciation pattern (Experiment 1), and then extended the work by investigating whether preferences for the teacher’s pronunciation can be modulated by attributing “favorable” versus “unfavorable” social characteristics to the teacher regarding their teaching experience, teaching effectiveness, and linguistic background (Experiment 2). We found that participants still tended to prefer the teacher’s pronunciation, but that the degree of preference was reduced when the teacher had been characterized unfavorably. We thus provide evidence that preferences for speech input from teachers are modulated by beliefs about the social characteristics of the teacher, presenting a challenge for asocial models of pronunciation learning and contributing to our understanding of linguistic stereotyping and its impact on language teaching and learning.

articles.title: Failure Feedback: Vehicle for the Transmission of Stereotypes About Intellectual Ability
articles.authors: Grace Huang Murphy; Uliana Solovieva; Lin Bian
articles.abstract: Stereotypes linking intellectual ability to particular social groups (e.g., boys) emerge early in childhood, constraining the aspirations of certain groups such as girls. Yet little is known about how children acquire these stereotypes. The present research investigated whether parental responses to children’s failure serve as a pathway through which stereotypes about intellectual ability are communicated. In Experiment 1 (N = 312; 54% women), parents responded to a child, identified as either a boy or a girl, who repeatedly failed a challenging intellectual task. Parents most frequently provided two types of feedback: persistence (which encouraged continued effort) and redirection (which suggested pursuing alternative activities). Following the initial failure, parents were more likely to encourage persistence for the boy but to redirect the girl. Across repeated failures, parents also continued to provide more redirection to the girl than to the boy. In Experiments 2 and 3 (N = 96 and 124 children, respectively), 5- to 10-year-old children watched videos in which unfamiliar individuals or members of novel groups received either persistence or redirection feedback after failure. Across both experiments, children inferred that recipients of redirection feedback were less smart than recipients of persistence feedback. Moreover, children extended these inferences to groups, suggesting that differential failure feedback could contribute to the acquisition of group-based intelligence stereotypes. Together, these findings highlight failure as an important socialization context in which behavioral guidance can carry implicit evaluations of intellectual ability, providing a potential pathway through which intelligence stereotypes are transmitted.

articles.title: Does Person-First Language Reduce Stigma? Evidence Across Health Condition Labels From Two Experimental Studies
articles.authors: Elizabeth Kruse; Paige Amormino; David Dodell-Feder
articles.abstract: The stigmatization of mental health conditions remains a widespread problem. One proposed intervention involves reforming the language used to describe people with mental health conditions by using terminology that separates the individual from the label (i.e., person-first language) rather than language that defines the individual by the label (i.e., identity-first or identity-only language). Across two studies, we tested whether manipulating the language used to describe an individual alters multiple dimensions of stigma, including attitudinal stigma, trait-based stereotype judgments, and dehumanization, across a broad and intentionally heterogeneous set of labels spanning mental health and related conditions. In Study 1, language framing did not consistently influence attitudinal stigma across labels, with the exception of responses to psychopathy. In Study 2, language framing did not significantly influence perceived stereotype judgments or dehumanization for any label examined. Instead, the specific label used and, to a lesser extent, personal familiarity with mental health conditions showed the most consistent associations with stigma across both studies. These findings suggest that individual labels are embedded in distinct social schemas that shape perceptions independent of language framing, and that social or personal contact may be a more reliable pathway to reducing stigma than terminology reform.

articles.title: Auswirkungen von Künstlicher Intelligenz auf psychische Belastung in der Arbeitswelt – ein Überblick
articles.authors: Markus Langer; Annette Kluge
articles.abstract:
Der vorliegende Beitrag arbeitet den Forschungsstand zu den Auswirkungen des KI-Einsatzes auf psychische Belastungen und Ressourcen am Arbeitsplatz auf. Ein Leitgedanke ist die Ambivalenz: KI-Systeme können auf nahezu jeder Dimension gleichzeitig als Ressource und als Belastung wirken – als Produktivitätsgewinn und Überforderung, als Autonomiezuwachs und Kontrollverlust, als Kompetenzerweiterung und Dequalifizierung. Ob im Einzelfall das eine oder das andere überwiegt, hängt maßgeblich davon ab, wie ein KI-System gestaltet ist und genutzt wird und wie es in Arbeitsprozesse eingebettet und organisational begleitet wird.
Im Beitrag bestimmen wir den Neuheitswert aktueller KI-Systeme. Vieles ist eine quantitative Fortschreibung bekannter Automatisierungstechnologien; qualitativ neu sind jedoch Eigenschaften wie die eigenständige Generierung von Inhalten, die Einsetzbarkeit als Allzweck-Werkzeug, nahezu autonome Aufgabenbearbeitung, probabilistisches und lernendes Verhalten, menschenähnliche Interaktion, engmaschige Entscheidungen über Menschen, schnelle Update-Zyklen sowie die verbreitete informelle Nutzung. Für jede dieser Eigenschaften lassen sich konkrete Chancen und Risiken für die psychische Gesundheit ableiten.
Die empirische Synopse (Stand Frühjahr 2026) ordnet die Befunde in einer soziotechnischen Kontext ein: Einflussfaktoren auf organisationaler, arbeits- und technologiegestalterischer sowie personenbezogener Ebene wirken – vermittelt über Moderatoren und Mediatoren auf verschiedene Ergebnisgrößen. Als belastungskritisch erweisen sich beispielsweise unrealistische Erwartungen und fehlendes Change Management, algorithmisches Management mit Autonomie- und Kontrollverlust, Arbeitsverdichtung statt Entlastung, der Verlust sozialer Einbindung sowie Sorgen um Arbeitsplatz und berufliche Identität. Als Gelingensbedingungen werden beispielsweise KI-Kompetenzen und ausreichende Zeit- und Trainingsressourcen beschrieben.
Daraus leiten wir Handlungsempfehlungen auf drei Ebenen ab. Organisational sollte beispielsweise die KI-Einführung konsequent als menschzentrierter Veränderungsprozess verstanden werden;. Auf der Arbeits- und Technologiegestaltungsebene sind Autonomie und Kontrolle zu sichern, Arbeitsverdichtung zu überwachen, Tätigkeitszuschnitte im Sinne der SMART-Kriterien zu prüfen und Technologien so zu gestalten, dass menschliche Aufsicht gelingt. Auf Personenebene rücken KI- und metakognitive Kompetenzen, der Erhalt arbeitsfachlicher Fertigkeiten sowie die neue Kernaufgabe der effektiven menschlichen Aufsicht von KI-Systemen in den Vordergrund.
Dieser Beitrag zeigt, dass eine menschzentrierte, soziotechnisch gedachte Gestaltung und Einführung von KI-Systemen den technischen Fortschritt nicht ausbremst, sondern Arbeit reichhaltiger, gesünder und nachhaltiger macht – und ist die entscheidende Stellschraube dafür, dass KI zur Ressource statt zur Belastung wird.

articles.title: Media Selectivity Research in Light of Self-Defeating Tendencies: Towards a Novel Understanding of Media Effects on Well-Being
articles.authors: Nicole Bizzotto; Tobias Dienlin; Silvia Knobloch-Westerwick
articles.abstract: A critical gap persists in media uses and effects research: while existing work has predominantly focused on self-serving motivations for media selection, an expanding body of evidence suggests that individuals—including those with psychological vulnerabilities—may seek out online content that aggravates, rather than alleviates, distress. Drawing on scholarship on self-defeating tendencies in offline contexts, we argue that the same process may unfold in mediated environments, especially on social media: when negative self-concepts are salient, users may gravitate toward content that validates these self-views, even at the expense of their well-being. We focus on mental health content as an illustrative case in which these dynamics become particularly visible and harmful, while arguing that similar processes apply to other domains. To guide this line of inquiry and offer a more comprehensive account of media selection processes and their implications for well-being, we extend the established Selective Exposure Self- and Affect-Management (SESAM) model by incorporating self-defeating motivations and outline a research agenda.

articles.title: Dyadic Social Dynamics in Separation-Related Anxiety: Multimodal Arousal Synchrony Between 4-Year-Olds and Their Mothers
articles.authors: Leonard Konstantin Kulisch; Laurin Plank; Anna Exner; Silvia Schneider; Sabine Seehagen; Armin Zlomuzica; Babett Voigt
articles.abstract: Separation anxiety disorder (SAD) is an early-onset disorder linked to adverse outcomes into adulthood. To advance SAD etiology, this study examined how parental risk factors relate to dyadic social dynamics. Seventy-two four-year-olds (50% girls, 93% primarily German-speaking) and their mothers (74% holding a Bachelor’s degree) participated in a standardized separation paradigm. Parental reports, heart rate, and machine-learning-based measures of facial and vocal arousal were assessed. The announcement of separation increased children’s physiological (ꞵ=.17) and vocal arousal (ꞵ=.13). Within individuals, physiological and vocal arousal were coordinated (r=.18–.20), while across dyads, facial (r=.15) and vocal arousal (r=.09) showed consistent synchrony. Physiological synchrony emerged selectively in dyads with higher maternal anxiety (r=.31) but was unrelated to absolute arousal or SAD symptoms. Anticipatory physiological synchrony was negatively associated with child vocal arousal during separation (r=-.44). Early separation-related anxiety appears embedded in dyadic processes, shaped by vocal arousal transmission and maternal anxiety symptoms.

articles.title: Attitudinal, Experiential, and Trait-based Correlates of Inceldom
articles.authors: Robyn Mooney; Millie Hargreaves; Brandon Sparks
articles.abstract: To prevent radicalisation into the involuntary celibate (‘incel’) community, it is critical to understand individual differences underlying inceldom. This exploratory research aimed to examine relationships between inceldom and attitudinal and trait-based risk factors for extremism. Study 1 explored relationships between misogyny, right-wing authoritarianism (RWA), social dominance orientation (SDO), and incel ideology endorsement in a male community sample (n = 65). Using another male community sample (n = 282), Study 2 examined associations between autistic traits (social-sensory sensitivity and monotropic processing), childhood traumatic experiences (CTEs), misogyny, and incel traits. Results showed that in Study 1, misogyny and RWA positively predicted incel ideology endorsement, while SDO was negatively predictive. In Study 2, CTEs and both aspects of autistic traits were positively associated with incel traits, and these associations were mediated by higher levels of misogyny. Self-identified incels also scored higher than non-incels on incel traits, misogyny, CTEs, and social-sensory sensitivity, but they did not differ on monotropic processing. The findings from these studies can help inform effective, tailored prevention programs and deradicalisation support systems for those wishing to leave the incel community.

articles.title: Linguistic Affiliation and the Structure of Cultural Values: Evidence from the World Values Survey
articles.authors: Meriem Boukhris; Farah Benzarti; Peter Wad Sackett; Montassar Ben Messaoud; Gabriel Renaud
articles.abstract: The values of a society are determined by a plethora of factors, including history, geography and culture. A resource to monitor such values is the World Values Survey, a survey about the predispositions of individuals across 66 societies from various geographic regions. While some analyses have been conducted on this dataset, several questions dealing with circumstances rather than values were not filtered out e.g. ”I feel unsafe at night” and the types of analyses conducted were limited. We removed such situational questions and kept the 199 questions related solely to values, and submitted the resulting data to several supervised and unsupervised numerical analyses. We find that linguistic affiliation provides a strong organizing dimension of cultural-value similarity. We observe a split primarily along morality and religion, accounting for 23.9% of the variance, and in second place along confidence in institutions, accounting for a further 13.5%. We analyzed bilingual countries like Kazakhstan and Canada. We find that English-speaking Canadians are closer to other English-speaking countries than they are to French-speaking Canadians. While the USA initially appeared as an outlier within the English-speaking world, stratifying respondents by Democratic and Republican affiliation revealed deep internal divisions. Strikingly, Americans identifying as Democrats were closer, in terms of values, to other English-speaking nations, especially English-speaking Canadians, than they were to US Republicans.

articles.title: KUAI-Kids: Developing a Measurement Instrument for Children’s Knowledge, Use, and Attitudes Toward Generative AI Chatbots
articles.authors: Sarah Malone; Carmen Koehler; Kristin Altmeyer; Dominik Thüs; Marina Dombrovskaia; Johannes Hartig
articles.abstract: The increasing presence of generative artificial intelligence in children’s lives highlights the need for age-appropriate measurement instruments to assess their knowledge, use, and atti-tudes toward these technologies. This study introduces and validates KUAI-Kids, a question-naire on ChatGPT knowledge, use, and attitudes for children in middle childhood and early adolescence (ages 7 to 14; N = 310), based on a previously validated adult scale but with sub-stantially revised and extended items for children. Confirmatory factor analyses supported uni-dimensional structures for the Knowledge and Use scales, both showing good model fit and internal consistency. For the Attitude scale, the originally assumed unidimensional structure was not supported. Instead, factor analyses identified two distinct dimensions, Enthusiastic and Cautious Attitudes toward ChatGPT. Both Attitude subscales demonstrated good model fit and reliability. Latent correlations revealed expected associations: Knowledge and Use were mod-erately positively correlated; Enthusiastic Attitudes were strongly associated with Use, while a moderately strong correlation was observed between Cautious Attitudes and Knowledge. Ex-ploratory analyses indicated higher Enthusiastic Attitudes in boys and higher Knowledge, Use, and Cautious Attitudes scores in older students. The KUAI-Kids offers a psychometrically sound tool to study children’s engagement with AI chatbots and to support AI literacy assess-ment, the evaluation of educational interventions, and evidence-based development of AI-related educational policies. Limitations include the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI technologies and the fact that many children in the sample had little or no direct experience with ChatGPT.

articles.title: How Childhood Adversity Alters Social Information Processing and its Effect on Social Functioning: A Systematic Review
articles.authors: Hannah Dorsman; Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Antoinette Haverhals; Pauline Wessels; Peter Bos; Eamon McCrory; Anne-Laura Van Harmelen
articles.abstract:
Background: Childhood adversity (CA) affects millions of children worldwide and may change how children perceive and respond to social cues in ways that are adaptive in adverse environments but maladaptive later in life. These maladaptive effects may be particularly pronounced during adolescence, a sensitive period of social reorientation and neurodevelopment. This pre-registered systematic review examined whether CA shapes the way young people process social information, and whether these changes are linked to difficulties in social functioning during adolescence.
Methods: We searched Web of Science, PsycINFO, and PubMed for studies assessing CA before age 18, social information processing across five domains, and social functioning in youth aged 10-24.
Results: Although 6657 studies were identified, only 11 met inclusion criteria. These examined threat-related processing (n=5), emotional reactivity and regulation (n=5), and reward processing and learning (n=3). CA was associated with alterations in social information processing across most domains. If associations between social information processing and social functioning were directly tested, they were generally supported. Evidence spanned different stages of adolescence, but associations with social functioning were tested almost exclusively in early-to-mid adolescent samples.
Conclusions: We find preliminary support for a model where CA is associated with alterations in social information processing which then leads to poorer social functioning. These findings were based mostly on longitudinal samples in early-to-mid adolescent samples, however, prospective examinations of this model were rare. These findings suggest that interventions targeting social information processing may be a promising avenue for supporting adolescents with experiences of CA.

articles.title: Socialization in the Spotlight: Early Parent-Infant Synchrony, Mind-Mindedness, and Children’s Later Expressions of Shyness
articles.authors: Christopher Riddell; Milica Nikolic; Agneta Fischer; Itir Onal Ertugrul; Moniek Zeegers; Susan Bögels; Cristina Colonnesi
articles.abstract: Owing to their burgeoning understanding of the social world, the early childhood years represent a critical developmental period in which children's first expressions of shyness take shape. Nonverbal expressions of shyness have been argued to take two forms: positive shyness, characterized by smiling with a gaze and/or head aversion, and negative shyness, characterized by negative affect with a gaze and/or head aversion. Although early parental socialization practices are known to shape children’s emotions, few studies have examined how these influence shyness expressions beyond infancy. In a sample of 120 Dutch children and their parents, we examined two potential socialization mechanisms of preschool children’s expressions of shyness: positive affective synchrony (measured at 4-months) and mind-mindedness (measured at 12- and 30-months). We assessed these facets separately with both mothers and fathers during free-play tasks, and children’s expressions shyness during a public performance. Mothers’, but not fathers’, positive affective synchrony was associated with lower levels of negative shyness in childhood, consistent with a potentially protective role of early synchrony. Fathers' appropriate mind-mindedness, however, was unexpectedly associated with less positive and more negative shyness, while mothers' non-attuned mind-mindedness was associated with more positive shyness. Together, our results highlight the importance of early parent-child socialization practices in infancy for later expressions of shyness in childhood but suggest that these operate in context dependent ways.

articles.title: Dynamic coordination of speech and gesture in the brain
articles.authors: Jiachen Yao; Cecilia Husta; Linda Drijvers
articles.abstract: Face-to-face communication relies on the continuous integration of auditory signals, such as speech, and visual signals, such as co-speech gestures. Rather than serving as an add-on to spoken language, gestural information has been shown to actively shape how the brain constructs meaning. A central question is how the brain achieves integrating gestures with speech. This is not a trivial problem, as auditory and visual signals are often noisy, temporally misaligned, variable in length, and ambiguous, yet interlocutors still seem to understand each other effortlessly. This chapter will review evidence from neuroimaging (e.g., fMRI, MEG, (dual-)EEG, fNIRS) and brain stimulation (e.g., TMS, tDCS, tACS) methods, both from a within- and a between-brain perspective. Together, these methods have begun to outline a distributed and flexible brain network that supports the integration of speech and gestures. We will discuss how these brain networks coordinate the integration of speech and gestures, and how speech-gesture integration unfolds over time, in both clear and adverse listening conditions.

articles.title: Humans learn to distinguish imagination from reality with age
articles.authors: Andre Sahakian; Stefan van der Stigchel; Nadine Dijkstra; Surya Gayet; Christoph Strauch
articles.abstract: Telling apart what is the product of one's imagination and what is a true sensory experience (i.e., reality monitoring) might feel trivial to most. Yet it remains unclear whether reality monitoring is an innate ability (like breathing, or aversion to pain) or whether it is a learned skill (like speaking, or walking). Here we extend the age range of participants tested by Dijkstra and Fleming (2023) with young children from the age of 5. In a close replication we tested how likely participants were to report actually seeing a faint left or right tilted grating in dynamic noise, depending on whether they were concurrently imagining the same or an orthogonal grating. We found clear evidence that confusion of imagery and perception steadily declined to none with age - independent of perceptual ability or (subjective) imagery vividness. We empirically show that the ability to tell apart imagination from reality develops over age. These findings provide new insights on how we learn to keep apart imagination from reality, which has important implications for the development of psychopathology.

articles.title: ChirPing: A Social Media Simulation Platform Developed for Scientific Research
articles.authors: Nadia Said; Lena Plötz; Nicole Antes
articles.abstract: Experimental research on behavior on social media platforms typically relies on two methodological approaches, each with advantages but also limitations. Experimental studies, while having the advantage of giving researchers full control over the content presented and allowing for direct assessment of other variables of interest, often lack ecological validity, as behavioral intentions are only weakly predictive of actual sharing behavior. Studies conducted directly on live platforms, by contrast, offer ecological validity. However, the lack of control over the experimental environment makes it difficult to draw causal inferences. To address those issues, social media simulation platforms have gained increasing popularity in research. However, these platforms vary widely in usability and flexibility: some require more advanced programming skills, while others are fairly easy to use but may be limited in their use cases. Here we present our social media simulation platform, ChirPing, a new tool embedded within the widely used experimental research platform SoSci Survey. The main advantage of our platform is that it is part of an established platform; thus, researchers can easily integrate it into their surveys and adjust it within a familiar tool environment. Furthermore, our platform is highly customizable, allowing researchers to systematically manipulate experimental parameters (e.g., content presentation and post order). Allowing researchers to examine, for example, causal effects on behavioral outcomes such as sharing, engagement, and decision-making.

articles.title: Dyadic JITAIs in Health Behavior Change: Key Components and Design Principles
articles.authors: Inbal Nahum-Shani; Lex Hurley; Ziping Xu; Carolyn Yoon; Jean-Philippe Laurenceau; Susan A Murphy
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The widespread adoption of digital technologies offers unprecedented opportunities for delivering accessible and affordable health behavior interventions. Advances in mobile and wireless technologies have the capacity to collect rich and granular data about people’s states and contexts and utilize this information to intervene in (near) real-time in everyday life.
