science as perceived benefits. Based on these insights, we propose recommendations for
researchers, editors, and funders to streamline RR workflows, ensure sustainable incentives,
and expand capacity building beyond Western contexts. Overall, the OSR initiative
demonstrates that modest, well-structured incentives can meaningfully foster transparent,
rigorous, and reproducible research practices within underrepresented subfields of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Hunger and Concentration in Daily Life: Inter-Individual Differences and Eating-Related Variation but No Robust Average Association
articles_hidden.authors: Christoph Bamberg; Julia Reichenberger; Jens Blechert
articles_hidden.abstract: Momentary reductions in concentration may affect daily functioning. In addition to external distractors, bodily signals might divert attention from ongoing tasks. Hunger might not only signal short dips in energy supply but also trigger distracting interoceptive sensations. We focus on hunger as a frequent sensation that is regularly regulated through food intake and therefore may display a complex relation to concentration. To test the relation between hunger and concentration, 64 participants in an experience sampling study reported their momentary concentration, hunger, and food intake six times daily for four weeks. Using Bayesian multilevel within between models, we assessed the hunger concentration association and, in exploratory analyses, whether this relation differed depending on prior food intake. We found no robust average hunger concentration association, with a Bayes Factor supporting the absence of a systematic population level within participant association. At the same time, the association varied considerably between individuals. Prior food intake did not clearly change the association overall. In exploratory meal-specific-analyses, more negative hunger concentration associations were estimated after breakfast and lunch compared with assessments without the respective meal. Thus, the momentary hunger concentration relation in daily life was characterised by considerable inter-individual differences and possible dependence on specific meal contexts. These findings suggest that everyday concentration may be shaped less by hunger per se than by individual differences and the context in which hunger occurs.

articles_hidden.title: Benchmarks for Associative Learning Models
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik R Bach; Ralph R. Miller; Jose E. Callejas-Aguilera; Hilary Don; Kurt Fraser; Mihaela Iordonova; Jessica C. Lee; Josie Linnell; Huaiyu Liu; Evan James Livesey
articles_hidden.abstract: Associative learning, like many mature fields of behavioural science, is endowed with a nearly unfathomable wealth of empirical data. These arise from multiple experimental procedures and animal species. To assess any proposed theory of associative learning, decisions must be made about which behavioral phenomena to account for. However, there is currently no systematic approach to selecting observations within this body of evidence. Here, we propose benchmarks for theories of associative learning by organizing phenomena according to their robustness across experiments, their generality across procedural variations, domains, and species, and the degree to which they occur under broad but clearly specified circumstances. We queried the expert community for phenomena to be included, reviewed the relevant literature, classified the phenomena into four categories of robustness and generality, and compared our classification with a second survey of the expert community. We identified 92 benchmark phenomena, of which 21 are domain- and species-general, and 24 are species- and/or domain-specific but highly robust across procedures. Strikingly, some textbook phenomena that have motivated influential and general associative learning theories are not among these. The remaining 47 phenomena were either constrained to particular experimental procedures or of inconclusive generality. Some of their implementational boundary conditions appear to be informally known but were rarely investigated systematically. In summary, our review provides a comprehensive evaluation of the current evidence, which will support theory building while also re-focusing research into areas in which evidence is lacking.

articles_hidden.title: Misplaced Evidence? A Reflexive Thematic Analysis of Clinicians’ Reflections on the Connection Between Psychotherapy Research and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Renate Schwarzbach; Merle-Marie Pittelkow; Lisa Kiltz; Sarah Tol; Rink Hoekstra; Theo Bouman; Marieke Pijnenborg
articles_hidden.abstract: The gap between research and clinical practice, known as the scientist-practitioner gap, poses a persistent challenge in clinical psychology. Although existing research suggests that effective engagement with research can be challenging for clinicians, there is limited understanding of the specific barriers, obstacles, and potential solutions as perceived by clinicians themselves. In this focus group study, we explored junior clinicians' perceptions, attitudes, and interactions with clinical research, specifically targeting Dutch mental health psychologists following postgraduate training (n = 32). Through reflexive thematic analysis, we investigated their relation to research in clinical psychology, their perceived value of research, barriers to engagement, and suggestions for the future. Clinicians reported multiple barriers including difficulties in accessing, understanding, and applying research in practice, as well as skepticism about its relevance. We summarize clinicians’ personal opinions and motivations regarding research, systemic issues such as insufficient organizational support, research priorities not matching demands in practice, and methodological limitations of conventional psychotherapy research. With this study, we stressed the need for enhanced communication between researchers and clinicians, methodological considerations, and greater inclusion of clinicians’ perspectives in research processes.

articles_hidden.title: An eye-tracking study investigating the processing of numerical referential expressions when subset interpretations are unavailable
articles_hidden.authors: Ellen Spencer; Kevin Paterson; Ascension Pagan; Helen Breadmore
articles_hidden.abstract: A numerical referential expression can be interpreted either as a subset of an introduced set or as a new set of entities. Previous research shows that adult readers generally prefer subset interpretations. This study used eye-tracking to investigate how readers process numerical expressions when a preferred subset interpretation is unavailable (e.g., “Two dogs were playing in the garden. Three dogs were barking”). It also examined whether processing differed between bare cardinal (e.g., ‘three’) and noun-phrase (e.g., ‘three dogs’) expressions. The experiment included four conditions: subset interpretations available or unavailable, with either bare cardinal or noun-phrase expressions. Eye movements were analysed to compare reading behaviour across expression types and referential contexts. Results showed that when subset interpretations were unavailable, reading was disrupted more strongly for bare cardinal expressions, particularly in later processing measures. This disruption was absent for noun-phrase expressions, suggesting that nouns may support the establishment of new referents. Individual differences also influenced processing: higher reading motivation and more positive attitudes were associated with greater text engagement and reduced disruption during new-set interpretations, while greater vocabulary knowledge and mathematical competence were associated with more efficient early processing.

articles_hidden.title: Democratizing diffusion decision models: A comprehensive tutorial on developing, validating, and fitting diffusion decision models in Python with FlexDDM
articles_hidden.authors: Kyle J. LaFollette; Joy Fan; Alessandra Puccio; Heath A. Demaree
articles_hidden.abstract: Diffusion decision models let researchers explain both choices and response times as the product of a single evidence-accumulation process, but building custom, time-varying versions of these models remains difficult for most behavioral scientists. Manipulations that unfold within a decision, such as an early automatic impulse in a conflict task or a boundary that collapses under time pressure, often call for process components that change over the course of a trial. These components rarely have a closed-form likelihood and usually require programming skills that many researchers and students lack. We introduce FlexDDM, a graphical, point-and-click software environment for building custom diffusion decision models without requiring users to work primarily in a programming language. FlexDDM organizes the modeling process into five linked modules that mirror an analysis workflow. Users map and filter their data, formalize process functions for model parameters, simulate synthetic data from specified parameter distributions, validate a model through parameter recovery, model recovery, split-half reliability, likelihood profiles, and curvature diagnostics, and fit empirical data using Fokker-Planck or simulation-based backends. Locked templates for the fixed-time DDM and time-varying alternatives give users editable starting points while keeping only the psychologically meaningful code visible. FlexDDM can serve both research applications and classroom instruction, via this tutorial and an included in-software walkthrough where students can manipulate sliders to observe how parameter changes reshape predicted behavior. By lowering the programming and providing a user-friendly graphical interface, FlexDDM aims to make process-level explanations of choice and response time accessible to a wider range of behavioral scientists.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of the Youth Mental Health Quotient (Youth MHQ): A Comprehensive Assessment of Mental Health & Wellbeing in 12–17 Year Olds
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Newson; Oleksii Sukhoi; Tara Thiagarajan
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: The Mental Health Quotient (MHQ) is a 47-item, transdiagnostic, web-based self-report assessment of mental health wellbeing that has previously been validated in adult populations (Newson & Thiagarajan, 2020; Newson et al., 2022, 2024). The Youth MHQ adapts the same 47 items to an eighth-grade reading level for use with adolescents aged 12–17. Methods: We evaluated the psychometric properties of the Youth MHQ using 9,916 responses collected from 12- to 17-year-olds in the United States during 2025. Evidence of convergent and discriminant validity was assessed via item-pair correlations; sampling stability was assessed as the coefficient of variation (CV) of the overall MHQ score across ten randomly drawn subsamples of n = 500; and validity evidence based on relations to other variables was examined using (1) score-range mappings to DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for ten major psychiatric disorders and (2) a functional measure of the ability to attend school and complete schoolwork. Results: Item pairs expected to be conceptually related showed high correlations (e.g., Relationships with Others and Social Cooperation, r = 0.64; Self-Image and Self-worth & Confidence, r = 0.64), while conceptually unrelated items showed near-zero correlation (Susceptibility to Infection and Empathy, r = 0.06), supporting convergent and discriminant validity. Sampling stability of the overall score was reasonable (CV = 17%) but markedly lower than that previously reported for the adult MHQ (CV = 4.6%). MHQ scores were systematically related to both DSM-based clinical criteria across the ten disorders and to the functional measure of school participation. Conclusions: The Youth MHQ demonstrates good convergent and discriminant validity and meaningful validity evidence based on relations to other variables in a large US adolescent sample, supporting its use as a comprehensive transdiagnostic assessment of mental health and wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: Supervision, Category Structure, and Selective Attention in Category Learning: A Comparative Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Hyungwook Yim; Leyre Castro; Jay I. Myung; Edward A. Wasserman; Vladimir Sloutsky
articles_hidden.abstract: We investigated the interactions between supervision, category structure, and selective attention in category learning. We compared human adults and pigeons in a category learning task, where we manipulated the category structure (dense vs. sparse) and the level of supervision by corrective feedback (low vs. high). Results showed a benefit of supervision across species, which was particularly strong in learning the sparse categories. Moreover, both species benefitted from category structures that had multiple category-relevant dimensions (i.e., dense categories). In addition, human adults, who have a more advanced ability to attend selectively, showed faster learning and better generalization overall. Finally, attention was optimized to the category-relevant dimension in the sparse category only in human adults. Subsequent computational simulation of the data indicated that these patterns were well explained by a parameter that controls the ability to flexibly switch attention to category-relevant dimensions.

articles_hidden.title: Predictive Priority Shapes Human Statistical Learning in Multi-Regularity Environments
articles_hidden.authors: Shelley Xiuli Tong; Mei Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning enables prediction by extracting temporal dependencies and guiding attention based on spatial probabilities. Yet natural environments often contain multiple regularities at once, raising the question of how the cognitive system integrates or prioritizes competing sources of structure. Across five experiments using an integrated color-location visual search task (N = 245), we examined how participants learned concurrent color-color transitions and color-location distributions. The results showed that statistical learning is not a passive combination of all available regularities, but a prioritization process. Temporal conditional statistics generally dominated spatial distributional statistics, although learning was stronger when both regularities supported the same underlying structure. In contrast, single regularities were acquired only when they did not compete with more complex multi-regularity inputs. These findings suggest that statistical learning is adaptive and selective, prioritizing information that best supports behaviors in complex environments.

articles_hidden.title: Do Youth Offending Labels Matter? The Impact of the Label “Young Serious Offender” on Public Attitudes Toward Youth Justice
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Yesberg; Clare-Ann Fortune; Hasi Kolongahapitiya
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on the impact of crime-first labels on public attitudes has focused almost exclusively on sexual offending. This pre-registered conceptual replication of Harris and Socia (2016) examined the effect of the label 'young serious offender' on support for punitive youth justice policies and beliefs about rehabilitation. Using an experimental design, 393 adult residents of New Zealand and Australia were randomly allocated to receive statements using either 'young serious offender' or the person-first alternative 'young people who have committed serious offences'. Contrary to our hypotheses, we found no evidence the label influenced attitudes relative to the person-first alternative, and no consistent moderation effects were observed. Exploratory analyses identified political orientation, ethnicity, and educational attainment as significant predictors of both punitive attitudes and belief in rehabilitation. These findings suggest crime-first labelling effects may only appear where strong stigma and well-established stereotypes already exist (e.g., sexual offending). However, this null result reflects only a single, one-off exposure in a survey context. The introduction of the Young Serious Offender designation in New Zealand embeds crime-first language into policy, with potentially cumulative effects that a one-off exposure cannot capture. Future research should use longitudinal designs to examine repeated exposure to labels over time.

articles_hidden.title: Mindfulness-Based Instruction Does Not Improve Real-Time fMRI Neurofeedback Efficiency in Problematic Alcohol Use
articles_hidden.authors: Jingying Zhang; Falk Kiefer; Peter Kirsch; Martin Fungisai Gerchen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rt-fMRI NF) targeting ventral striatal (VS) cue reactivity has been proposed as a tool to support volitional self-regulation in individuals with problematic alcohol use, but training effects remain inconsistent. Regulation strategy is one potentially important but underexamined factor that may influence NF success. This pre-registered randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study investigated whether mindfulness-based instructions could enhance rt-fMRI NF regulation of VS cue reactivity.
Methods: Ninety individuals with problematic alcohol use (AUDIT score > 8) were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) VS NF with mindfulness-based instructions, (2) VS NF with neutral instructions, or (3) sham NF (primary auditory cortex) with neutral instructions. Participants completed two training sessions within one week. VS activation during alcohol cue exposure, craving, and associations with trait mindfulness and drinking refusal self-efficacy were assessed.
Results: No significant group differences or run-by-group interactions were observed in VS activation across NF runs. Craving ratings did not significantly change over the intervention period and did not differ between groups. VS regulation success was not significantly associated with trait mindfulness or drinking refusal self-efficacy.
Conclusions: The present study found no evidence that rt-fMRI NF reduces alcohol cue-related VS activity or craving, even when combined with mindfulness-based instructions. These findings converge with a parallel RCT targeting VS cue reactivity in AUD patients (Halli et al., 2026), and further suggest that downregulating VS cue reactivity via rt-fMRI NF is particularly challenging.

articles_hidden.title: The Psychology of AI and God
articles_hidden.authors: Miranda Stiehl; Danica Dillion; Adam Waytz; Kurt Gray
articles_hidden.abstract: Silicon is becoming sacred. Chatbots interpret scripture and channel the divine, and people treat AI like a religious advisor, seeking out counsel and moral advice. This brief guide explores how people make sense of the intelligence and sacredness of AI and God—and predicts what might happen when technology and God touch within our minds. We briefly explore concepts of mind perception and sacredness before empirically mapping various entities along the dimensions of Mind (intelligence) and Sacredness: God, AI, average human, priest, philosopher, crow, carrot, and robot. While God is seen as maximally intelligent and sacred, AI is seen as moderately intelligent and minimally sacred. However, current events show that AI is becoming more intertwined with the sacred, and we outline four futures for AI’s relationship with God: Messenger, Killer, Rival, and Spirit. We close with future directions and what sacred silicon might mean for how we perceive ourselves.

articles_hidden.title: Language-Based Affect Assessments Capture Experiment-Induced Changes Beyond Rating Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Oskar Bång; Zhuojun Gu; August Nilsson; Veerle Celine Eijsbroek; Clara Wiebel; Adithya V Ganesan; Katarina Kjell; H. Andrew Schwartz; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell
articles_hidden.abstract: Language-based assessments (LBAs) have shown strong convergent and criterion validity cross-sectionally and longitudinally. However, no study has tested the ability of LBAs of affect to capture experiment-induced changes (i.e., causal validity). In this randomised mixed-design experiment, participants (N=892) completed a Mood Induction Procedure comprising different conditions (church, shopping mall, and park) using physical locations (N=153) and online video clips (N=739). Participants reported their pre- and post-induction affect through open-ended responses and ratings (i.e., the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule; PANAS). Using large language models and machine learning, we compared how accurately PANAS and language responses classified the experimental conditions. The LBA derived from the language responses exhibited significantly higher accuracy compared to the PANAS scores in classifying the conditions in both the training set (cross-validated AUC=.74 vs. .63), the online holdout set (AUC = .76 vs. .70), and the offline holdout set (AUC = .67 vs. .53). Apart from showing higher predictive accuracy, we assessed LBAs of specific affective dimensions (valence, arousal, and basic emotions). These analyses revealed that positive valence was most strongly expressed in the park condition, while anger was particularly elevated in the mall condition. Further, we visualized the language differences across conditions, showing more calm and peaceful expressions in the park condition and more tired and bored expressions in the mall condition. These findings support the causal validity of language-based affect assessments and its ability to provide insights into affective states. We discuss the potential of using LBA in experimental psychological research.

articles_hidden.title: All mental disorders as personality disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Orestis Zavlis
articles_hidden.abstract: In this piece, I make the case that all mental disorders can be understood as personality disorders. To do so, I begin with a minimal definition of “personality” and then show how it leads to the paradoxical, yet also logical, conclusion that all mental disorders are equally “personality disordered”.  I then close by suggesting that clinical researchers should study all mental disorders as personality disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Does global slowing explain age effects in inhibitory control?
articles_hidden.authors: Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; John Jonides; Taraz Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: A long-standing debate in the study of cognitive aging concerns whether aging results in a selective deficit in inhibitory control beyond a general slowing of cognitive processing. Previous studies have obtained mixed findings, in part because the typical free response time paradigm lacks the specificity required to disentangle component processes underlying inhibitory control. Here, we apply a novel forced-response paradigm and a computational model to disentangle these processes to test if aging results in overall speed differences or a selective deficit in inhibitory control. 50 older adults and 57 younger adults completed a “forced-response” arrow flanker task. We find strong evidence that older adults demonstrate a global slowing of processing, without any selective deficit in inhibitory control. Furthermore, we demonstrate global slowing is sufficient to explain the mixed findings in previous free RT studies. Overall, these results highlight the utility of using a theory-informed, fine-grained approach to study inhibitory control.

articles_hidden.title: Relaxed SEM-Based Out-of-Sample Predictions
articles_hidden.authors: Aditi M. Bhangale; Julian David Karch; M.J. de Rooij
articles_hidden.abstract:
Predictive modeling is growing more popular in psychological research. Until recently, prediction rules were limited primarily to traditional regression and machine learning approaches. Many of these approaches, however, fail to incorporate complex theories about the data (e.g., multiple manifest variables measure a single underlying construct) and thereby do not impose theory-driven restrictions on model parameters used for prediction. Structural equation models (SEMs) incorporate this information and combine measurement and regression to produce restricted covariance matrices for prediction. Recently, a SEM-based prediction rule for continuous data was proposed and was found to be robust against non-normality but sensitive to model misspecification. This sensitivity to model misspecification follows from the failure to model dependencies among variables, which can bias the estimated covariance matrix and produce inaccurate predictions. To address this, we propose a relaxed SEM-based prediction rule, which uses a data-driven compromise between the unrestricted sample and model-implied covariance matrices to produce predictions. We compared relaxed SEM to existing rules in a simulation study and found that it outperformed other SEM- and regression-based rules and performed comparably to elastic net for large training set sizes. In our empirical example, relaxed SEM improved upon SEM- and regression-based prediction, but did not outperform elastic net. 

Keywords. prediction, structural equation modeling, model misspecification, cross-validation, machine learning

articles_hidden.title: Eye Gaze Reveals How People Flexibly Combine Abstraction and Mental Simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Sosa; Aria Zhang; Samuel J. Gershman; Tomer David Ullman
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite the ubiquity and importance of intuitive physical reasoning, the computations underlying this commonsense ability are in dispute. Some researchers believe that people use a general-purpose mental simulation engine, while others think that people use specialized physical heuristics or abstractions. More recent proposals have suggested people switch between (or combine) these different cognitive strategies. Here, we show that these two modes of physical reasoning are associated with different patterns of eye movements. Participants were shown brief animations of an object in motion, and asked questions about the object's future location. During periods likely to involve mental simulation, people's gaze moved in small increments, in line with step-by-step unfolding of the object's path. During periods likely to involve abstraction, people's gaze moved in larger increments, as though jumping from the beginning to the end of a linear path. These results suggest that intuitive physics can flexibly combine mental simulation and abstraction in real time.

articles_hidden.title: The Development of a Multidomain Metacognition Experiment: a Pilot and Feasibility Study
articles_hidden.authors: Domenic Groh
articles_hidden.abstract:
Evidence for a common metacognitive ability across cognitive domains remains mixed. Previous cross-domain studies have often used similar first- and second-order response formats across tasks, making it difficult to separate common metacognitive variance from common method variance. In addition, a reanalysis of the tasks used by Mazancieux et al. showed comparatively high performance and little systematic difficulty modulation, limiting their usefulness for individual-differences research.
The present feasibility study therefore developed revised experimental tasks for a later multidomain investigation of metacognitive monitoring. Episodic memory, visual perception, and executive function were retained in modified form, while the culturally specific semantic-memory task was replaced by a mindfulness-based attentional monitoring task. First-order response formats and metacognitive judgments were varied across tasks, using judgments of learning, the Perceptual Awareness Scale, retrospective confidence ratings, and post-decision wagering.
Across small participant groups, the tasks were iteratively modified according to performance, participant feedback, and procedural problems. The final versions reduced the strongest ceiling effects and produced greater variation in performance while remaining feasible to complete. The memory iterations additionally showed that participants could report uncertainty while still answering correctly under a 2AFC format, supporting its replacement by a 3AFC structure. At the same time, intermediate memory and executive-function versions showed that increased difficulty could also produce substantial frustration and therefore had to be balanced against task burden.
The resulting task structures provide the basis for a subsequent full-scale experiment examining whether metacognitive monitoring contains a common latent component across cognitive domains.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Layered Framework of Environmental Experience: Integrating Sensory, Perceptual, and Semantic Processes
articles_hidden.authors: Dylan Chau Huynh; Aja Khalid Hussein; Farzaneh Behzadi; Amir Kalantarifard; Lars Brorson Fich; Andreas Møgelmose; Simone Kühn; Klaus Gramann; Zakaria Djebbara
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental experience is shaped by sensory stimulation, perceptual organization, and semantic meaning, yet these dimensions are often studied in isolation or reduced to broad environmental categories. This fragmentation limits our ability to explain how environments are experienced, how bottom-up and top-down processes interact, and how person-environment relations can be studied in a mechanistically informative way. Here, we provide an integrative review of work spanning embodied cognition, predictive processing, environmental psychology, and related traditions, and use this synthesis to develop a human-centered framework of environmental experience. In this framework, environmental experience unfolds across three analytically separable but experientially intertwined dimensions: sensory, perceptual, and semantic. The sensory dimension concerns immediate stimulation and salience; the perceptual dimension concerns the organization of environmental input into coherent, action-relevant structure; and the semantic dimension concerns learned meaning, cultural interpretation, familiarity, and contextual relevance. We argue that these dimensions are not sequential stages, but parallel, co-active, and mutually constraining aspects of lived environmental engagement. We then outline methodological implications for studying both dimension-specific contributions and their interaction, emphasizing convergent, multimethod, and temporally sensitive designs spanning behavioral, physiological, neurocognitive, and computational approaches. The framework provides an integrative basis for moving beyond static or overly coarse descriptions of environments and toward a more precise account of how environmental experience emerges across brain, body, and world.

articles_hidden.title: Recognizing strengths in individuals with ADHD: Exploring experiences and applications in clinical practice
articles_hidden.authors: Amy De Roubaix; Jennifer de Smidt; Lessa Madelief Schippers; Rob Abels; Patricia van Casteren; Barbara Franke; Corina Greven; Pieter Hoekstra; Petra Hurks; Akke Meilink
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Growing recognition of strengths associated with ADHD has stimulated interest in strength-based approaches. Highlighting these strengths may promote well-being and self-acceptance and help counter stigma. Although incorporating strengths into ADHD care may enhance positive outcomes, little is known about how ADHD-related strengths are currently recognized, valued, and applied in clinical practice. This study examined whether and how strengths are discussed in Dutch ADHD care, the perceived importance of attention to strengths, factors needed to support flourishing, associations with stigma, and characteristics of adults associated with reporting strengths related to ADHD.

Method. In co-creation with a Dutch ADHD advocacy organization, we conducted a mixed-method study and developed a survey containing open- and closed-ended questions on strengths associated with ADHD, attention to strengths in clinical care, support needs, and stigma. All members with ADHD were invited to participate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and tests of associations between experiencing strengths, stigma, and participant characteristics, while qualitative response were analyses thematically. 

Results. Among 224 respondents, 87.1% reported experiencing strengths associated with their ADHD. Participants who reported such strengths had received their diagnosis at a younger age than those who did not. Strengths were discussed more often during treatment (50.4%) than during diagnostic assessment (36.2%), mainly in the context of identifying and utilizing personal strengths. Experiencing strengths was associated with having discussed them in treatment, although the effect size was small. Most participants (78.6%) considered attention to strengths essential. A supportive and understanding environment was most frequently identified as necessary for strengths to flourish (73.2%). No association was found between experiencing strengths and reported stigma.

Conclusion. Most respondents experienced strengths associated with ADHD and considered attention to these strengths important. However, strengths are not systematically addressed in clinical care. Participants emphasize that understanding and acceptance of ADHD are key conditions for enabling strengths to flourish.

articles_hidden.title: Optimizing Behavioral Strategy Selection during Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Procrastination using Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Devon LoParo; Magdalena Pietruch; Weronika Maria Browarczyk; Joachim Kowalski; Jarosław M. Michałowski; Marek Wypych
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To determine whether machine-learning models using baseline self-report data could
personalize selection between two behavioral strategies embedded within cognitive-behavioral
therapy (CBT) for procrastination.

Methods: Participants were 256 Polish-speaking university students aged 18–26 years (M=22.4;
73.0% women) who completed active treatment in two preregistered randomized trials
(development sample, N=173; external validation sample, N=83). Participants received five
weekly group CBT sessions with identical psychoeducation and cognitive restructuring but
different behavioral modules: Realistic Planning and Timely Beginning (RPT) or Working Time
Restriction (WTR). Separate partial least-squares regression models used 483 baseline
demographic and self-report items to predict posttreatment Aitken Procrastination
Inventory–Revised (API-R) scores under each strategy. Predicted between-strategy differences
and Youden-index cutoffs generated recommendations: RPT, WTR, Either, or Neither. Because
treatment assignment was randomized, outcomes could be compared between participants whose
assigned treatment matched versus mismatched their model-derived recommendation.

Results: In the development trial, matched participants had lower posttreatment API-R scores
than mismatched participants (p=5.6×10−24; d=1.90) and higher likely-response rates
(p=1.8×10−15; RR=4.6). In the validation trial, each treatment-specific model explained 9% of
outcome variance. Matched participants again had lower API-R scores (p=.009; d=.53) and
higher response rates (p=.04; RR=1.3). Differences remained at six months (p=.033; d=.40).

Conclusion: Together, these findings indicate that personalization of procrastination treatment
can be achieved by modeling differential response to specific behavioral components rather than
entire treatment packages, supporting precision intervention in procrastination and beyond.
Further, explorative examination of predictors suggests that individuals may benefit from a
mechanism-informed, but not strictly mechanism-deterministic, precision framework.

articles_hidden.title: The popBAT: A New Beat Alignment Task to Assess Beat  Perception Abilities in Children
articles_hidden.authors: Francesca Cantoni; Zoé Mandernach; Erika Godde; Anna Fiveash; Barbara Tillmann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Beat processing is a fundamental skill for music and speech processing, as well as motor 
coordination. Existing tools testing beat perception, such as the seminal Beat Alignment Test 
(BAT), mostly use beat keepers that are external to the music, and may be too long to be 
engaging for children. We here developed the popBAT: a novel, child-friendly test using 
groovy pop-music excerpts, a musically integrated kick drum as the beat keeper, and a cover 
story, all aiming to enhance ecological validity and children’s engagement. Across four 
experiments, the popBAT was validated in adults (Exp. 1-2) and 7- to 8-year old children (Exp. 
3-4). In adults, the kick drum significantly increased subjective ratings of “pleasure”, “wanting 
to move”, and “pulse clarity”, compared to a triangle timbre playing the beat. In children and 
adults, popBAT performance was significantly above chance level, and popBAT performance 
correlated positively with performance in a previously used BAT implementation (adapted from 
Dalla Bella et al., 2017), confirming its convergent validity. In Experiment 4, popBAT 
performance significantly correlated with chronological age and reading performance, further 
confirming the link between beat perception and reading abilities. The popBAT provides a 
short, engaging, and ecologically valid measure of beat perception in children. Its success in 7- 
and 8-year-old children supports its use for investigating the developmental trajectories of 
rhythm processing and its role in language abilities, offering a promising tool for both research 
and clinical settings.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness Beyond the Brain: The Role of the Autonomic Nervous System in Non-ordinary States of Consciousness
articles_hidden.authors: Lana Porter; Valerie Bonnelle; Marieke Schölvinck; Martha N. Havenith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Non-ordinary states of consciousness (NOSCs), whether entered via psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis or other means, show striking therapeutic promise by improving well-being and reducing psychopathology across diverse conditions. While the neuronal dynamics underpinning such therapeutic shifts in consciousness have to some extent been mapped, research has mainly focused on the central nervous system (CNS). In contrast, the contribution of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) to NOSCs remains largely unexplored. At the same time, growing evidence indicates that beyond simply regulating bodily functions, the ANS mediates a range of processes directly linked to the core effects of many NOSCs, from emotional regulation to interoception and cognitive function.

In this review, we delineate the potential role of the ANS in shaping NOSCs, and discuss pathways by which ANS responses may support the cortical dynamics associated with NOSCs. Based on these insights, we propose a framework whereby inducing physiological stress within a conducive context supports the emergence of NOSCs, and the coexistence of high arousal and relaxation, i.e. of both sympathetic and parasympathetic tone, serves a hallmark of peak NOSCs. Finally, we highlight opportunities for future research to pinpoint these dynamics further, and offer an outlook on how understanding the ANS dynamics linked to NOSCs can allow us to induce NOSCs more safely, optimize their therapeutic impact, and provide cost-effective yet powerful physiological tools to monitor and facilitate these states in real time.

articles_hidden.title: The role of childhood neurocognition in eating disorder state transitions: findings from the ABCD cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Jenni Leppanen; Karina Allen; Marja Kaila-Vanhatalo; Kate Tchanturia; Ian Kelleher
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Neurocognitive difficulties have been proposed to play a role in the development and progression of eating disorders (EDs). However, prospective evidence from general population samples is limited. This study examined whether childhood neurocognition predicted the development of threshold or sub-threshold ED over 6 years in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) cohort.
Method: We analysed data from 11,378 children aged 8 – 11 years from the ABCD Study. ED states were derived from parent-reported Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia data at baseline and annual follow-ups. Neurocognition was assessed with the NIH Toolbox Cognition battery at baseline. Multi-state models were used to estimate ED state transitions and the impact of childhood neurocognition. 
Results: Across the observation periods, the most probable state to stay in or transition to was the no ED state and the probability of transitioning from no ED to sub-threshold or threshold ED state was 0.5 – 1%. Better working memory performance was associated with a small but significantly lower probability of transitioning from sub-threshold ED to no ED. Better performance on the episodic memory task was associated with a small but significantly lower risk of transitioning from no ED to sub-threshold ED. 
Discussion: Childhood neurocognition showed limited influence on later ED state transitions in this general population sample. Working memory and episodic memory were the only cognitive domains associated with specific transitions, suggesting that these functions could be relevant to early ED risk and recovery and further investigation is warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Linking Trait Items of Self-Control to Broader Conceptualizations in Daily Life  Using Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Anabel Büchner; Kai Tobias Horstmann; Marie Hennecke
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research suggests that self-control in everyday life is composed of different components (frequency, intensity, and successful resolution of self-control conflicts), and that individuals seem to differ in their abilities to resolve different types of self-control conflicts (initiation, persistence, inhibition). To date, however, it is unclear how established trait measures capture individual differences regarding these different components and types of self-control. We apply machine learning techniques to experience sampling data (N = 491; 9,634 measurement occasions) and identify which items from various trait scales best predict the different components and types of self-control in daily life. Commonly used trait items indexed all components to some extent, but most strongly successful conflict resolution. Contrary to our expectations, we were unable to predict the frequency, intensity, or successful resolution of inhibition conflicts, despite various trait measures being primarily developed for this conflict type. By comparing the most important predictors, we found meaningful theoretical differences between the components and types. We conclude that applying a broader conceptualization of self-control offers novel opportunities for exploring diverse routes to successful goal attainment and discuss theoretical and methodological implications of the findings for future research on trait self-control.

articles_hidden.title: Gradual Progress or Breakthrough Moments? Antecedents and Consequences of Sudden Gains in a Digital Neuroticism Intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Olaru; Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Rosalie Andrae; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Sudden gains—large and abrupt improvements in symptoms between consecutive sessions—are a well-documented phenomenon in psychotherapy research and reliably predict better treatment outcomes. Personality trait change, in contrast, is typically seen as a gradual process, and whether such sudden gains also occur and matter in the context of volitional neuroticism change is still unclear. In this preregistered study, we used daily and weekly measures of neuroticism to examine whether sudden gains occur during a 6-week digital neuroticism intervention embedded in an 8-week intensive longitudinal study (N = 427), and tested divergent claims from two theories on sudden gains in psychopathology. Sudden gains occurred in 11.2% (weekly) and 16.9% (daily) of participants, exceeding the rates that would be expected based on gradual change and noise, but far below the rates reported in psychotherapy research. Consistent with findings from psychotherapy, these gains occurred more frequently for participants with stronger state fluctuations overall but occurred equally often across conditions targeting neuroticism at the state, habit, or trait level. While gains coincided with large improvements in self-control, self-efficacy, self-esteem, and self-concept clarity (0.37–0.68 SD), we did not find robust evidence for an effect on neuroticism trait change. In contrast, gradual progress across the days and weeks of the intervention predicted stronger neuroticism trait changes. Our findings suggest that breakthrough moments or sudden shifts are less common and less consequential in volitional personality trait change than in the treatment of psychological disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian Hierarchical Models for Longitudinal Meta-Analysis in Sports Science: A Practical Tutorial Using brms
articles_hidden.authors: Sandro Balbino Júnior; Ahlan Benezar Lima; Humberto M. Carvalho
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analysis in sports science has predominantly focused on cross-sectional comparisons, leaving the temporal structure of longitudinal evidence largely unexploited. This tutorial introduces Bayesian hierarchical longitudinal meta-analysis as a principled framework for synthesizing repeated-measures data and illustrates its implementation using the R package `brms`. We demonstrate a complete analytical workflow---from model specification and prior selection to convergence checks, posterior predictive checks, and reporting—using a simulated dataset based on pubertal stature growth in male youth athletes. The worked example highlights how polynomial growth models recover biologically meaningful parameters, such as age at peak height velocity, with full uncertainty quantification. Additionally, we compare three prior specifications using leave-one-out cross-validation to test robustness. Fully annotated code scripts are provided, providing researchers with the practical tools and methodological reasoning necessary to apply longitudinal Bayesian meta-analysis to their own work in sports science and related fields.

articles_hidden.title: Confidently Neutral: Cognitive States of Neutrality in Auditory Perceptual Decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Luzie Kallfaß; Mara Wolter; Carla Ludig; Christoph Korn; Verena Wagner; Yulia Oganian
articles_hidden.abstract:
Theories of perceptual decision-making attribute neutral decisions to internal states such as inattention or low confidence, detached from sensory properties of the stimulus. Consequently, forced-choice paradigms do not allow for neutral decision outcomes, even under ambiguity. In contrast, epistemology posits multiple distinct neutral states, notably mere indecision – an intermediate state associated with low confidence and continuous information gathering – and settled indecision – a final state reached by actively suspending judgment after deliberation. Here, we tested whether distinct neutral states can be identified in perceptual decision-making. We induced perceptual ambiguity in a speech discrimination task using German vowel minimal-pair words, e.g., satt/Saat (“full”/“seed”), acoustically manipulated to range from low to high ambiguity. On each trial, participants could categorize the stimulus as one of the two words, request its repetition (indicating mere indecision), or select a final neutral response (indicating settled indecision). In Experiment 1 (n = 36), repetition requests and final neutral responses occurred most frequently for ambiguous stimuli, reflecting stimulus acoustics. Repetition requests were often followed by final neutral responses, indicating sequential evidence accumulation. In Experiment 2 (n = 37), embedding targets in speech-shaped noise increased final neutral responses for less ambiguous targets, showing that settled indecision can be elicited by external noise. Experiment 3 (n = 38) showed comparable metacognitive confidence ratings for final neutral and categorized responses. Overall, our results support the existence of distinct neutral
states (mere and settled indecision) in perceptual decision-making and call for their integration in models of perceptual decisions under uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: Ensemble clustering: A practical tutorial
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline X. Gao; Shengqi Wang; Ye Zhu; Myriam Ziou; Shu Mei Teo; Catherine L Smith; Derek Chiu; Aline Talhouk; Sue M. Cotton; Dominic Dwyer
articles_hidden.abstract: Cluster analysis is an explorative analytical method, serving as a critical tool in psychology, psychiatry and related fields to map heterogeneous data into meaningful subgroups. Despite their extensive historical use, traditional clustering techniques suffer from a lack of stability, robustness, and generalisability. These issues stem from the inherent difficulties of the clustering optimization problem as well as the stochastic nature of algorithm optimizers. To address these challenges, we demonstrate the use of methods utilising ensemble learning techniques to combine clustering results from different algorithms, model specifications, and/or sampled sub-datasets to form a single, more reliable consensus of clustering solutions. We detail ensemble clustering principles, variations in base clustering generation models, and consensus methods. Detailed introductions in existing R libraries and practical examples using R code are provided to guide users in both implementing and optimising ensemble clustering models. We then include simulation studies of real-world data to demonstrate the substantial benefit of ensemble clustering compared with single-run clustering models. The resources presented here will enable researchers to apply advanced clustering techniques to decompose heterogeneous and complex psychological data into stable subgroups.

articles_hidden.title: The relationship between mental time travel and aesthetic experience: a scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Yizhen Zhou; Hideaki Kawabata
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental time travel (MTT), the ability to project oneself backward to remember past experiences or forward to anticipate future events, shares neural correlates with aesthetic experiences within the default mode network. Previous research has demonstrated that mental imagery, a representational component of MTT, is deeply intertwined with aesthetic experience. However, a comprehensive overview of how retrospective (i.e., autobiographical/episodic memory) and prospective (i.e., episodic future thinking) components of MTT interact with aesthetic experiences is lacking. Guided by Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, this scoping review identified 16 studies published between 2004–2026. Overall, evidence demonstrates a dynamic, bidirectional relationship between the retrospective component of MTT and aesthetic experiences: aesthetic appreciation facilitates episodic memory encoding and consolidation; furthermore, autobiographical memory and self-relevance appraisals drive aesthetic experiences. Empirical research on prospective MTT in aesthetic contexts remains limited.

articles_hidden.title: Pilot Results of the Reintegrative Protocol in the Treatment of Binge Eating
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph Nicolosi; Christopher Rosik
articles_hidden.abstract: Experiencing a traumatic event, or a series of traumatic events, may increase the probability of subsequent development of binge eating and Binge Eating Disorder (BED). BED is the most common eating disorder in the United States, affecting some 2%-4% of people yearly. Due to the large prevalence of this disorder, as well as the burden BED puts on those living with it, effective treatment practices for treating BED are necessary. To date, there has been no research specifically examining the novel reintegrative protocol in a clinical setting as a treatment modality for BED. The purpose of this small, multiple-baseline pilot study was to explore the practicality and efficacy of the reintegrative protocol in treating BED by treating traumatic memories of individuals who engage in binge eating. Overall, the reintegrative protocol demonstrates promise as a tool for affect regulation and the treatment of BED. While implementing the protocol was feasible, the results varied among the 6 heterogeneous subjects and therefore, further research is required.

articles_hidden.title: Humanlike representation of social networks in large language models
articles_hidden.authors: Jae-Young Son; Daniel Carstensen; Serra Elizabeth Favila
articles_hidden.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have made great progress in their general reasoning capabilities, reasoning about social relationships has remained a challenge. In contrast, humans are naturally skilled at reasoning about how people are connected to one another, even in large, complex social networks. Recent research in cognitive science suggests that a key component of human social intelligence is the ability to represent social networks using multistep abstraction, which integrates knowledge of both direct and indirect social connections, and therefore supports inferences about network members’ social proximity to one another. Here, we test whether LLMs represent social networks using similar computational principles. In Study 1, we converted an existing human social navigation task into text and recorded LLM responses to the same problems humans were tasked with solving. LLMs’ behaviors closely mirrored those of human participants, and were best-explained by Katz communicability, a model of multistep abstraction that captures how humans represent and navigate social networks. In Study 2, we tested whether these multistep representations persisted in a task where they offered no benefit—and were in fact detrimental to task accuracy—and found that LLMs continued to show a multistep signature even in this context. These findings suggest that multistep abstraction may be a core property of how LLMs represent relational information, closely paralleling accounts of human cognitive maps.

articles_hidden.title: Impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on Canadian men and women with depressive and anxiety disorders: Time trend data from 9 waves of the iCARE Study
articles_hidden.authors: Marianne Berthiaume; Christina Bertachas; Mariam Atoui; Simon Bacon; Kim Lavoie
articles_hidden.abstract:
Importance: Psychosocial, employment and health impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic merit further examination among those with a mental health condition, as previous research shows these individuals were already vulnerable to these outcomes prior to this health emergency. 
Objective: To examine the 2-year psychosocial, employment, and health risk behaviour impacts of COVID-19 on Canadians adults with anxiety and/or depressive disorders, as a function of sex. 
Design, Setting and Participants: Nine cross-sectional online surveys from the iCARE Study were conducted between November 2020 and September 2022, weighted for age, sex and province. Participants were Canadian adults recruited through an online polling firm.
Main Outcomes and Measures: Rates of participants who reported significant psychosocial, employment, and health risk behaviour impacts as a result of COVID-19, and changes over a 2 year period. Formulation of the hypotheses preceded data collection. Measures included mental health status, psychosocial impacts of COVID-19 and changes in health risk behaviours. 
Results: Respondents (N = 27 142) were 52.6% being women with a mean age of 48.4 (SD 16.87) years. 24.33% reported being diagnosed with anxiety and/or depression disorders (N = 6411). Those with a mental health condition, versus those without, reported significantly greater emotional distress [ORadj (95% CI) = 3.84-5.57 (3.56-6.01)], interpersonal conflicts [3.39 (3.00-3.83)], employment loss [2.03 (1.82-2.27)], income reduction [1.90 (1.73-2.09)] and worse health behaviours (e.g., smoking [2.78 (2.52 to 3.06]), drug use [3.24 (2.96 to 3.54)]), and limited access to medical care [2.54 (2.32 to 2.78)]. Impacts on mental health, conflict, job/income and access to medical care decreased overtime (all p’s <.001), while difficulty affording food increased (p=0.02). Women with these disorders, compared to men, reported more emotional distress [OR (95% CI) = 1.17-1.39 (1.05-1.55)] and worse diet [1.36 (1.21-1.52)] and physical activity levels [1.24 (1.12-1.38)], but were less likely to report increased vaping [OR .67 (.57-.79)], alcohol [.86 (.76-.97)] and drug use [.79 (.70-.90)].
Conclusion and Relevance: Findings indicate that government initiatives aimed at mitigating the multidimensional impacts of a pandemic should prioritize individuals with mental health conditions, with women needing more psychosocial and health behaviour support, and men needing more substance use support.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging Word Knowledge from Everyday Language
articles_hidden.authors: Layla Unger; Emma James
articles_hidden.abstract: Within the first few years of life, children go from nonverbal infants to fluent users of hundreds of words. This feat unfolds as children are immersed in a sea of words in conversations, stories and other language contexts. In principle, word contexts might support word learning because words similar in meaning tend to occur in similar contexts. Thus, a child who knows some fruit words and has heard them in the context of "juicy" might learn that a "juicy mango" is also a fruit even without ever seeing a mango. Indeed, cutting-edge large language models leverage just these context cues to form rich representations of words. Yet we do not know whether these cues are an important driver of real-world word learning. We quantified context cues in children’s everyday English language input and found that they did reliably predict real-world word learning, above and beyond other established predictors. These findings illuminate how everyday language scaffolds word learning.

articles_hidden.title: Complex systems methods in ageing research: An overview of emerging approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriela Lunansky; Lotte P. Brinkhof; Ingrid A. van de Leemput; René J Melis; Marcel Olde Rikkert; Geeske Peeters; Rick Quax; Jeroen Uleman; Almar Andreas Leonardus Kok
articles_hidden.abstract:
The application of complex systems science is gaining traction in the field of ageing research. A complex system is a large collection of components whose dynamic interactions lead to 'emergent properties' that cannot be understood or predicted based on knowledge of the components in isolation. Here we conceptualise human ageing as resulting from integrated, multi-scale systems characterised by dynamic interactions within and between biological, behavioural, functional and environmental domains. 
Complexity science provides tools to study these joint dynamics, allowing researchers to address research questions that examine (1) interactions across levels or domains, (2) dynamic processes over time, or (3) emergent behaviour of the system as a whole, which is not reducible to individual components. Studying complex systems can benefit from these methodological tools, which are still underexplored in gerontology and geriatrics. With this article, we intend to inspire and support researchers in the field of ageing to explore the potential of complexity science methods for their own research. 
We explain four different methodological approaches to study complex systems: causal loop diagrams, system dynamics modelling, psychometric network analysis, and dynamical indicators of resilience and complexity. For each of these approaches, we explain their purpose and theoretical assumptions, provide examples from the scientific literature, and discuss their strengths and limitations. As it remains challenging to operationalise complexity-driven research questions and select appropriate methods from the growing range of available methodological approaches, particularly for researchers unfamiliar with them, we hope to have lowered this threshold.

articles_hidden.title: Mentalizing from self and friend perspectives: Relations between neural similarity, affective similarity and social anxiety symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Alicia Vallorani; Kathryn A. McNaughton; Marisa N. Lytle; Michael Hallquist; Elizabeth Redcay; Koraly Perez-Edgar
articles_hidden.abstract: Social interactions are dynamic and complex, relying on tracking variation in your own and your partner’s affective and mental states. Being “in-sync” neurally and building a shared consensus can mark successful social interactions. In addition, social anxiety can impact social experiences. We used a novel, naturalistic paradigm to investigate relations between inter-brain neural similarity within mentalizing regions, affective similarity and social anxiety symptoms. Undergraduate student friend pairs (N = 34, 85% White, 65% Women) engaged in a social interaction while videos previously captured from their individual perspectives were recorded. Participants watched clips of the social interaction from both their own perspective (their personal view of the social interaction) and their friend’s perspective (their friend’s personal view of the social interaction) while fMRI data were collected. They rated their affect after each clip. Inter-brain neural similarity was computed across three conditions: 1) Same-Stimuli: both participants viewed identical visual stimuli as in a traditional neural similarity paradigm, 2) Self-Perspective: both participants viewed the clip from their own perspective like the originally experienced social interaction and 3) Friend-Perspective: both participants viewed the clip from their friend’s perspective, a novel perspective. Participants self-reported their social anxiety symptoms and affective similarity captured affect rating concordance within dyads. In contrast to the Same-Stimuli condition, when participants viewed the clips like they originally experienced social interaction (Self-Perspective), greater affective similarity was associated with greater inter-brain neural similarity. When participants viewed the clips from a novel perspective (Friend-Perspective), participants lower in social anxiety symptoms exhibited greater inter-brain neural similarity with greater affective similarity; whereas, participants higher in social anxiety symptoms exhibited greater inter-brain neural similarity with less affective similarity. The results suggest stimuli from socially relevant perspectives, rather than identical stimuli, may reveal more nuanced brain-behavior dynamics, allowing for a better understanding of individual differences in socioemotional experience.

articles_hidden.title: Active information sampling versus yoked observation in location probability learning
articles_hidden.authors: Emma; Vanessa G. Lee
articles_hidden.abstract:
Past experience guides spatial attention: locations that frequently contain a target become
prioritized, demonstrating location probability learning (LPL). However, the role of active
control over information sampling and delivery in LPL remains unclear. Using a paradigm that
requires deliberate information sampling and a yoked design that then restricts self-directed
sampling, we investigated whether LPL can arise in the yoked case. In a three-stage experiment
conducted in 2025, we created a yoked search task: one participant controlled what they saw
during search, and another viewed the active participant’s display. In Stage 1, active participants
(P1) moved the mouse to search for a T-among-Ls while their vision was restricted to the 3.3º
around the cursor. Unbeknownst to them, the target frequently appeared in one high-probability
quadrant. In Stage 2, yoked participants (P2) searched the screen recordings from P1, without
controlling information sampling. Despite having no control in Stage 2, P2 developed an
attentional preference for the high-probability quadrant, which persisted in an unbiased Stage 3
testing phase. However, at the group-level, P2 learned only when yoked to recordings from a P1
who showed learning. Thus, observational learning can give rise to spatial attentional changes.

articles_hidden.title: The evolution of pain and associated anxiety, depression, and suicide was profoundly impacted by predation
articles_hidden.authors: Edgar T. Walters
articles_hidden.abstract: Predation is a powerful evolutionary selection pressure, but its roles in shaping human behavior are not understood. Predators often injure prey in unsuccessful attacks, and they selectively target injured and otherwise impaired prey. Injury commonly causes anxiety-like hypervigilance, which has been shown in squid to increase survival from predatory attack. It also induces persistent hyperactivity of primary nociceptors, which in mammals drives pain and anxiety. In social mammals and some eusocial insects, injury can elicit group antipredator defense and woundtending responses, usually from closely related kin. Accelerated evolution of affective pain is proposed to have occurred in social mammals to facilitate communication of need for support. This function probably evolved rapidly in hominins because of the abundance of large predators and the necessity of cooperative group defense for otherwise relatively defenseless individuals. Affective pain and its empathetic recognition by group members became increasingly useful as cooperative protection and care facilitated the recovery of temporarily incapacitated members to help the group. Such social functions may explain unusual human nociceptor properties that promote persistent pain. When hominin groups were small and predatory threat relentless, the value to the group of each member would have been high. Severe pain and depression could indicate to a member their incapacity and burden to the group, potentially motivating suicidal behavior, while ready access to predators would have made suicide easy. Thus, suicide motivated by intolerable pain and depression could have been under positive selection (genetic and cultural) in cooperative bands of hominins living alongside dangerous predators.

articles_hidden.title: A Specialized Model versus a Frontier Model in Emotional Support: Blind Evaluation by Psychology Professionals
articles_hidden.authors: Alejandro Vaca Serrano; Alberto Vaca Escribano; José María González de Echevarri
articles_hidden.abstract:
General-purpose conversational assistants are also used for emotional support and mental health concerns, even though they were not designed as clinical interventions. In this work we evaluate whether a model specialized in emotional support is preferred, by psychology professionals and under blind conditions, over a frontier model. We compare Pía, the conversational system of the TerapIA application (https://terapiaconpia.com), with the most recent version of OpenAI's ChatGPT — a general-purpose, large-scale frontier model, in the versions GPT-5.5 Instant and GPT-5.6 Sol depending on the period, both with the health and mental-health improvements publicly announced by OpenAI. Both systems receive the same system message, an extensive prompt designed by clinical psychologists for this domain, and the same conversational context, and both are run without explicit reasoning (reasoning disabled). The analysis is carried out on irreversibly anonymized data. Over n=771 blind comparisons corresponding to 101 real conversations of 100 distinct users, evaluated between 19 June and 7 August 2026, Pía was preferred in 52.7% of cases against 39.7% for the reference system (7.7% ties), which amounts to a tie-adjusted preference rate of 56.5% (95% CI bootstrap by conversation: [51.0%, 61.9%]; p=0.017). The observed advantage does not appear to be explained by a preference for longer responses: Pía produces responses less than half as long as the reference system. Nor by greater scale or general capability, since the reference system surpasses Pía in both. An exploratory analysis by position of the turn within the conversation shows preference indistinguishable from parity in the first third (49.8%) and clearly above it in the middle third (60.6%) and the final third (58.4%), with a significant positive trend (p=0.022); his pattern is compatible with differences between systems becoming more visible when more conversational context is available, without the design being able to identify the responsible mechanism. A second exploratory analysis by risk level A second exploratory analysis by risk level of the conversation shows a
descriptive upward pattern that does not reach statistical significance.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond WEIRD and White: Building a Globally Inclusive Science of Sport Leadership
articles_hidden.authors: Radhika Butalia; Filip Boen; Nicholas de Cruz; S. Alexander Haslam; Rolf van Dick; Katrien Fransen
articles_hidden.abstract: Research in the social sciences overwhelmingly relies on participants drawn from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies despite the fact that these populations represent about 12% of the world’s population. Moreover, these samples are disproportionately White. Although this limitation has been widely discussed in the social sciences, its implications for sport science remain underexamined. In this expert statement, we use sport leadership research as a test case to illustrate why moving beyond WEIRD and White dominance is critical to building a more inclusive and representative science of sport. First, we discuss how cultural and social contexts shape leadership expectations, perceptions, and effectiveness, thereby calling into question the appropriateness of applying theories developed in WEIRD samples to other contexts. Second, we synthesise the current state of the literature and highlight recent advances, particularly insights from the Cross-Cultural Research on Leadership in Sport (CROLIS) programme. Drawing on these insights, we provide practical and methodological recommendations and identify priorities for future research that together offer a roadmap for building a science of sport leadership in which diverse populations, cultural contexts, and knowledge systems shape equitable knowledge production.

articles_hidden.title: Memories that remain: Image memorability transfers to scene descriptions
articles_hidden.authors: Diana Kollenda; Yee Lee Shing; Katharina Dobs; Benjamin de Haas
articles_hidden.abstract: Some images remain in memory while others fade quickly. Memorability reflects an observer-independent, intrinsic property of an image, which can be predicted by computational models. While semantic content has been proposed as the critical determinant of memorability, it is challenging to disentangle image content from visual features on display. Here, we find that the memorability of scene images transfers to short textual descriptions of those scenes, whether generated by humans or multimodal large language models. Furthermore, new images produced with generative AI from descriptions alone reproduce the memorability of original images. Together, these findings show that semantic content, including interrelations captured in scene descriptions, accounts for a meaningful portion of the variation in scene memorability, and that language serves as an efficient compression of memory-relevant visual content.

articles_hidden.title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-environmental Behaviors
articles_hidden.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hege Landsvik
articles_hidden.abstract: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies (N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Further, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people's moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

articles_hidden.title: Using the Interpersonal Circumplex in Therapeutic Planning and Intervention for Individuals Experiencing Acculturative Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Serena Z Chen; Aaron L. Pincus
articles_hidden.abstract: We integrate theories and models of acculturative stress and interpersonal behavior to help advance research and practice for clients experiencing acculturative stress. We briefly review Contemporary Integrative Interpersonal Theory (CIIT) and the interpersonal situation framework as an empirically validated heuristic model for case conceptualization and psychotherapy. We then apply CIIT to therapeutic planning and intervention for individuals experiencing acculturative stress, including a clinical example and clinical recommendations.

articles_hidden.title: Large language models for depression assessment from brief daily diaries
articles_hidden.authors: Whitney R. Ringwald; Aman Taxali; Mike Angstad; Colin Vize; Chandra Sripada; Aidan G.C. Wright
articles_hidden.abstract: Closely tracking changes in depression is important for clinical research and practice. However, intensive longitudinal depression assessment relies on self-report surveys that have major limitations.  Scoring depression from natural language with large language models (LLMs) could resolve these shortcomings.  This study tested the validity of depression rated by LLMs from daily video diaries. We studied 108 participants selected for mental health treatment status (45% in treatment).  Participants completed a clinical interview and 14-21 days of depression surveys and video diaries.  Daily depression scores were estimated by LLMs from diary transcripts. LLM ratings converged with self-report depression within-person (r=.45;95% CrI[.40, .49]) and when averaged across days for an overall depression score (r=.61;95% CrI[.43,.75]). Averaged LLM ratings correlated with depression symptom severity ascertained by clinical interview (r=.53;95% CrI[.35, .68]).  LLM-rated depression and self-report had similar profiles of associations with daily functioning variables (profile r=.98 within-person; r=.94 between-person).  Multivariable regression results showed LLM ratings predicted daily functioning variables (partial βs=|.12|-|.28|) and interview-rated depression (partial β=.33;95% CrI[.07, .58]) over and above self-reports, suggesting LLMs capture clinically-relevant information that self-reports miss. Findings establish a strong foundation for a depression assessment approach that addresses shortcomings of self-reports while satisfying the unique demands of intensive longitudinal monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Insomnia and Emotion Dysregulation Across the Perinatal Period: Daily and Longitudinal Associations with Anxiety and Depression
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Barrett; Benicio Frey; David L. Streiner; Sheryl Green
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Insomnia is prevalent during pregnancy and the postpartum period and contributes to vulnerability for anxiety and depressive disorders during this time. However, the mechanisms linking sleep disturbance to depressive and anxiety symptoms remain unclear. Emotion dysregulation (ED) and pre-sleep arousal have been proposed as key transdiagnostic processes. This is the first study to integrate daily and longitudinal methods to examine these mechanisms across the perinatal period.
Methods: Data were drawn from a randomized controlled trial evaluating two brief interventions for insomnia during pregnancy and the postpartum. Seventy-five pregnant individuals were assessed across pregnancy and the postpartum using trait measures and 7-day daily surveys at three timepoints. Regression models examined whether prenatal insomnia, ED, and their interaction predicted postpartum depression, anxiety, and worry. Multilevel models tested within-person associations between daily sleep and next-day symptoms, with ED as a moderator, and cluster bootstrap mediation analyses examined pre-sleep arousal as a mediator of sleep–symptom associations.
Results: For postpartum anxiety symptoms, higher prenatal insomnia and ED independently predicted symptoms, with a significant interaction (β = .28, p = .003). For postpartum depressive symptoms, only the insomnia × ED interaction was significant (β = .23, p = .045). For postpartum worry, only baseline worry predicted outcomes. At the within-person level, sleep quality and sleep onset latency predicted next-day anxiety and depression; ED did not moderate these associations. Mediation analyses indicated that daytime anxiety and depressive symptoms predicted poorer sleep quality, sleep onset latency, and sleep efficiency through increased pre-sleep arousal.
Conclusions: Findings support a pathway linking insomnia and ED to perinatal anxiety and depression. Results suggest that prenatal ED is associated with heightened vulnerability to the mental health consequences of insomnia and identify pre-sleep arousal as a key mechanism linking daytime affect to sleep disruption. Clinical implications for perinatal mental health are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Anxious avoidance as disrupted exploration
articles_hidden.authors: Vanessa M Brown; Alexandre Dombrovski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Avoidance is a hallmark of anxiety. Exposure treatments often help overcome
avoidance, yet why avoidance persists without external reinforcement remains unclear.
We propose that one contributing factor is a failure to adaptively use uncertainty when
deciding whether to explore choices with unknown outcomes. Using reinforcement
learning and explore/exploit paradigms, we examined whether anxious individuals
misestimate the value of exploration. We tested this hypothesis against alternatives—
uncertainty intolerance, punishment sensitivity, and stochastic choice—in a task where
optimal behavior required both increasing and decreasing exploration. Consistent with
our hypothesis, people high in anxiety failed to adjust exploration based on uncertainty,
instead either under-exploring or over-exploring. This deficit was distinct from
intolerance of uncertainty and remained after controlling for other internalizing
symptoms. These findings suggest that anxious avoidance may stem from
misestimating uncertainty and the value of exploration, pointing to new treatment targets
focused on improving adaptive use of uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental changes in the weighting of prosodic cues
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Amanda Seidl; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract:
