In a preregistered simulation with pooled correlations matched by calibrated design, the estimator separated minority-carried community edges from planted incoherent edges ("distractors") with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of .985 versus .469 for raw correlations (paired difference +.516, 95% confidence interval [+.506, +.526]). A concentration-only variant of the estimator remained at chance while a coherence-only variant matched the full estimator — the separation is due to the coherence factor alone. Community recovery by the full pipeline showed no improvement at n = 600: by design, both pipelines drew their candidate edges from the same raw-correlation filter, so reweighting could not restore true edges that the selection step had already discarded.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual adaptation to human-likeness in voices
articles_hidden.authors: Christine Nussbaum; Sebastian Goerke; Ibrahim Vefa Arslan; Stefan R. Schweinberger
articles_hidden.abstract: With synthetic voices now being a part of everyday life, it is important to understand how the perception of synthetic voices is shaped and modified through exposure. Therefore, we employed an adaptation paradigm to test whether perception of human-likeness is amenable to short-term perceptual encounters. In three experiments, we presented morphed target voices on a human-synthetic-continuum in three conditions: without prior adaptation, and after repeated exposure to adaptor voices that all were either synthetic or human. Experiment 1 (N = 26) was conducted online, Experiment 2 (N = 31) was a full replication in the lab, and Experiment 3 (N = 36) employed an adjusted procedure with blocked and reduced adaptor exposure to test the robustness of effects. In all experiments, we observed consistent contrastive aftereffects: After adaptation to synthetic voices, ambiguous voices were more often classified as human. After adaptation to human voices, the same ambiguous voices were more often classified as synthetic. Intriguingly, in Experiment 1 and 2, contrastive aftereffects were even larger in trials which employed digital caricatures (i.e., 25%-exaggerated human or synthetic voices) as adaptors, even though caricatures themselves were not consistently rated as more human (or synthetic, respectively) compared to original voices. While the adaptation effect survived the adjusted procedure (Experiment 3), substantial modulations by caricatured adaptors were no longer observed. Together, these findings provide robust evidence that impressions of vocal human-likeness are not only determined by the acoustic features but are the result of a complex interplay with listeners and their recent perceptual experiences.

articles_hidden.title: Bidirectional Interaction Between Working Memory and Long-Term Memory Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Jingyao Cheng; Yiheng Qiu; Keisuke Fukuda; Yingtao Fu; mowed shen; HUI CHEN
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans routinely coordinate distinct representations from working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM) to construct and update internal models of the world. However, the nature of cross-system interaction between these representations remains poorly understood. To address this, we developed a novel visual memory task in which participants maintained a briefly presented color in WM while retrieving a color from LTM, testing how representations from different systems influence one another. Across three experiments (N = 120) and computational modeling, we demonstrate that interaction between WM and LTM is bidirectional yet asymmetric: LTM representation is attracted toward WM, whereas WM representation is repelled from LTM. These opposing biases reveal distinct representational mechanisms underlying WM and LTM, and we further discuss their implications for the prevailing account of memory distortions and a potential explanation.

articles_hidden.title: Stimulus selection and sample-size calculation for statistical test of hierarchical cognitive model
articles_hidden.authors: Kazuya Fujita
articles_hidden.abstract: Sample-size calculations are essential for ensuring adequate statistical power. However, these calculations are rarely performed in elaborate models, specifically hierarchical cognitive models in which Bayesian cognitive models for human data are used. We used a population-level Fisher information matrix (PFIM) proposed in the field of pharmacology to develop and demonstrate experimental stimulus selection and sample-size calculations within a hierarchical cognitive model. In Simulation Study 1, we confirmed that PFIM could accurately predict statistical power. Further, a high correlation was observed between the logarithm of the Bayes Factor and the predicted statistical power. In Simulation Study 2, we outlined the process of determining the number of participants and trials after the selection of the optimal experimental stimulus in that the statistical power is maximized. Despite the time-intensive nature of parameter estimation, the sample-size calculation was achievable within a realistic timeframe (e.g., to 2–3 days). The proposed method has low computational load and enables sample-size calculations for elaborate hierarchical cognitive models. Further this method can be applied to a wide range of models.

articles_hidden.title: When Mood Turns Attention Inward: Affective and Cognitive Pathways Linking Negative Mind Wandering and Attentional Control
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholaus P. Brosowsky; Emma Dueck; Stephanie Lauren Souliere; Nicholas Daniel Evans; Liam Yeo; Josephine Nicholson
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative mood is associated with both attentional failures and increased mind wandering, but the mechanisms linking mood, thought, and performance remain unclear. In particular, it is unknown whether mood-related performance costs arise primarily from changes in attentional control or from changes in the content of thought. We examined these possibilities in 585 undergraduate participants who completed positive, neutral, or negative mood inductions followed by a sustained attention task with intermittent thought probes. Probes assessed both the intentionality (intentional vs. unintentional) and emotional valence (positive, neutral, or negative) of off-task thought. Structural equation models were used to examine pathways linking mood induction, post-induction affect, mind wandering, task performance, and post-task mood. Negative mood was associated with poorer task performance both directly through post-induction affect and indirectly through increases in negatively valenced mind wandering. These indirect effects were observed for both intentional and unintentional negative mind wandering and generalized across measures of perceptual sensitivity, commission errors, and reaction-time variability. Negative mind wandering also predicted poorer subsequent mood, whereas positive and neutral mind wandering did not. These findings identify negatively valenced thought as a common mechanism linking mood to both sustained-attention performance and subsequent affect.

articles_hidden.title: Negative Urgency, Not Negative Affect, Mediates the Association Between Sleep Problems and Eating Disorder Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Franco; Emily R. Linn; Noa A. Bregmann; Stacey M. Schaefer; Richard Davidson; James I. Hudson; Kristin Javaras
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: There is increasing evidence suggesting that sleep problems may cause alterations in
eating behavior (e.g., poor sleep quality is linked to eating disorders (EDs) and ED symptoms).
However, little is known about the mechanisms by which sleep problems may increase ED
symptoms. Sleep deprivation has been linked to elevated negative urgency (NU; the tendency to
act rashly in response to extreme negative affect [NA]), and NA. Both are consistently linked to
higher ED symptoms and potentially mediate the association between sleep problems and ED
symptoms. This study examined whether NU and NA mediate the relationship between sleep
problems and ED symptoms. Method: Female-identifying introductory psychology students at a
midwestern university (n = 119) completed self-report measures of impulsivity (UPPS-P), ED
symptoms (Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale), and sleep problems (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality
Index), and a task-based measure of NU (total commission errors for negatively-valenced
distractors in the CANTAB Affective Go/No-go Task). Mediation analyses included bias-
corrected and accelerated confidence intervals estimated via non-parametric bootstrap. Results:
Sleep problems were significantly associated with (Box-Cox-transformed) ED symptoms
(B=0.26, p<0.01). Self-reported NU mediated a significant proportion of the association between
PSQI sleep problems and transformed ED symptoms (Proportion = 61%; p<0.01), but task-based
NU (Proportion = 4%; p=0.73) and NA (Proportion = 23%; p=0.74) did not. Discussion: Poor
sleep may increase ED symptoms partly due to increasing trait-like NU, but not via task-based
NU nor NA. Trait-like NU may be an important mechanism linking sleep problems and eating
disturbances.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Open-Weight Large Language Models for Structured Depression Assessment from Clinical Interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Jeffrey M. Girard; Gaossou Youssouf Kebe; Louis-Philippe Morency; Fernando De la Torre; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: The administration of semi-structured clinical interviews for depression assessment is resource-intensive and susceptible to rater drift. While large language models (LLMs) offer potential for automated quality assurance, reliance on proprietary models creates data privacy barriers incompatible with secure clinical workflows. This study evaluates a privacy-preserving pipeline using open-weight LLMs to perform item-level scoring of the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) directly from interview transcripts. The sample included 541 video-recorded English-language interviews with 277 psychiatric inpatients diagnosed with diverse affective and psychotic disorders. Benchmarking 25 architectures, we found that an indirect scoring strategy, where models predict individual item scores that are subsequently summed, significantly outperformed direct total score prediction. This suggests that decomposing the assessment into intermediate reasoning steps improves performance. The best-performing models achieved “good” error rates and “excellent” correlations with trusted human labels, approaching established benchmarks for human inter-rater reliability. To determine the active ingredients of effective prompting, we conducted an ablation study. Results revealed that descriptive cues (scoring criteria) were the primary driver of performance, whereas few-shot examples provided negligible additional benefit, suggesting that zero-shot prompting is a viable, efficient strategy. However, error analysis identified a multimodal gap, where text-only models struggled more with items dependent on nonverbal behavior. We conclude that open-weight LLMs demonstrate strong potential to serve as secure “digital second opinions,” representing a promising step toward augmenting clinical decision-making without compromising patient privacy.

articles_hidden.title: Monocular stereopsis, pinholes, and the perils of classroom theorizing:  A response to McIntosh (2025).
articles_hidden.authors: Dhanraj Vishwanath
articles_hidden.abstract: Monocular stereopsis is a compelling perceptual effect wherein viewing a picture of a 3-dimensional scene with one eye through an aperture generates a perceptual impression of depth similar to binocular stereopsis. Here I provide a critique of a recently published report on the topic in the journal i-Perception (McIntosh, 2025).  In the report, the author claims to adjudicate on explanations of the monocular stereopsis effect and the phenomenology of stereopsis more broadly construed.  The author suggests, based on an informal test comparing pinhole and aperture viewing of a picture during a fifteen-minute classroom lecture break, that the monocular-aperture effect is best explained by a 100-year-old description of the phenomenon. I show that McIntosh’s report reveals a lack of understanding of the modern empirical facts and theoretical concepts relevant to this scientific debate and neglects the rudimentary demands of conducting an interpretable perceptual test.

articles_hidden.title: Changing Contributions of Emotion and Reward Information to Learning Through Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Leah Somerville
articles_hidden.abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8-22 years completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hampered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially hindered by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

articles_hidden.title: Agency enhances episodic memory across the broader experience
articles_hidden.authors: Tej Bhoga; Zachariah Reagh; Angelique I. Delarazan
articles_hidden.abstract: Agency, the ability to exert control over one’s own experience, enhances memory relative to passive observation. However, it remains unclear whether agency only benefits information that one directly acts on, or if its benefits extend to the fidelity that the broad experience is represented in memory. Across two experiments, participants encoded objects and their locations while exploring a series of rooms, either controlling object placements themselves (Active) or observing the same sequence of events without control (Passive). Memory was assessed using the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), along with tests of object-spatial placement and descriptive recall. Critically, mnemonic discrimination required retaining perceptual details beyond what the object-spatial placement task demanded. In Experiment 1, agency enhanced basic object recognition, mnemonic discrimination, and object description recall, but not object-spatial placement. Experiment 2 used a within-subjects design, a recognition-based spatial test with lower retrieval demands, and attention ratings collected throughout encoding. Agency again enhanced mnemonic discrimination, and its benefits extended to object-spatial placement and recall of both object and room descriptions. These effects remained after accounting for self-reported attention during encoding. Together, the findings show that agency enhances mnemonic discrimination on the MST and suggests that its benefits extend beyond information falling within the scope of participants’ direct control, influencing both the detail of individual object representations and memory for the broader context in which they were encountered.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding the Impact of Psychological Interventions for Psychosis in Daily Life: Experience Sampling Methodology as an Adjunct Outcome Measure in Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Clementine Jane Edwards; Ginette Lafit; Joanne R Beames; Morwenna Rickard; Simone Burger; Alyssa Jongeneel; Elise van der Stouwe; Wim Veling; Eric Granholm; Anita Schick
articles_hidden.abstract:
Retrospective outcome measures are widely used in mental health clinical trials. Yet, these gold-standard measures may not capture fully how subjective experiences and behaviours unfold and relate to each other in everyday life context. Experience Sampling Methodology (ESM) offers a complementary approach by collecting repeated assessments in daily life. The ESM allows the measurement of proximal, dynamic and context-dependent outcomes while interventions are being delivered, while classical scales administered in clinics capture retrospective aggregates of experiences over a defined period of time.
In this paper, we draw on learnings from psychological therapy trials in psychosis that applied ESM as an outcome measure to support the wider adoption of this approach in intervention studies. We offer practical suggestions for incorporating ESM into clinical trial design and conduct, including the development of specific momentary research questions, selection and adaptation of questionnaire items, sampling schedules, participant briefing and debriefing, and approaches to maximising compliance and data quality. We also discuss key analytic and conceptual issues, including the interpretation of ESM findings alongside traditional retrospective interviews and self-report measures.
ESM assessments can provide unique insights into mechanisms, variability, context and timing of change in daily life, helping to clarify not only whether an intervention works, but how and when it has an impact. Used to address these research questions through questionnaires and schedules that harness the value of assessments during daily life, ESM can strengthen the evaluation and subsequent development of mental health treatments by capturing meaningful change in the settings in which people live their lives.

articles_hidden.title: Parenting sense of competence and dynamic physiological self-regulation before and during parent-child conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Prakash Thambipillai; Salome Vanwoerden; Amy Byrd; J. Richard Jennings; Stephanie Stepp; Vera Vine
articles_hidden.abstract: Parenting sense of competence encompasses both parenting self-efficacy, or parent’s appraisal of their parenting skills, and parenting satisfaction, the affective feelings of gratification from parenting. Parents’ sense of competence may be linked to psychophysiological self-regulation during challenges, which for parents of adolescents with emotion dysregulation difficulties may begin during the anticipation of conflict. 162 clinically-referred, parent-adolescent dyads (adolescents: Mage = 12.59, SD = .59, range 10-14 yrs, 47% girls, 41% African American, 60% minoritized race/ethnicity; caregivers: Mage = 40.35, SD = 7.23, 94% female, 40% African American, 48% minoritized race/ethnicity) completed an ecologically valid, conflict protocol, including a 2-minute conflict anticipation and 8-minute conflict discussion, during which their respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) was recorded. Results of dynamic growth curve models indicated that parenting satisfaction, but not self-efficacy, was associated with parents’ RSA trajectories,  = .33, SE = .12, p = .005, and this effect was robust to respiration adjustment and relevant behavioral confounds. Lower satisfaction was associated with greater anticipatory RSA withdrawal followed by sharp RSA augmentation at conflict onset; higher parenting satisfaction was associated with a more flexible RSA trajectory, beginning with anticipatory augmentation followed by modest, theoretically appropriate withdrawal at conflict onset. Parents’ self-regulation before and during conflict may be especially relevant to the experience of parenting.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of a German Version of the Barcelona Music  Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ)
articles_hidden.authors: Kim Meyer; Charlotte Jolmes; Madita Jodes; Willi Moxter; Lena Rölz; Maël Roth; Lars Rogenmoser
articles_hidden.abstract:
The Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ) is a widely used self-report measure of 
individual differences in music reward sensitivity. Although the instrument has been adapted 
into several languages, no validated German version has previously been available. The 
present study translated and psychometrically evaluated a German adaptation of the BMRQ 
in a sample of 471 German-speaking adults. 
A split-sample approach was used to conduct confirmatory and exploratory factor analyses. 
Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original five-factor structure comprising Musical 
Seeking, Emotional Evocation, Mood Regulation, Sensory-Motor, and Social Reward. 
Exploratory analyses broadly reproduced this structure, although overlap emerged between 
Musical Seeking and Social Reward. Internal consistency estimates for the BMRQ dimension 
scores and overall score ranged from acceptable to good. Associations with reward-related 
motivational tendencies provided evidence for convergent validity. 
Scores were distributed across a broad range of the scale and showed moderate negative 
skewness, reflecting a tendency toward higher levels of music reward. 
Overall, the present findings support the German BMRQ as a psychometrically sound 
instrument for assessing individual differences in music reward sensitivity in German
speaking populations.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Divorce and Partner Bereavement: Personality and Trajectories of Change in Life Satisfaction and Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Thao Kieu; Liselotte den Boer; Wiebke Bleidorn; Yu Xie; Jaap J. A. Denissen
articles_hidden.abstract: Dissolutions of romantic relationships can elicit diverse reactions across various aspects of well-being, but they also offer an opportunity to examine which factors promote resilience and identify individuals at risk. In this preregistered multi-sample longitudinal study, we examined the heterogeneity in life satisfaction and mental health changes around and during divorce or partner bereavement, and whether personality (i.e., traits and resilient versus nonresilient personality profiles) may explain individual differences in change trajectories. Data from 1,306 divorcees and 1,150 bereaved partners were drawn from nationally representative panel studies in the Netherlands (N = 12,551), Germany (N = 10,830), and China (N = 28,628), and analyzed using growth mixture modeling. Four life satisfaction trajectories and three mental health trajectories were identified for each event. Recovery and resilience emerged as the most common trajectories across events, outcomes, and samples. Among personality factors, neuroticism was the most consistent predictor of a lower likelihood of belonging to a resilience trajectory. This study advanced the generalizability of findings across diverse loss-based events, populations, and aspects of well-being. The findings further underscore the  influence of neuroticism in shaping, and potentially complicating, psychological adjustment surrounding divorce and partner bereavement.

articles_hidden.title: Displacement, Parenting, and Self-Development in Syrian Refugee Children: A Longitudinal Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Hend Eltanamly; Fiona McEwen; Elie Karam; Sander Thomaes; Michael Pluess
articles_hidden.abstract: Millions of children worldwide endure forced displacement, with profound implications for their psychological well-being. This study examines how forced displacement impacts self-development (i.e., self-esteem and self-efficacy) among Syrian refugee children (N=1576; Mage=11.00; SD=2.30) and their mothers (Mage=38.28; SD=8.97), in Lebanon. Over a one-year follow-up with N=1000 children linear-mixed analyses show that a relatively well-resourced refugee environment is associated with higher self-esteem and self-efficacy cross-sectionally, but does not predict changes in self-development over time. Parenting, however, has distinct effects on self-esteem over time: maternal acceptance buffers against the adverse effects of poor refugee environments on self-esteem, whereas psychological control and abuse at home exacerbate these negative impacts. No such longitudinal effects were found for self-efficacy.

articles_hidden.title: From team rationality to morality:  Implicit joint plans carry moral force
articles_hidden.authors: Arthur Le Pargneux; Fiery Andrews Cushman; Hossam Zeitoun; Nick Chater
articles_hidden.abstract: Collaboration is essential to social life. Sometimes teams, families, companies, and other organizations agree on explicit rules governing such collaboration, and these are backed by moral force: To violate the rule is wrong. Other times, however, we find ways to collaborate on the fly, without rules or norms, or even explicit communication. This often requires inferring a joint plan — imagining “what coordination would we agree to, if we could?” — and playing our surmised role. Is it also considered morally wrong to violate an implicit or inferred joint plan? In five preregistered experiments (n = 1,506), we show that deviating from an inferred joint plan is perceived as morally problematic, even without prior communication or agreement. In other words, just as the agreements we actually make are morally binding, so too are the patterns of conduct that we infer our social partners would agree upon.

articles_hidden.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles_hidden.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 52% in 2025. Among 392 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 152 times; only 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 40% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 42% referenced a missing file — shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Trajectories of Pro-Environmental Behavior in Adolescence:  A Cross-National Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: Stathis Grapsas; Andrik Becht; Lukas Baumann; Sander Thomaes
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for the formation of sustainable lifestyles. However, evidence on the development of pro-environmental behavior in adolescence is limited and inconsistent, suggesting either an inverted U-shaped developmental dip or a developmental increase. In the present longitudinal study, we pitted against each other the dip and increase hypotheses in early to mid-adolescent samples across three countries (four annual measurements in the Netherlands, three in China and Colombia) and two behavior types (private and public sphere). We also examined the potential presence of youth subgroups with different trajectories of pro-environmental behavior and how these youth subgroups differed in levels of baseline sustainability motive-alignment (perceptions of pro-environmental behavior as granting autonomy and peer status). Findings provide a more nuanced picture than either hypothesis alone predicts. Latent growth models mostly revealed developmental stability, except for a linear increase in private behavior in Colombia. Latent class growth models revealed no subgroups in China and Colombia. In the Netherlands, these analyses revealed, for both behaviors, a subgroup of engaged youth with higher, stable levels, and a subgroup of temporarily disengaged youth showing a dip towards mid-adolescence. Baseline motive-alignment positively predicted pro-environmental behavior across waves and characterized the pro-environmentally engaged subgroups of youth. Together, these findings show relative developmental heterogeneity across youth subgroups and call for tailored interventions that align pro-environmental behavior with adolescents’ developmentally salient motives.

articles_hidden.title: Substitution, addition, or stepping-stone? Exploring the temporal associations between the consumption of alcoholic and alcohol-free beverages among Dutch university students
articles_hidden.authors: Kirsten van Hooijdonk; Lise Dams; Tirza van Noorden; Jacqueline Vink
articles_hidden.abstract: Background and aim. Stimulating the use of alcohol-free beverages is portrayed as one strategy to reduce excessive alcohol use and alcohol-related harm among students in higher education. This strategy relies on the assumption that students drink alcohol-free to substitute alcohol (i.e. “substitution effect”), while other possibilities like drinking alcohol-free in addition to alcohol (i.e. “addition effect”) or alcohol-free acting as a step-up to consume (more) alcohol (i.e. “stepping-stone” effect) have largely been neglected. Consequently, this preregistered study aimed to examine bi-directional temporal associations between the quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free use among university students (Aim 1). Next, these bi-directional temporal associations were examined in subgroups: females vs. males (Aim 2) and members vs. non-members of student associations (Aim 3). Design. Observational study, utilizing Wave 2, Wave 3, and Wave 4 of Radboud University’s Healthy Student Life study. Data were collected May-July 2022, 2023, and 2024. Setting. The Netherlands. Participants. 9,951 university students of which 6,790 students had only cross-sectional data, while 2,383 and 778 students participated in 2 and 3 surveys, respectively. At Wave 2, participants’ mean age was 23 (SD = 4.0). 70% were female, 17% were members of a student association, 13% were international students, and 57% were enrolled in a bachelor programme. Measurements. At all waves, participants self-reported the frequency and quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free beverage consumption, using two (adapted) items of the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test – Consumption (AUDIT-C). Additionally, participants self-reported on: gender, student association membership, living situation, relationship status, and other substance use. Last, information on biological sex, age, educational programme, and (inter)national status were received from the university administrative records. Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models were utilized to study reciprocal effects between the quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free use, by decomposing observed scores in between-person differences and within-person dynamics. Findings. None of the analyses, in the total sample (Aim 1; b between .02 and .03, p between .414 and .779) nor in subgroups (Aims 2-3; b between -.001 and .12, p between .192 and .988), provided support for within-person cross-lagged effects between the quantity of alcohol and alcohol-free use. Conclusions. No evidence was found for substitution or stepping-stone effects, which (indirectly) suggests that students generally drink alcohol-free as an additive to alcohol, rather than as a substitute or stepping-stone. Additional research is needed to strengthen the evidence on the effects of consuming alcohol-free beverages on alcohol use and health in general.

articles_hidden.title: Alpha Oscillations Reflect Curiosity During Information-Seeking
articles_hidden.authors: Hanna Julku; Sebastian Österman; Caitlin Dawson; Kaisa Elovaara; Jaana Simola
articles_hidden.abstract: Curiosity is a fundamental driver of information-seeking, but its electrophysiological correlates are poorly understood. To investigate how curiosity and information quality affected neural activity during information-seeking, we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants collected information in a multi-armed bandit task. Participants (N=60) read statements of varying scientific quality to decide their stance on health-related topics. After reading each statement, participants rated their state curiosity level, the usefulness and clarity of the statements, and their confidence of the usefulness rating. We also measured participants’ trait curiosity (N=53) with a questionnaire and asked whether they had searched for more information about the topics after the experiment. The EEG analyses included a cluster-based permutation analysis (N=60), which indicated two clusters where alpha power differed between information quality categories: frontal and parietal. Then, by using generalized linear mixed effects modeling (N=53), we tested whether information quality, trait and state curiosity, other statement related ratings, and thinking about or searching for more information about the topics after the laboratory experiment predicted alpha power in these clusters. A decrease in frontal alpha power was associated with an increase in state curiosity and deprivation sensitivity dimension of trait curiosity. A decrease in parietal alpha was related to an increase in deprivation sensitivity and searching for more information about the topics. These results show that lower alpha power reflects higher curiosity and the strength of cognitive engagement during information-seeking.

articles_hidden.title: Long-Term Outcomes of Childhood ADHD Stimulant Use Trajectories
articles_hidden.authors: N.E. van der Plas; Siri Noordermeer; Catharina Hartman; Pieter Hoekstra; Nanda Rommelse; Emma Sprooten; Jaap Oosterlaan; Marjolein Luman
articles_hidden.abstract: Stimulant medication is the first-line pharmacological treatment option for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, long-term effects remain unclear. Therefore, we explored long-term (>12 years) outcomes of childhood stimulant medication use, using data from the Dutch NeuroIMAGE cohort. Childhood (up to Mage=16.14, SDage=3.48) stimulant treatment trajectories were detected using K-means clustering based on age at initiation, stop age, total and maximum daily dose, and duration and variability of stimulant use in 324 children. The trajectories were compared across seven domains of adult outcomes (controlling for multiple testing) including psychiatric status, behavioral and emotional functioning, academic and professional functioning, adaptive functioning, neurocognitive functioning, physical health, and healthcare service use. At follow-up, 143 adults with childhood ADHD (Mage=28.34, SDage=3.74, 65% males) were part of three stimulant treatment trajectory groups: early-and-intense (n=46), late-and-moderate (n=63), and stimulant-naïve (n=34). The three groups did not differ on any of the 51 adult outcomes and findings did not change after controlling for age and sex, except that a significant group difference emerged for callous and unemotional traits (behavioral and emotional functioning domain). More specifically, the early-and-intense and late-and-moderate groups had more favorable scores compared to stimulant-naïve group, although this may partly reflect pre-existing group differences. The main findings did not change after controlling for ADHD medication use at wave IV. Overall, stimulant medication use in childhood did not predict long-term outcomes in those with childhood ADHD in our sample, suggesting that there may be no lasting effects of stimulants on many long-term functional outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Does treatment engagement explain symptom improvement after multimodal therapy for irritable bowel syndrome? Exploratory process analyses of the SHARK study
articles_hidden.authors: Maximilian Hinse; Harald Matthes
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Multimodal programmes combining psychoeducational, mind–body and body-oriented components improve symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), but the processes underlying improvement remain largely unknown. We examined three process variables routinely available in real-world multimodal care — treatment attendance, self-reported long-term treatment engagement, and change in anxiety and depressive symptoms — to establish what such observational data can, and cannot, reveal about mechanisms.
Methods
Secondary, exploratory analyses of the single-arm SHARK study (DRKS00016890). Adults with IBS (Rome IV) who attended at least 8 of 12 group sessions of a multimodal programme were analysed at post-treatment (n = 36) and 12-month follow-up (n = 17). Path models estimated (1) attendance and post-treatment IBS symptom severity (IBS-SSS), adjusted for baseline; (2) the association structure linking perceived effectiveness (PE), treatment engagement (TE; retrospectively reported frequency of home practice) and 12-month severity; and (3) associations between change in anxiety (GAD-7), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) and IBS-SSS. Bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 samples), multiple imputation (m = 50) and case-exclusion sensitivity analyses were used. A Monte Carlo simulation informed sample size for a planned randomised controlled trial.
Results
Attendance did not predict post-treatment severity (b = 17.6, p = .149), with variance restricted above the eight-session threshold. PE was strongly associated with TE (a = 0.54, 95% CI [0.33, 0.79], p < .001) — the only finding robust across sensitivity analyses. The exploratory indirect effect of PE on 12-month severity via TE was indistinguishable from zero (b = 47.6, 95% CI [−37.4, 157.8]) and positive in sign, i.e. towards higher severity. TE was bivariately uncorrelated with follow-up severity (r = .01) but correlated with baseline severity (r = .38); given the near-collinearity of PE and TE (r = .78), the opposing b and c’ paths formed a suppression pattern consistent with severity-driven practice rather than an engagement effect. Excluding one participant shifted the estimate to 84.5, 95% CI [7.6, 199.7], demonstrating single-case fragility at n = 17. Short-term IBS symptom change was statistically independent of concurrent change in anxiety and depressive symptoms.
Conclusions
No process variable explained symptom outcomes in this small, uncontrolled sample, and retrospective engagement ratings were empirically inseparable from perceived effectiveness and illness severity. These data do not establish mechanisms; they establish how mechanisms must be studied — with prospective, behaviour-proximal engagement measurement, baseline treatment expectancy, disorder-specific rather than generic affective mediators, stratification by psychological comorbidity, and pre-registered, simulation-powered mediation analyses within a controlled design.

articles_hidden.title: Men report lower perceived social support and a stronger association between childhood adversity and internalising problems than women in young adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Zenna Liekens; Peter Prinzie
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental health problems show marked sex/gender differences in young adulthood, with women reporting higher levels of internalising problems and men higher levels of externalising problems. Childhood adversity is one of the strongest predictors of later mental health problems, whereas social support is an important protective factor following childhood adversity. However, it remains unclear whether associations among childhood adversity, perceived social support, and internalising and externalising problems differ between men and women during young adulthood.

Using data from 331 young adults from the Flemish Study on Parenting, Personality and Development (aged 22–27 years; Mage = 24.8, 58% women), we examined whether childhood adversity was associated with internalising and externalising problems, whether these associations were moderated by social support, and whether these patterns differed by sex/gender. Next, we compared perceived social support across different support sources (friends, romantic partners, mother, father, and siblings) while again testing for sex/gender effects.  

Childhood adversity was positively associated with externalising problems and internalising problems. When adjusting for perceived social support, the positive association between childhood adversity and internalising problems was stronger for men compared to women. Social support had a main effect on internalising and externalising problems but did not moderate the association between childhood adversity and mental health outcomes. Perceived social support was highest among romantic partners, followed by friends, mothers, fathers, and siblings. Men reported lower levels of perceived social support than women across all support sources, but no significant sex/gender differences were found on cumulative childhood adversity or internalising/externalising problems. 

Together, these findings suggest lower levels of perceived social support and a stronger association between childhood adversity and internalising problems for men compared to women. Furthermore, we show that social support may function as an independent protective factor for mental health in young adulthood rather than as a buffer against the effects of childhood adversity.

articles_hidden.title: Model Checking for Vector Autoregressive Models
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Joran Jongerling; Björn S. Siepe; Sacha Epskamp; Lourens Waldorp
articles_hidden.abstract: Time series have become pervasive in psychological science, and Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models are now among the most popular tools for studying within-person dynamics in such data. However, researchers rarely check systematically how well a VAR model fits their data. This is problematic because model misfit can lead both to incorrect interpretations of model parameters and to missed structure in the data that would be theoretically interesting. We provide a tutorial that explains the theory behind model checking, discusses the most common types of VAR model misspecification in psychological time series, and introduces diagnostics for detecting them using plots and simulations. In addition, we provide code to extract predictions and residuals from popular software packages, along with the new R-package VARcheck, which allows researchers to create extensive diagnostic plots with only a few lines of code. We then apply these tools to assess the fit of a multilevel VAR model estimated on a typical empirical dataset of emotion measurements from 179 people over three weeks. We conclude by discussing three complementary ways in which model checking can advance psychological science using time series.

articles_hidden.title: When Real Danger Lowers Anxiety: A Test of Phantom Anxiety Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles_hidden.abstract:
One paradox of contemporary anxiety psychopathology is that gains in safety and quality of life do not yield proportional decreases in anxiety-related problems at the population level. This paper introduces Phantom Anxiety Theory (PAT), according to which the human anxiety system includes both a reactive component and an endogenous vigilance component. This yields a counterintuitive prediction: genuine danger may reduce anxiety-related indicators, whereas safer periods may be associated with greater search interest in anxiety-related content.
This prediction was tested by analysing 56 flood and 13 earthquake events across five highly developed countries with a combined population of 289 million. For each event, Google Trends search interest in the Topic “Anxiety” was compared in the most affected region with analogous periods one and two years earlier. 
Consistent with PAT’s differential predictions, “Anxiety” search interest declined after floods but rose after earthquakes. The two disaster types differed significantly in the direction of change, while control topics failed to replicate this pattern. These findings support the hypothesis that the human anxiety system may operate in two complementary modes and remain active without an adequate threat object. They may help explain why reductions in objective stressors do not necessarily reduce anxiety-related phenomena.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness and emotions in non-human animals: Are laypeople more or less skeptical than experts?
articles_hidden.authors: Bastian Jaeger; Stefan Leach; Matthew Zipple
articles_hidden.abstract: Consciousness and the capacity to experience affective states, such as pain, pleasure, fear, and hunger (i.e., sentience) are seen as key determinants of an individual’s moral status, a view that is shared by scientists, philosophers, and laypeople. Whether (and which) non-human animals are believed to possess these capacities can therefore have important consequences for how they are treated. In this registered report (study design registration: https://doi.org/10.71240/lcyc.238674), we measured people’s attributions of consciousness and emotions to a diverse set of animals, testing whether laypeople overattribute (as suggested by research on anthropomorphizing) or underattribute these mental capacities to animals (as suggested by research on motivated mind denial). Animal consciousness and emotions are famously challenging to study. In the absence of an unambiguous benchmark against which people’s beliefs could be compared, we tested whether laypeople, a nationally representative sample of 600 U.S. participants, are more or less skeptical about animal consciousness and emotions than scientific experts, a sample of 100 behavioral ecologists, evolutionary biologists, and other animal researchers. We find that, compared to scientific experts, laypeople were less likely to attribute consciousness (-8 percentage points), and substantially less likely to attribute emotions (-21 percentage points) to non-human animals. Laypeople were on average more confident in their beliefs than scientific experts.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Assurance: Theoretical Refinement, Scale Development, and Future Research
articles_hidden.authors: Atsuki Ito; Matthias S Gobel; Kosuke TAKEMURA
articles_hidden.abstract: Expectations that others will cooperate are critical for sustaining intragroup cooperation. Although extensive research has emphasized trust—expectations of cooperation based on others’ traits and intentions—as a strong predictor of cooperation, assurance—expectations grounded in incentive structures—has received little empirical attention. The present research aims to establish a theoretical and methodological foundation for assurance research. First, we propose that assurance can be understood as a process through which perceived incentive structure gives rise to expectations of others’ cooperation and ultimately promotes cooperation. Second, across three studies using American and Japanese samples (total N = 1,589), we developed the Perceived Assurability Scale, a reliable measure of perceived incentive structure underlying assurance and demonstrated that perceived assurability predicts workplace cooperation independently of perceived trustworthiness. Third, we propose future research directions regarding how group contexts are translated into cooperation through psychological processes captured by the concepts of trust and assurance.

articles_hidden.title: State of Social Cognition Research: Challenges, Future Directions, and Efforts Toward Consensus Building
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Bürgi; Anabela Cantiani; Beatriz Catoira; Mado Gautier; Ilenia Gori; Annika Konrad; Lara Maliske; Annabel Nijhof; Arthur Pabst; Ekaterina Pronizius
articles_hidden.abstract: Social cognition research has become a key area of cognitive science, producing a wealth of theories, methods, and empirical findings. However, the field faces significant challenges that constrain further progress and broader impact. As a group of social cognition researchers from various theoretical and methodological backgrounds, we came together to identify issues we consensually  consider  most  pressing,  highlight  their  negative  consequences,  and  suggest ways forward. We thus offer a synthesis of core issues that are typically treated separately in the literature,and  translate  them  into  a  shared  agenda  for  the  field.  Major  conceptual challenges  include  substantial  variation  in how  social  cognition  is  defined,  subdivided,  and labeled,   alongside   a   limited   understanding   of   its   basic   structure.   Methodologically, shortcomings  include  inadequate  assessment  and  reporting  of  psychometric  properties  of measurement tools. Furthermore, ecologically valid interactive paradigms are still scarce, and the clarification and experimental control over the processes underlying measurement scores remain   insufficient.   We   argue   that   progress   requires   both   humility   and   courage: acknowledging  our  field’s  theoretical  fragmentation  and  methodological  limitations,  and embracing complexity through multimethod, interactive, and computational approaches. We further introduce our community building initiative as a facilitating step toward achieving these objectives through consensus initiatives, open science practices, and large-scale collaborative research.

articles_hidden.title: Making Room for Autistic Identity: An Experimental Investigation of Self-as-Context with Autistic Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren Lawson; Olivia Corda; Miranda Mirabile; Laura Therese Broadbent; Simon Bury
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Autistic adults experience higher rates of mental health difficulties than non-autistic adults, driven in part by marginalisation, minority stress and internalised stigma. Self-as-context, a core process of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, may offer a way to loosen the grip of identity-related distress, but it has not previously been tested experimentally in an autistic sample.
Method: In a preregistered online randomised experiment, 101 UK-based autistic adults recruited via Prolific were allocated to an 8-minute self-as-context skills video or a time-matched neutral video control (final N = 93). Participants completed baseline measures, wrote about a time they felt out of place due to being autistic, viewed the intervention or control video, re-read their account, and then viewed a calming video, completing momentary state measures after each of five phases. Data were analysed using 2 (condition) × 5 (phase) mixed ANOVAs.
Results: After re-reading their account, the self-as-context condition reported significantly lower state shame than controls (Mdiff = −1.52, p = .036, ηp² = .048). The between-condition difference in state self-compassion at that point was non-significant (Mdiff = 0.34, p = .062), although the self-as-context condition scored higher immediately after the intervention (p = .046) and at the end of the study (p = .030). Significant condition × phase interactions emerged for state self-compassion, F(3.04, 276.84) = 6.14, p < .001, ηp² = .063, and state experiential avoidance, F(3.40, 309.14) = 5.22, p = .001, ηp² = .054, with the self-as-context condition reporting lower experiential avoidance from the intervention onwards (ps ≤ .010). No effects were found for state self-as-context.
Conclusions: A single brief, self-paced self-as-context exercise reduced state shame and showed promise for improving self-compassion and reducing experiential avoidance in autistic adults reflecting on identity-related distress. These first experimental data support self-as-context as a therapeutic target for this population and brief online delivery as feasible; replication with larger samples and validated self-as-context measures is needed.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Currents of Mindfulness: Tracing Mindfulness’s Use and Influence in Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Takeshi Hamamura; Min Maung; Anuradha Baminiwatta; Jun Chih; Suzanne Gilbey; Monica Gumulya; Masaru Kanetsuki; Trevor Mazzucchelli
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Mindfulness is now widely studied and applied in psychology, yet its use and adaptation in non-Western contexts remain underexplored. This study examines how mindfulness is discussed and studied within Japanese scholarly literature. 

Methods: A two-pronged approach was employed: a scoping review of English-language publications to identify prevailing research patterns (Study 1), and a topic modelling analysis of Japanese-language literature to explore themes (Study 2). 

Results: Findings from both analyses indicate that mindfulness in Japan is predominantly framed within therapeutic and wellness-oriented contexts in clinical, educational, and occupational settings. At the same time, culturally grounded adaptations were observed, including the incorporation of practices such as Naikan, Zen meditation, and martial arts, alongside thematic emphases on relational and psychosomatic processes. However, explicit engagement with cultural adaptation was relatively limited, raising questions about the extent to which local cultural contexts are informing or being overlooked in the adaptation process. 

Conclusion: As mindfulness continues to circulate globally, findings from this study highlight the need for context-sensitive approaches that engage with both global frameworks and local conceptual traditions.

articles_hidden.title: Loneliness and Perceived Cognitive Function: Evidence from a Large-Scale Daily Study
articles_hidden.authors: Martina Luchetti; Antonio Terracciano; Selin Karakose; Justin Brown; Hannah Lovett; Samia C. Akhter-Khan; Damaris Aschwanden; André Hajek; STEPHAN; Angelina Sutin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Loneliness is linked to poor cognition and dementia risk. Yet, little is known about how loneliness relates to perceptions of cognitive functioning in daily life, particularly among individuals at-risk for dementia. We examined within-person and between-person associations between daily loneliness and subjective cognition and tested moderation by cognitive status, dispositional loneliness, and sociodemographic characteristics.
Research Design and Methods: Data were from 2,540 adults aged 40 years and older (Mage= 63; 59.6% female; 32.7% with subjective cognitive decline [SCD]; 7.3% with cognitive impairment, no dementia [CIND]), who completed 8 daily assessments of loneliness, subjective cognitive functioning, forgetting, and forgetting-related irritation and interference.
Results: Participants with higher mean daily loneliness reported worse cognitive functioning and greater odds of forgetting over the study period. On days when participants felt lonelier than their average, they reported poorer cognition. Daily loneliness was not associated with forgetting on a given day but was associated with greater forgetting-related irritation and interference. While participants with SCD or CIND reported higher daily loneliness, associations did not differ by cognitive status, dispositional loneliness, or socio-demographic factors. There was limited evidence of lagged associations.
Discussion and Implications: Loneliness was negatively associated with subjective cognition between persons and within persons. Associations were consistent across normal cognition, SCD, and CIND, suggesting loneliness may be relevant to subjective cognition regardless of clinical stage. The higher daily loneliness among SCD and CIND participants underscores the need to address psychosocial well-being in efforts to promote cognitive health and support dementia prevention strategies.

articles.title: Mental Representations Beyond Survey Responses: Evidence from Gendered Wording
articles.authors: Nora Müller; Lynn-Malou Lutz; Oshrat Hochman; Lisa Hummel Jäckel
articles.abstract:
This study examines the effects of different gender formulations on respondents mental representations of the
people referred to in survey questions, responses to survey questions, and conventional indicators of questionnaire quality.
Using data from a cognitive pretest (N = 466), we compare the generic masculine that is, the use of masculine role nouns to
refer to people regardless of gender, which remains common in German surveys with a gender-inclusive formulation using the
gender colon and a gender-inclusive neutral formulation. The results show that the linguistic formulation used in survey items
significantly affects respondents mental representations of the people referred to in the survey questions. Compared with both
gender-inclusive formulations, the generic masculine leads to a substantially lower likelihood that respondents include women
in their mental representations. Although wording substantially affected respondents mental representations, responses
differed modestly but significantly across wording conditions only for the politician competence item, whereas responses to
the income question remained stable across wording conditions. Likewise, neither perceived readability nor response times
differed systematically between wording conditions. These findings suggest that relying solely on conventional indicators of
survey quality may overlook meaningful differences in the reference groups respondents have in mind when answering survey
questions, even when observable survey responses remain largely unchanged. Overall, the findings demonstrate the value of
considering respondents’ mental representations alongside conventional indicators of questionnaire quality when evaluating
alternative questionnaire formulations, as conventional survey outcomes alone may overlook meaningful cognitive differences
between wording conditions.

articles.title: Republican, Cosmopolitan, Collective, Threshold: The Political Formations of European Port Cities and Their Democratic Fate
articles.authors: Mudassar Munir
articles.abstract: Port cities across Europe are changing. The docks have been automated, fishing industries have contracted, and the working communities that once organised political and social life around maritime labour have been substantially transformed. This paper asks what these changes mean for the political and social formations that European port cities historically produced. Existing scholarship has established that European port cities constitute a distinctive urban formation, one that developed specific political and social characteristics through centuries of maritime life. The paper examines four recurring political and social formations associated with European port cities: a republican disposition, cosmopolitan pragmatism, collective risk culture, and threshold consciousness. It asks whether these formations are disappearing, taking new institutional forms, or being reworked in ways that preserve their language while changing their democratic substance. The paper focuses on European port cities within the Atlantic, North Sea, and Mediterranean maritime traditions. What is happening to these formations matters not only as a question of urban history, but also as a question of democratic life in contemporary European cities.

articles.title: It's her! Investigating relationship development with social AI chatbots
articles.authors: Nadja Rupprechter; Tobias Dienlin
articles.abstract:
As AI chatbots become integrated into various aspects of everyday life, users increasingly
form parasocial relationships with their digital companions. To understand how such relationships
emerge, we examined how perceived human-likeness fosters parasocial attachment to AI
chatbots. We test a relationship process model in which human-likeness—conceptualized as a
meta-factor comprising anthropomorphism, authenticity, and social presence—promotes
parasocial attachment via user gratifications and interaction behavior. In a preregistered survey of
598 chatbot users from 64 countries, structural equation modeling showed that perceived humanlikeness
was a strong predictor of parasocial attachment. As predicted, this effect was partially
mediated by increased gratifications and interaction. Additional qualitative responses illustrated
how chatbots provide emotional support, role-play, and productivity benefits, alongside concerns
about dependence, social withdrawal, inappropriate behavior, and privacy. Together, the findings
identify human-likeness, gratifications, and interaction as central drivers of parasocial attachment
to AI chatbots.

articles.title: High Agreement, Different Stories: How LLM Classifiers Reshape Demographic Patterns in Survey Data
articles.authors: Chris Soria
articles.abstract: What we learn from open-ended survey data depends on who—or what—does the coding. Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to democratize qualitative analysis, but do high agreement rates translate into equivalent thematic findings? This study compares eight LLMs to human annotators on a multi-label coding task using 3,200 responses from the UC Berkeley Social Networks Study, comprising over 19,000 coding decisions. Although LLM-human reliability does not match human-human reliability overall, LLMs approach human performance on simpler tasks and can serve as useful additional coders for generating consensus labels. Compared to a gold-standard human consensus, models achieve 82–97% per-category agreement, but macro F1 is lower and response-level similarity is lower still: even the best model reproduces the full human label set for fewer than 60% of responses. Yet high agreement masks thematic divergence. Models systematically over-identify themes, assigning 66% more categories per response, especially for categories requiring greater interpretive judgment. Models also show lower agreement for some demographic groups. These gaps are partly explained by response characteristics such as length, clarity, and atypicality, but the main driver is over-classification itself: models add false positives at a nearly constant rate, so groups whose answers carry fewer themes lose the most precision. At the sample level, models largely preserve the overall thematic narrative: human and model category rankings correlate strongly (pooled Spearman's ρ=0.75), and top-performing models achieve approximately 80% directional agreement on demographic patterns. Concrete behavioral questions, such as reasons for moving or strategies for making friends, show especially strong alignment. Yet systematic over-classification can still shift narratives about how specific groups behave, leading researchers to report patterns that the human gold standard does not support.

articles.title: Cloud Capital's Hidden Thirst: Scope 2 Water and the Geography of US Data Center Electricity
articles.authors: Atoshi Golder
articles.abstract: Data center operators report water use as a facility-level question, disclosing on-site metrics while omitting the water consumed in generating the electricity they purchase — their Scope 2 water footprint. This paper quantifies that omission at the eGRID-subregion level and traces its consequences for a standardized data center load. Comparing EPA eGRID 2018 against eGRID 2023 on an identical pipeline, I find that generation-weighted national water intensity fell 17.1% over the five years in which data center electricity demand accelerated, but that the decline was uneven: several subregions gaining generation share fell more slowly than the national average, and SERC Virginia/Carolina — host to the largest data center market in the world by inventory — fell only 7.7%, less than half the national pace. Combining eGRID generation data with consumption-basis water coefficients, I estimate a total of 1,350.6 billion gallons of operational water consumption embedded in contiguous-US electricity generation across all end uses in 2023, and show that an identical data center's embedded footprint varies approximately 3.2-fold by grid region under common technology-factor assumptions. I then construct a Water Dependency Index and adjust it by a territorial water-scarcity score built from the World Resources Institute's Aqueduct basin indicators, on the principle that identical consumption imposes different costs depending on where it occurs; the adjusted index ranks SERC Virginia/Carolina first in the nation. No widely adopted disclosure framework requires standardized, location-based reporting of electricity-embedded water. The paper proposes extending location-based Scope 2 carbon accounting, which is structurally analogous, to water.

articles.title: Improving Efficiency in Egocentric Network Surveys: A Reproducible Qualtrics Template from Design to Analysis
articles.authors: Ruizhe Liu; Mark Girson; Christopher McCarty; Eleonora Rossi
articles.abstract: How can researchers collect social network data in the field and laboratory settings without imposing excessive technical or logistical burdens? This work presents an improved and reproducible approach for collecting ego network data with alter–alter ties using Qualtrics and for preparing the resulting data for network analysis. By leveraging built-in functions of Qualtrics, this approach reduces the effort required to construct and administer large sets of alter attributes and alter–alter tie questions. An offline pilot dataset demonstrates that the instrument functions reliably in low-connectivity environments, and an accompanying data-processing workflow converts Qualtrics exports into network data suitable for analysis in R. Together, this approach lowers barriers to field-, and lab- based social network data collection, mitigates limitations associated with limited programming background and unfamiliar network software, and supports more consistent integration of network measures into broader survey-based research across disciplines.

articles.title: Theory of Carried Gaps in an Organizational Transformation
articles.authors: Jérôme Mendoza-Trussart
articles.abstract:
Organizational transformations are generally analyzed through change strategies, support mechanisms, resistance, or adaptation capacities. These approaches remain essential, but they sometimes leave a decisive question in the background: what happens to the gap between what the transformation requires and what the organization actually makes possible?

The Theory of Carried Gaps proposes that organizational gaps do not disappear when they are not addressed by the system. They can be displaced, absorbed, compensated for, and ultimately carried by individuals or collectives. Managers, experts, committed teams, or key actors then provide, often without an explicit mandate or proportionate recognition, the regulation necessary for continuity of activity.

The central contribution of the theory is to shift the focus: rather than considering only the difficulty experienced by an individual, it becomes possible to ask which organizational gap is being carried so that the system can continue to function. The managerial action then consists in making these gaps and their carrying mechanisms visible, enabling the organization to take back what it has left to individuals.

articles.title: “When I Turned 18, It All Ended”: Age Control, Migration Regimes and Radical Social Work
articles.authors: Nikoleta Gerontaki; Dimitra - Dora Teloni
articles.abstract:
* This is a post-peer-review, pre-copy edited version of an article published in Critical and Radical Social Work. The definitive publisher-authenticated version is available online at: Critical and Radical Social Work Journal https://doi.org/10.1332/20498608Y2026D000000141

What are the experiences of former unaccompanied minors in Greece in the process of transitioning to adulthood, what rights are infringed in the process, and how do their voices resist to silence and exclusion? Drawing on qualitative research conducted in 2024 with 10 young refugees, aged 18-22 years, based on semi-structured interviews analysed through thematic analysis, the article focuses on experiences of rights and social services from the perspective of radical social work. Findings demonstrate that the process of becoming an adult is frequently followed by loss of the basic services, which leaves dangerous conditions of living and infringement of the rights to housing, healthcare, education, and legal assistance. The participants' reflections on the policies in place show regret and gratitude for low levels of assistance, highlighting logics of deserving and undeserving care. Rights as a privilege at 18 years old become more akin to a right than an entitlement.

articles.title: Advancing open research information: exploring the persistence of proprietary bibliographic databases
articles.authors: Tanya Lee; Kathleen Gregory; Alexander Rushforth
articles.abstract:
Purpose – “Research information”, which informs how research is searched,
conducted, monitored, and evaluated, is usually made available in proprietary
databases in ways which often restrict its use. Recently, there has been a movement
towards opening research information through the creation of systems such as
OpenAlex, but their adoption remains inconsistent. In this study, we explore challenges
which university stakeholders face in switching from proprietary to open databases for
research information.

Design/methodology/approach – We conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with
university stakeholders in the Netherlands, a particularly proactive environment in the
Open Research Information movement. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic
analysis and informed by literature in platform capitalism and infrastructure studies.

Findings – The analysis shows that even in seemingly progressive environments,
systemic change remains challenging. Longstanding routines, technical dependencies,
and embedded practices present challenges for universities to disengage from
proprietary databases and their complementary services. Concerns about the viability
and further development of open databases became apparent through the context of
collective action dilemmas perceived by interviewees. Importantly, we find that platform
capitalism, a framework often employed in analyzing proprietary companies, is not
sufficient to explain these hesitancies. 

Originality/Value – Our findings highlight the challenges faced in an under-researched
area of open science: the adoption of open research information. Our study is relevant
to open science advocates and for institutions struggling with similar challenges. Our
analysis makes a conceptual contribution through treating claims about the platform
dominance of proprietary databases as empirical questions and highlighting the
importance of stakeholder agency, contingency and variation.

articles.title: Gambling Industry Political Engagement, 2020–2026: A Proof-of-Concept for Auditing of Political Transparency Data using a GPT-assisted Pipeline.
articles.authors: James Close
articles.abstract:
Background: Commercial political activity is increasingly recognised within the broader framework of commercial determinants of health. However, UK gambling-related political engagement is fragmented across separate transparency systems. This study examined whether a GPT-assisted, independently reconciled workflow could integrate these records and provide a more complete picture of disclosed political activity.
Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted of UK gambling-related political engagement from 1 January 2020 to 25 August 2026 across three streams: (1) Electoral Commission political donations; (2) MPs’ declared hospitality/gifts and funded visits; and (3) ministerial meetings within the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport / Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). GPT was used to retrieve, structure, link and classify records against a reference frame of gambling organisations, which was derived from multiple public sources, including Gambling Commission registers, Companies House records, company and trade-body information, and historical ownership and corporate-relationship evidence. After classification, each of the three streams underwent an independent GPT reconciliation pass, followed by bounded human adjudication of unresolved cases. A final audit compared the final donations and hospitality datasets with previous UK journalism and civil-society reporting.
Results: The principal analysis identified 127 donations with confirmed active commercial gambling connections, worth £7.73 million, from donors with a confirmed material commercial gambling connection active on the donation date. Of this value, 85.4% went to the Conservative political family and 13.0% to Reform UK. MPs declared 176 qualifying hospitality/gift events involving 71 MPs, worth £236,162, plus four funded visits. The ministerial-meeting census contained 272 gambling-related events, of which 86 involved principal commercial-industry actors. Across the 138-group company universe, meeting frequency was positively associated with both donation frequency (Spearman ρ=.390; p=.00004) and hospitality frequency (ρ=.487; p=.00001), although these associations are observational and non-causal. In the final audit against previously reported figures, 291 of the observed donation/hospitality records had no apparent or obvious match in the prior-reporting examined; and one genuine omission in this analysis was identified and corrected (related to hospitality). 
Conclusions: Systematic linkage across transparency systems revealed a scale and pattern of gambling-connected political activity that is not apparent from individual registers or prior headline reporting. GPT made this integration tractable, but independent reconciliation and human adjudication were essential. Integrated monitoring of political activity may therefore be important for understanding the commercial determinants of health in gambling and other harmful commodity industries.

articles.title: Produção científica de um programa de educação ambiental no licenciamento federal: Análise bibliométrica do PEAPescarte
articles.authors: Vitor de Moraes Peixoto
articles.abstract:
O licenciamento ambiental federal obriga as operadoras de petróleo a financiar programas de educação ambiental, executados por universidades públicas ao longo de mais de uma década. Avalia-se o efeito socioambiental desses programas; não se mede o conhecimento que eles deixam. Este artigo faz esse levantamento para o PEA-Pescarte por revisão sistemática PRISMA 2020, que reúne acervo
institucional, auditoria de planilha e busca em três bases: 356 obras em 382 registros de 284 autores, descritas por cinco redes. A colaboração se organiza pelo pertencimento ao programa, não pelo organograma de pesquisa, e se concentra num articulador. A citação interna só se torna visível na leitura dos textos completos. O corpus, as redes e o protocolo ficam públicos em https://pescarte-acervo-7402cb.gitlab.io, produto deste artigo. Este artigo é resultado de pesquisa financiada pelo Projeto de Educação Ambiental (PEA) Pescarte que é uma medida de mitigação exigida pelo Licenciamento Ambiental Federal, conduzido pelo IBAMA.

articles.title: Dimensions of Division: Structuring Ideological Polarization During Poland’s Democratic Backsliding
articles.authors: Marta Kołczyńska; Maciej Sychowiec; Oliwia Szczupska
articles.abstract: Research on democratic backsliding increasingly views mass polarization as a mechanism that facilitates democratic erosion. This study examines trajectories of ideological polarization in Poland between 1997 and 2023, a period encompassing democratic backsliding whose onset is typically dated to 2015. Using repeated issue-based questions from the Polish National Election Study (POLNES), we distinguish three aspects of polarization: radicalization of individuals’ positions on single issues, issue alignment (system-level correlation of issue positions across different domains), and issue partisanship (the extent to which issue positions are explained by party preferences). We find no evidence of increased single-issue radicalization over the studied period. By contrast, both issue alignment and issue partisanship increased, particularly on socio-cultural issues, with little change on economic issues. These trends are not linear: they emerge around the 2011 election and persist thereafter. This pattern is  consistent with theories that view changes in mass polarization as facilitating conditions for democratic backsliding. Additionally, our findings highlight the heterogeneous nature of polarization and show that focusing on single issues or unidimensional ideological scales can obscure important changes in the structure of mass belief systems.

articles.title: Influence of Media Modality on Language Learning
articles.authors: Claire Wu
articles.abstract: This paper seeks to examine which form of television media, anime or live action, best aids Japanese language acquisition in English speakers. While this study focuses on the Japanese language, the literature review covers similar studies on the effect of media exposure on English, Korean, and Turkish vocabulary acquisition. In this study, participants were randomly sorted into two groups, an anime viewing group and a live-action viewing group, and were given Japanese vocabulary words to translate both before and after a media exposure phase. Participants in the live-action group gained more vocabulary words on average compared to participants in the anime group. Animated TV allows students to learn at their individual skill level and may better benefit beginner language learners since it often includes more frequent words in the lexicon. On the other hand, the higher language complexity in live-action TV makes it more suited towards intermediate language learners. This study demonstrates that L2 (target language) television, particularly live-acted L2 television, is an effective tool for vocabulary acquisition and reinforcement. In language learning environments, students could benefit from L2 television consumption to aid and accelerate L2 language acquisition.

articles.title: Adaptive Solutions: An interdisciplinary Study of Human and  Organizational Adaptation during the Covid-19 Pandemic.
articles.authors: Claudia Hölter
articles.abstract:
This exploratory qualitative study examines how professionals and organizational leaders connected to the Brazilian pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors experienced and responded to adaptive challenges arising from organizational disruption during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study adopts an interdisciplinary perspective at the intersection of Business, Organizational Psychology, and Organizational Studies, conceptualizing adaptation as a process involving both organizational responses and changes in human behavior, relationships, expectations, and established ways of working.
The study combines a focused literature review with six semi-structured interviews conducted between July and September 2022 with professionals working across pharmaceutical/medical affairs, commercial operations, human resources, marketing and sales, information technology, and Agile transformation.
