The analysis was organized around five interconnected domains: leadership, Agile management, Agile HR management, performance management, and knowledge management. Particular attention was given to the distinction between technical challenges, which can be addressed through existing expertise and established procedures, and adaptive challenges, which may require changes in behaviors, assumptions, relationships, and patterns of interaction.
The findings indicate that organizational disruption exposed limitations that could not always be addressed through technological or procedural interventions alone. Participants described changes in work structures, stakeholder relationships, leadership practices, collaboration, prioritization, communication, and employee support. Agile practices were described as one mechanism for enabling shorter learning cycles, greater collaboration, distributed decision-making, and adaptation to changing stakeholder needs. At the same time, the interviews suggest that Agile practices were more meaningful when accompanied by attention to people, relationships, communication, leadership, and the capacity to reconsider established ways of working.
The study contributes to interdisciplinary research on human and organizational adaptation by connecting external disruption with individual and collective responses within organizational settings. Rather than presenting Agile management as an independent solution, the findings suggest that adaptive capacity emerges through the interaction of human behavior, leadership, organizational practices, knowledge processes, and changing environmental demands. The study offers exploratory implications for organizational psychology, organizational behavior, leadership, human resource management, and organizational change research.
Keywords: human adaptation; organizational adaptation; adaptive challenges; organizational change; organizational psychology; leadership; Agile management; knowledge work; pharmaceutical industry; COVID-19.

articles.title: AUKUS: Public Opinions
articles.authors: kerry liu
articles.abstract: This study examines the AUKUS security partnership, established in September 2021, with a focus on public opinion and its relation to national policy in Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Using weekly Google Trends data from September 2021 to July 2025, the research identifies differences in public attention and the key drivers shaping perceptions of AUKUS. Australians emphasise costs and uncertainties; the British prioritise economic opportunities and diplomatic influence; and Americans focus on strategic considerations. China-related factors—particularly the perceived China Threat—play a central role in shaping public sentiment in Australia and the United States, whereas in the United Kingdom, a combination of China influence, employment concerns, and the Global Britain agenda drives attention. The study also considers policy implications, finding a strong alignment between public opinion and government policy across the three countries. While the core AUKUS narrative centres on the UK, the United Kingdom may also play a leading role in setting the policy agenda. These findings demonstrate the utility of time-series digital data for assessing public perceptions and offer a novel approach for understanding the interaction between public sentiment and foreign policy.

articles.title: Responsible AI Risk Governance in Public Service Organizations—Insights from a Meta-Synthesis
articles.authors: Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller; Menno J. Hoppen; Gjalt De Graaf
articles.abstract: The use of AI in public service provision can reshape citizen-state interactions, introducing new risks and challenges to ensure safe, inclusive, and just applications that do not discriminate against vulnerable citizens. This study examines how public service organizations govern these risks. Drawing on a meta-synthesis of AI risk governance scholarship (n=56), we synthesize the empirical evidence from a value-based risk governance perspective. We identify four governance challenges: (1) establishing substantive pre-assessment before adoption; (2) enabling informed, plural, and revisable appraisal; (3) ensuring meaningful human oversight during implementation; and (4) preserving organizational ownership in ensuring that monitoring and feedback are connected to correction and learning. For each challenge, the synthesis identifies failure patterns and proposes solutions on how to avoid them. Integrating these findings, we develop a novel evidence-based AI risk governance framework for public organizations. Advancing the discourse on technology risk governance and administrative burden in the age of AI, this study provides an organizational explanation for AI risk governance success and failure, offering insights for theory and practice.

articles.title: Weathering the Crisis:  How American Insurers Planned for Climate Change, 2012-2023
articles.authors: Edoardo Di Vincenzo; Daniel Hirschman
articles.abstract: How did the American insurance industry respond to the growing threat of climate change? We show that insurers were confident in their ability to quantify increased climate risks and either raise rates or exit risky geographies and thus maintain profitability. This strategy was plausible given the short term of property insurance contracts: homeowners might have 30-year mortgages, but home insurance contracts are typically one year. At the same time, insurers continued to underwrite and invest in fossil fuel companies and engaged very little with climate policy. This analysis extends prior research on the “tragedy of the horizon” in the relationship between finance and climate change and contrasts with predictions that insurers should be natural supporters of climate change policy.

articles.title: Officials Hedge, Public Doubts: The Certainty Gap in China's AI-Education Discourse (2020–2026)
articles.authors: Danchen Xu
articles.abstract: Chinese universities have launched a wave of “AI+X” programs that train students in professional domains—architecture, journalism, accounting, teaching—to use generative AI tools, often before any consensus exists that AI-assisted learning improves educational outcomes. Empirical research to date finds no reliable improvement in grades, documents cognitive offloading, and leaves long-term learning effects unmeasured. This paper asks whether that disconnect between institutional acceleration and empirical uncertainty surfaces in discourse: do official and public articulations of AI’s role in education differ in epistemic certainty, and is any such gap innate or emergent? We construct two corpora spanning 2020–2026—official discourse (policy documents and official-media posts, n = 691) and public discourse (Weibo, n = 11,345)—and measure four dimensions of epistemic stance (certainty markers, presupposition, hedging, and tolerance of uncertainty) using a hybrid design that pairs a transparent dictionary with LLM zero-shot coding, cross-validated at a mean Cohen's κ of .926. Three findings stand out. First, before ChatGPT the two corpora were epistemically indistinguishable, replicating Zeng, Chan, and Schäfer’s (2020) “striking similarity”; the gap emerged only after 2023. Second, the gap is not unidirectional: official discourse presupposes AI’s value more (D2 = 82.8% vs. 77.2%; policy documents 90.7%) yet hedges and acknowledges uncertainty significantly more than the public does (D3 and D4 reversed)—a pattern we term institutional hedging. Third, public epistemic stance is bimodal (absolute assertion or absolute doubt), whereas official discourse is layered across premise and expression. Time-series and difference-in-differences analyses locate two shocks—ChatGPT (2023) broke the stance layer (public D2 fell from 82% to 52%), and DeepSeek-R1 (2025) deepened the expression layer (D3 reached its series maximum)—suggesting the public underwent an epistemic learning process, first learning to doubt and then to qualify. We contribute a measurable, multidimensional discourse variable for the certainty gap and a hybrid coding template for large-scale epistemic-stance annotation.

articles.title: Partisan disparities in the production and uptake of science
articles.authors: Alexander C Furnas; Jian Gao; Yian Yin; Dashun Wang
articles.abstract: Scientific institutions are designed to produce and evaluate claims through shared evidentiary and disciplinary standards, yet they are embedded in an increasingly polarized society. This fundamental tension raises the question of whether scientists’ partisan alignment is associated with the production, circulation, and uptake of scientific knowledge. Here we integrate campaign-finance records, faculty rosters, voter-registration data, an original survey of approximately 7,000 active U.S. scientists, bibliometric data, and measures of uptake in policy documents, patents, and news coverage to map the partisan composition of the scientific workforce, the knowledge it produces, and its uptake within and beyond science. We find that U.S. science is politically asymmetric without being ideologically homogeneous: scientists who make political contributions are overwhelmingly Democratic-aligned, and this asymmetry has widened over time, yet the broader workforce includes many Independents and substantial ideological heterogeneity within partisan groups. Among scientists with strong, behaviorally observed partisan alignments, Democratic- and Republican-authored papers are systematically distinguishable in semantic content across all fields, even after conditioning on fine-grained topic and year. Differences in total scientific citation rates are modest and have narrowed over time, whereas citations occur more often within the same partisan author communities than expected under topic- and year-preserving null models. Uptake beyond science also varies by partisan authorship and domain, with the clearest directional selectivity among ideological think tanks. These findings reveal an uneven profile of partisan association across U.S. science, visible in published content and directional attention, but comparatively limited in aggregate scientific recognition. This profile is consistent with a scientific system in which shared evaluative standards coexist with political structure in the production and circulation of knowledge, with implications for science’s capacity to remain a common evidentiary resource in a polarized society.

articles.title: Where Can Older Workers Go? Regional Restructuring and Occupational Opportunity
articles.authors: Sebastian Hanika; Chiara Natalie Focacci
articles.abstract: This paper examines how occupational restructuring within local labour markets shapes the employment opportunities of older workers. Using longitudinal Swedish register data covering workers across 69 functional local labour markets between 2017 and 2023, we show that greater occupational restructuring is associated with greater occupational narrowing among older workers. This relationship is moderated by local labour market characteristics. Thicker and more dynamic labour markets, with greater occupational diversity and job churning, provide broader opportunities for occupational adjustment. The findings highlight the importance of regional opportunity structures for old-age employment in ageing economies.

articles.title: What Survives Multilingual Competition? Ecology-Dependent Selection in World Englishes and Heritage Grammars
articles.authors: Kunmei HAN
articles.abstract: World Englishes and heritage languages both develop under multilingual conditions. One is usually studied through community-level contact-variety stabilization, the other through individual bilingual restructuring. It remains unclear whether the same feature-level pressures predict outcomes across these two ecologies. This exploratory study tests a simple selection model in which perceptual salience, contextual frequency, form–meaning transparency, cross-linguistic congruence, and regularity are expected to favor the survival or expansion of a variant. A manually audited pilot dataset contains 24 world English/contact outcomes and 21 heritage-language outcomes. Contact outcomes are coded from eWAVE; heritage outcomes are traced to primary experimental or corpus studies. Ordered-logit models provide no robust evidence for a general salience advantage. The results suggest that a shared feature-pool selection framework of multilingual restructuring may be conditioned by ecology. For world Englishes, the findings point to a stabilization logic in which recoverability, structural support, source availability, and repeated community use can outweigh raw perceptual prominence.

articles.title: To adopt or not to adopt? Moving beyond a binary conceptualization of farmer’s adoption decisions
articles.authors: Emma Chris Luka Windey; Tina Venema; Agnes van den Pol-van Dasselaar; Hens Runhaar
articles.abstract: Sustainable Farming literature often frames adoption as a binary choice, overlooking decision-making complexity. Drawing on innovation studies, this paper introduces a framework for analyzing adoption decision processes. We examined two types of species-rich grasslands (SRG) as case studies, covering the following decision stages: persuasion, decision, rejection, implementation, confirmation, and discontinuation. We conducted a survey among Dutch dairy farmers (n = 91) and assessed their current decision stage, drivers and barriers to SRG adoption, and farm characteristics. Results indicated that farm characteristics differed across decision stages in nature conservation collective membership for extensive-SRG (E-SRG), but did not differ significantly far any other characteristics for E-SRG, or for any characteristics in the adoption of productive-SRG (P-SRG). For E-SRG, significant differences emerged across stages for several drivers, but not barriers; rejectors stood out most distinctly. For P-SRG, both drivers and barriers varied significantly across stages. Drivers differed most between rejectors and recent implementers, while the confirmation stage was most distinct for barriers. These findings advance theory by showing the value of distinguishing decision stages in the adoption process. Practically, identifying farmer’ current decision stage can guide more efficient policy mixes, enabling targeted interventions that calibrate policy effort to actual needs.

articles.title: Anonymity In Contemporary Political Discourse: Implications of Citizenship And State
articles.authors: Abhay Pratap Singh Tomar
articles.abstract: This paper makes an attempt in bringing anonymity into contemporary political discourse as the issue is getting entangled in political debates more and more which is situated in the debate on anonymity that went on in the house of commons of UK parliament. Hitherto the state has enjoyed the monopoly over space but this paper suggests the rise of the internet and decentralised system databases creates cyberspace which defies the monopoly of state power. Further, it explores the implications for the state, citizenship and anonymity.

articles.title: Urban veg*ns and rural grillmasters? Local context has a moderate effect on meat consumption
articles.authors: Bram van Vulpen; Willem Rogier Boterman
articles.abstract: This paper deepens the role of what we call ‘local geographies of meat consumption’. The countryside is stereotypically portrayed as a conservative bastion with traditional, meat-centric meals on the table, while urban centres are viewed as progressive hotspots for vegetarians and vegans (veg*ns). Drawing on georeferenced survey data, we demonstrate with a multilevel regression analysis how local community is associated with meat-related diets in the Netherlands. This paper shows the relevance of going beyond the conventional urban-rural constellation, by incorporating a broader and more varied set of local context factors, including political culture, agriculture and food environment. In doing so, we account for individual characteristics such as gender, age, education, and political attitudes. The results show that there are local context effects, albeit to a modest degree. Individual characteristics, most prominently gender, are more strongly associated with veg*n diets. Nevertheless, independent of individual background, people living in highly progressive communities are more likely to follow a flexitarian diet, while those in areas with strong populist radical right support or intensive animal agriculture are more likely to be meat eaters. Our results suggest that the political and agricultural context of local community significantly influences the choice for meat-related diets, rather than urban-rural settings alone.

articles.title: Varieties of democratic vulnerability: a comparative study of checks and balances and popular acceptance of transgressions
articles.authors: Honorata Mazepus; Magnus Feldmann; Giovanni D'Agostino
articles.abstract:
The recent wave of democratic backsliding has demonstrated that liberal democracies are vulnerable to subversion by authoritarian leaders. Research showed that democratically elected leaders remove checks and balances that constrain their power. One of the explanations why leaders can violate democratic rules focuses on the response of citizens who trade off democracy for partisan and policy gains. This article investigates cross-country differences in vulnerabilities to democratic backsliding by comparing democratic priority profiles of citizens and the patterns of approval for transgressions of democratic rules. 
We use observational evidence from online surveys with large quota-based samples of citizens in a two-party presidential system (USA, N > 1700), a multi-party parliamentary system based on proportional representation with some semi-presidential features (Poland, N >1800), and a consociational parliamentary system based on proportional representation (Netherlands, N = > 2100). To complement observational evidence, we test experimentally some of these aggregate-level differences: next to partisanship and policy gains, we also manipulate different democratic transgressions (protest rights and decree powers) and measure their effects on government approval in the three countries. 
Our results show that citizens of different countries have different democratic priority profiles and differ in their disapproval of specific transgressions. Although overall transgressions are not rewarded, and citizens are mostly vigilant and disapproving of violating democratic rules, we find both observational and experimental evidence indicating that liberal democracies can have different vulnerabilities that relate to the democratic attitudes of citizens.

articles.title: Fossil-Fuel Plant Retirement Disputes and Grid Reliability During the Energy Transition: Evidence from Eddystone and J.H. Campbell
articles.authors: Peter C. Baker
articles.abstract: Recent fossil-fuel plant retirement disputes show how difficult it can be to maintain grid reliability while the energy grid is undergoing so many changes. This paper focuses on two plant retirement disputes, the Eddystone/PJM and J.H. Campbell/MISO cases, and analyzes the policies associated with maintaining grid reliability during the energy transition.  Throughout the analysis, it becomes evident that there is more to the conflict than a simple tradeoff between reliability and decarbonization.  There is a coordination problem between many governing organizations. Plant owners, state regulators, regional grid operators, FERC, NERC, and DOE all have different responsibilities, and their decisions do not always line up. A plant owner may decide that a facility is no longer economical while another institution later argues that it is still needed for reliability. Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act gives DOE the authority to prevent plant closures that are deemed necessary for reliability, regardless of the economics involving the plant.  However, this paper argues that authority should remain a temporary response to a specific reliability problem. If DOE keeps a plant operating, it should be able to show why that plant is needed, who will pay for it, and what has to happen before it can finally retire. The Eddystone and Campbell cases suggest that repeated emergency orders are not just a reliability issue. They are also evidence that retirement decisions and replacement resources are not being coordinated well enough.

articles.title: The Down Low Among Latino Men Who Have Sex With Men: A Review and Theoretical Analysis
articles.authors: Keith Robert Head
articles.abstract: Being on the "down low" (DL) describes men who identify as straight and secretly engage in same-sex encounters while maintaining heterosexual public identities. While the DL phenomenon has been discussed primarily in the context of African American men, Latino men in the United States experience similar patterns of sexual concealment shaped by cultural forces not experienced similarly by other groups. Relatively little is still known about how machismo, familismo, and religious values affect the sexual decisions and health outcomes of Latino men who have sex with men (MSM), and most existing research aggregates Latino MSM with other racial and ethnic minorities without examining their experiences separately. This article applies three theoretical frameworks to the DL among Latino men. The concealment-specific model is used to explore how the act of hiding same-sex behavior produces anxiety, depression, and ongoing self-monitoring, particularly within cultural settings where discovery threatens masculine standing and family belonging. Sexual configuration theory is used to examine why Western categories of gay and bisexual do not fit the way many Latino men understand their own sexuality, especially in cultural contexts where sexual role rather than partner gender defines sexual identity. Syndemic theory is used to examine how conditions such as homophobia, HIV stigma, substance use, poverty, and immigration status interact to worsen health outcomes for this population. The findings of this analysis suggest that DL behavior among Latino men is shaped by the interaction of cultural, psychological, and structural conditions and cannot be understood through any single framework alone. Applied in combination, these theories explain DL behavior among Latino men more fully than established Western approaches. This article is intended to support future empirical research and the development of culturally informed interventions for Latino MSM.

articles.title: Cognitive Expectations of Homophily in Village Social Networks
articles.authors: Eric Martin Feltham; Nicholas Christakis
articles.abstract:
Homophily, the tendency for individuals to associate with similar others, has long been
treated as a central principle of social organization. Yet people may overestimate its
importance in reasoning about their social networks. Here, we investigate individuals’
cognitive expectations of homophily and compare these expectations to actual homophily
among 10,072 adults in 82 isolated Honduras villages. We elicited subjects’ beliefs about
whether pairs of people in their village social networks were socially tied. We show that
people deploy cognitive heuristics that substantially overestimate homophily, including
based on wealth, ethnicity, gender, and religion. We also find that people exploit network
structure when predicting ties between others, independent of expectations about
homophily. Understanding cognitive homophily has implications for models of network
formation, interventions targeting social behavior and information diffusion, and the
maintenance of social inequality.

articles.title: The Retreat from Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: Language Change on Large U.S. Foundation Websites, 2019–2025
articles.authors: Chad M. Topaz; Benham Cobb; Frances Lu; Aniya Smith; Nathan Zekarias
articles.abstract: Following the murder of George Floyd in 2020, many U.S. organizations, including large private foundations, publicly foregrounded language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Beginning in 2023, a series of legal and political developments shifted the institutional environment: the Supreme Court’s ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), state-level anti-DEI legislation, and Executive Order 14151 (2025). Using the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, we construct a longitudinal corpus of archived web pages from thirteen large U.S. private foundations with established DEI vocabulary and track the frequency of sixty-seven DEI-related terms from 2019 to 2025. Among eight foundations with paired 2023 and 2025 data, six reduced their DEI word intensity; most terms present in the paired corpus declined, with race-related terms contributing the largest share of the drop. The aggregate decline on the full sixty-seven-term index is marginal (exact Wilcoxon p = .074, one-sided); evidence is stronger on the dictionary’s definitional core, the diversity-equity-inclusion triad and its variants (p = .031). The decline concentrates in the 2024–2025 window containing the January 2025 executive orders: eight of nine foundations fell (p = .020), with scattered movement earlier. Qualitative comparison of archived pages illustrates three pathways of retreat: elimination of equity framing, substitution of technical for justice-oriented vocabulary, and reduced prominence through site redesign. These patterns suggest institutional isomorphism operating in reverse—convergent abandonment amid shared political pressure—though our descriptive design cannot identify the mechanism. The findings establish an empirical baseline for tracking organizational communication about equity under political pressure.

articles.title: Digital Influencers, Gambling Perceptions, Behavior and Harm: What Do We Know? A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Anass El Mokhtari
articles.abstract:
Background: Digital influencers (DIs), including celebrities, social media influencers, tipsters, and gambling livestreamers, have become a prominent vehicle for online gambling promotion. This scoping review mapped the empirical evidence on how DI gambling content relates to gambling perceptions, behavior, and harm, with attention to livestreams and to groups at heightened vulnerability.

Methods: Guided by JBI methodology and reported following PRISMA-ScR, four databases and Google Scholar were searched for primary empirical studies published in English or Dutch between January 2016 and June 2026.

Results: Ten studies were included, all published since 2021, five quantitative and five qualitative, with seven conducted in Spain or Australia. DI content was widely perceived to increase the appeal and social acceptability of gambling, and tipster content was further linked to beliefs about skill and control. Evidence on behavior was more limited and largely self-reported. Only three studies applied validated harm instruments on outcomes, and only two addressed livestreams. Reported vulnerability concentrated in adolescents, women, and higher-risk gamblers, but followed largely from the populations sampled.

Conclusions: The evidence is concentrated on perceptions, limited for behavior and thin for gambling harm. All studies were observational, so selection and reverse causation cannot be excluded. Prospective research is needed for further insights, particularly on livestreams.

articles.title: Operating Model or Financial Structure? Profitability in Italian SMEs
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles.abstract: Research on small-firm profitability has organised itself around capital structure, leaving the operating model largely unexamined. This paper places both in one specification and estimates it three times — by panel methods, unsupervised partitioning and machine-learning regression — on 14,913 Italian firms observed between 2014 and 2025 across three regulatory regimes. Three findings emerge. The operating model dominates: the labour share of value added is stable across specifications, invariant across four clusters recovered from accounting data alone, and carries most of the out-of-sample predictive content. The capitalisation coefficient is not identified, changing sign across specifications; instrument failure traces to profit persistence. And the structure of profitability determination differs across the three populations, contradicting the common-mechanism premise underlying certification schemes.

articles.title: When the Diagnosis Breaks the Home: Paternal Abandonment and Maternal Endurance in Families of Children with Disabilities in Bangladesh
articles.authors: Syed Jabir Hossain
articles.abstract: In Bangladesh, literature shows that a child with a disability is considered to profoundly reorient family life around the mother, who becomes the primary and often only caregiver. A smaller but growing body of research has also documented the financial hardship, institutional barriers, and religiously-inflected stigma that already accompany this caregiving role. An examination of a dimension that is not closely studied in the context of Bangladesh, a child’s disability in marriage dissolution of the parents, extends that literature. In keeping with the secondary qualitative methodology that Cheong et al. (2023) propose, the study analyses eight past news narratives (2016-2026) in Bangladeshi media, which are publicly available. In these narratives, family members speak for themselves about raising a disabled child. Discourse analysis reveals three themes. First, mothers globally carry the structural weight of caring for the family, regardless of the father’s involvement. Second, some discourse suggests the child’s disability is sometimes ‘responsible’ for the father’s exit, which can occur before and/or after birth. Third, despair for the future collides with maternal agency, best seen through the mother who established her own school after being turned away from every single one. The analysis does not imply a causal link between disability and divorce. It shows how this link is narrated in the Bangladeshi public sphere. The analysis offers the narrated link as a focused question for future primary, interview-based research. As an exploratory secondary analysis, this piece recognises the limitation of the data being drawn from credible journalistic sources rather than high-quality interviews.

articles.title: Radiografía de la Accesibilidad Digital Municipal en Chile 2026
articles.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles.abstract:
La digitalización de los servicios municipales en Chile promete acercar el Estado a la
ciudadanía, pero revela una barrera crítica: la exclusión por diseño. Hoy, el acceso a la
información pública digital no es universal. Este informe expone los resultados de una
auditoría de accesibilidad web bajo estándares WCAG 2.1, aplicada a veinte plataformas
municipales de las regiones Metropolitana y del Maule. El estudio delimitó su alcance a
versiones de escritorio ya que esto permite establecer una línea base sobre la calidad del
código estructural. El objetivo fue medir empíricamente las barreras que aíslan a personas con
discapacidad visual y motriz, sugiriendo replicar esta metodología en futuros estudios
móviles.Los hallazgos revelan que la exclusión digital es sistémica y no obedece estrictamente a una
falta de presupuesto. Se detectó un severo bloqueo a la navegación motriz: el 50% de la
muestra no puede operarse mediante teclado, impidiendo el acceso a personas con
discapacidad motriz severa o usuarios de lectores de pantalla. Esta exclusión se agudiza en la
Región del Maule, donde el 60% reprueba esta métrica. A esto se suma una profunda brecha de
diseño visual, con 573 errores críticos de contraste lumínico que invisibilizan los textos para
personas con baja visión. Aunque el Maule presenta un 62% más de errores que la
Metropolitana, comunas de altos ingresos como Providencia y Las Condes también
reprobaron, demostrando que se prioriza la estética corporativa por sobre la legibilidad
universal.Finalmente, existen graves deficiencias en la gestión de contenidos. Destaca una invisibilidad
de la información operativa y transversal, al sumar más de 440 imágenes sin textos
alternativos (ALT), censurando el contenido gráfico para usuarios con ceguera. Además, se
advierte un fenómeno de accesibilidad performativa: el 20% de la muestra usa widgets o
botones flotantes que generan una falsa ilusión de inclusión. En la práctica, estas
herramientas institucionales no solucionan el código base excluyente generando nuevos
conflictos de interfaz para quienes dependen de tecnologías de asistencia.

articles.title: El Encuadre de la Responsabilidad Ciudadana: Comunicación Digital del Servel en la Elección Presidencial y Parlamentaria 2025
articles.authors: Jaime Elorrieta
articles.abstract:
Los organismos electorales enfrentan un desafío comunicacional distinto al de los partidos o candidaturas: deben informar y movilizar al electorado sin abandonar su mandato de neutralidad. Este informe examina cómo el Servicio Electoral de Chile (Servel) resolvió ese desafío en su publicidad digital durante la elección presidencial y parlamentaria de 2025, a partir del análisis de 101 anuncios publicados en Google Ads y Meta Ads.
Los resultados muestran que la comunicación del Servel es abrumadoramente práctica: el 85,1% de los anuncios se centra en información procedimental —dónde votar, qué documentos llevar, cómo revisar el rol de vocal de mesa— por sobre la apelación emocional, cívica o sancionatoria. Contra lo esperable, el tono no escala hacia la urgencia a medida que se acerca la elección; en cambio, mensajes puntuales como el llamado al deber cívico o la alerta contra la desinformación aparecen concentrados en momentos específi cos de la campaña, no en un crescendo progresivo. La advertencia sobre multas por no votar, pese a ser un rasgo central del sistema electoral chileno, ocupa un lugar marginal (3% de la muestra) en la comunicación digital del organismo.

articles.title: Evaluating the Theory of the AnthroShift:  How are Climate Shocks Related to Civic Engagement and Support for Climate Science in the US?
articles.authors: Dana R Fisher; Arman Azedi
articles.abstract: Since the theory of the AnthroShift was introduced in 2019, it has been increasingly seen as a theoretical lens through which to analyze social responses to climate change. This paper builds on this small but growing literature to assess the AnthroShift at the individual level.  We analyze a new dataset collected from a national sample of adults in the US to understand how experiencing climate shocks is associated with climate-change supportive attitudes and behaviors.  Specifically, we look at how self-reported experiences with climate shocks are associated with heightened levels of civic engagement and support for the science that documents climate change.  This paper is separated into three sections.  First, we review the theory of the AnthroShift, which explains how risk pivots can drive environmental behaviors, and connect it with the growing research that assesses the social effects of climate shocks.  Next, we describe our data, which were collected from a nationally representative sample of adults in the US in fall 2025 (n=1,068).  Third, we present the results of our analysis that document how individuals’ experience with climate shocks is strongly associated with civic and political engagement and support for climate science.  The paper concludes by discussing the implications of our findings for the relationship between climate shocks, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as for our understanding of the society-environment relationship and the sociological theory of the AnthroShift.

articles.title: When Belonging Comes Before Belief: Inherited Identity, Social Conformity, and the Difficulty of Looking Outside the Group
articles.authors: Syed Raheel Shahzad
articles.abstract:
People normally receive an identity before they are old enough to examine it. A child is born into a family, a language, a religious or non-religious environment, and a set of trusted authorities. By the time the person is able to compare different beliefs, one position already feels familiar and the others often feel foreign. This essay asks a simple social question: how much of what we defend comes from examination, and how much comes from belonging?

The argument is not that inherited beliefs are false, or that following experts is irrational. It is that social identity can make some questions costly to ask. Family ties, community approval, reputation, and fear of exclusion can narrow the range of views people seriously examine. A recent personal example from British Muslim life is used to illustrate the problem: communities with access to the same modern information may still follow different inherited authorities when deciding religious dates.

The wider point applies beyond religion. Political, national, family, and professional identities can work in the same way. The essay argues that genuine conviction is stronger when a person can examine alternatives without having to lose the social world to which he or she belon

articles.title: When Full Employment Is No Longer Necessary
articles.authors: Hong-Ming Chen
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence may reduce the economic necessity of some forms of cognitive labour faster than employment and social institutions can reorganize the time, identity and roles that work currently structures. Rather than forecasting mass unemployment, we ask what should be tested if that transition arrives unevenly or abruptly: how people are received after occupational loss, how newly available time becomes genuinely self-directed, whether AI can make heterogeneous, voluntary arrangements administratively feasible without turning personalization into obligation, whether unmet human needs can support voluntary new roles, and what it costs to keep the human last mile human. Employment organizes more than income, so occupational displacement is an institutional problem as well as an economic one. We set out a sequence — receive, stabilize, recover, choose — in which recovery is a legitimate state rather than a delay before activation, and in which voluntary reconnection is one possible exit among many. The central proposition is offered as a hypothesis rather than a finding: full employment may have functioned partly as a technology of standardization, while AI could make heterogeneity administratively affordable. Because the same capacity could also produce a more efficient workfare machine, we propose personalization without compulsory optimization as a governing constraint. AI may make matching cheap without making human contact cheap.

articles.title: Greenhouse Gas Mitigation and Climate Change Adaptation: Some Policy Alternatives for Nepal
articles.authors: Ambika P. Adhikari
articles.abstract: Many scientists consider climate change to be the most important environmental issue of this century. Although some controversy lingers about the extent of anthropogenic contribution to global warming, most scientists and experts agree that, due to the increased greenhouse gases (GHG) in the atmosphere, Earth’s average temperature is gradually rising, and the ensuing climate change is causing significant and mostly negative impacts on the environment and human population. Various studies show that average global temperatures have already risen by 0.8 degrees Celsius over pre-industrial levels. Scientists estimate that at this rate, the average temperatures are likely to rise by at least about 2 degrees Celsius by the end of the century. It is widely believed that a rise of more than 2 degrees Celsius in the average global temperature can bring serious adverse impacts to the global ecosystem and human welfare.

articles.title: Ukrainian Refugees in Switzerland: A research synthesis of what we know
articles.authors: Didier Ruedin
articles.abstract: The objective of this research synthesis is to collect and summarize the research literature on Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland. This is done through a systematic review, mostly in the form of a narrative review and with statistical indicators that are synthesized. Graphical summaries and an evidence gap map are provided to better identify the nature of evidence available and highlight areas where comparatively little is known about Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland. There is a wide range of evidence on Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland and their integration, although substantive and systematic gaps remain. The review provides a brief historical background, looks at the demographic composition of Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland, discusses economic integration, housing, education, social integration, crime and safety, health and well-being, and attitudes to Ukrainian refugees. Where feasible, changes over time are discussed. The demographic profile of Ukrainian refugees (many women, many children and elderly people, highly educated) is well documented, as are challenges to economic integration due to an insecure status and limited knowledge of local languages. Much less is known about cultural integration and political participation, for example. Given the size of the population and the ongoing war in Ukraine, more research on Ukrainian refugees is warranted, particularly in the direction of successful integration in a context where return in the near future seems increasingly unlikely, despite so-called dual-intent remaining the official focus. More research is also warranted in areas beyond economic integration that affect well-being and intentions to return.

articles.title: A Moment or a Movement? The Effects of Spatial Exposure to the 2017 Women’s March on Political Attitudes and Behavior
articles.authors: Colette Marcellin
articles.abstract: How do social movements affect the public in a polarized era? I examine how the 2017 Women’s March—the largest single-day protest in US history—affected Americans who were exposed to the march in their local communities. I theorize that crowd size moved residents’ political attitudes and behavior in a liberal direction, particularly among Republicans. Using an instrumental variables approach, I find that crowd size increased Republican women’s disapproval of Trump and both Republican women and Republican men’s Democratic vote choice in the 2018 midterm elections. This paper has important implications for understanding the effects of protests that reach a range of communities and focus on identity.

articles.title: Discussions of Race in Online Right-Wing Communities: A Cross-platform Computational Analysis of Reddit, Telegram, and Truth Social Using BERT and Structural Topic Modeling
articles.authors: Qin Li; Jack Gabriel Risien Wippell; Jasmine Hunt; Robert Bond; Joseph Tien; Nicole Yadon
articles.abstract: Race has long been a divisive fault line in American public discourse. Yet, political and societal changes have catalyzed the emergence of alternative collective identities, particularly in digital environments where alternative narratives can flourish. We examine right-wing social media spaces as forums in which racial discourse (specifically, that related to Black identities) is produced and contested through conversation, focusing on three platforms—Reddit, Truth Social, and Telegram—during Summer 2022. Structural topic modeling reveals six prominent themes: comparisons of the Black Lives Matter and January 6th protests; persistent discussions of race, crime, and violence; perceived racism within the Democratic party; broad discussion about ``wokeness''; race and health issues (abortion and infectious disease); and racial identity. While their relative prominence and framing vary, these themes appear across all three platforms. This indicates that racial narratives do not vary substantially across platforms. By extending the scope of social media platforms studied and foregrounding everyday conversations about race, this study advances academic understanding of how racial identities are both (re-)constructed and (re-)enforced online. In doing so, this study offers insights for political psychologists concerned with identity and its social underpinnings, as well as for scholars of race, political communication, culture, and collective behavior.

articles.title: Evaluating a task and map-based digital recording workflow for pedestrian archaeological survey
articles.authors: Katherine Peck; Grant Snitker
articles.abstract: Many Cultural Resource Management firms, public agencies, and research organizations use digital recording methods for archaeological pedestrian survey. However, some archaeologists may be reluctant to adopt a fully digital workflow because of cost or reliability concerns. In this paper, we propose a map-based and task-oriented digital recording workflow for archaeological survey, implemented in Avenza Maps. We first review the literature on digital field data recording workflows. Then, we describe our decision-making process and experience applying the workflow in the field. We also discuss the post-processing software we developed to quickly extract and organize field data to streamline creating final project deliverables. We argue overall that this method is low-cost, flexible, robust to data recording errors, and easy to implement and troubleshoot without advanced technical skills. Future digital recording implementations may also benefit from a map-based approach, even if they choose not to use this specific implementation.

articles.title: How Much Labelled Data Is Enough? A Simulation Study of Prompting Strategies for Unbiased and Reliable LLM-Based Annotation Workflows in Social Sciences
articles.authors: Qixiang Fang
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in (computational) social science to annotate text at scale. Typically, this approach requires researchers to provide (enough) gold labels, develop and evaluate candidate prompts, and decide on the most promising prompt. Meanwhile, many questions arise and remain unanswered: How much labelled data is enough? How should prompt evaluation be conducted? In particular, how can researchers prevent overfitting, an important consideration many social scientists are unfamiliar with. To address these questions, this paper reports a simulation study of prompt evaluation workflows for LLM-based text annotation. I compare intentionally biased yet often employed all-data reuse and validation-only baseline strategies with two defensible workflows: a two-way development/evaluation split and a three-way Explore--Select--Evaluate (ESE) workflow. Across 360 simulation scenarios and 360,000 workflow-level simulation results, all-data reuse and validation-only workflows produced positive reporting bias, especially under adaptive prompt development. In contrast, both two-way and ESE workflows had near-zero mean reporting bias and close-to-95% coverage. However, ESE did not generally select stronger prompts. In fixed-candidate settings, two-way selection outperformed ESE because ESE retained less data for formal prompt comparison without gaining any benefit from exploration. In adaptive settings, ESE reduced regret only modestly under some split ratios, while two-way workflows usually selected prompts with higher absolute true performance. The results suggest that a held-out evaluation set is essential, but that a separate Select stage should be used selectively rather than treated as universally optimal.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (III): From Banner Affiliation to Ethnicity—The Reconstruction of Modern Manchu Identity and Online Narratives of Manchu–Han Conflict
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article examines the formation of modern Manchu identity and its relationship to Manchu–Han tensions within the context of Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese internet in the 2020s. It begins by analyzing the Qing Eight Banner system, arguing that the banners were not a single-ethnicity organization in the modern sense, but a political and social system composed of multiple identity groups including Manchu, Mongol, Han-martial (Hanjun), and bondservant (baoyi) populations. After the fall of the Qing, the former banner affiliation was gradually reorganized within the modern ethnic classification system, producing the Manchu identity of today. The article further discusses the process of reconstituting modern Manchu identity since the 1980s, contending that this process involves both historical continuity and the influence of ethnic policy, local administrative factors, and practical interests. When ethnic identity becomes linked to the allocation of public resources, social policy, and historical narrative, it may shift from cultural identification toward an identity of social interest. The article maintains that contemporary Manchu–Han contradictions are not purely ethnic conflicts, but the product of the combined operation of historical memory, identity recognition, class differences, and material interests. Reducing the binding between ethnic identity and the distribution of public goods, thereby allowing ethnic identity to return more fully to the domain of cultural identification, may be an important direction for alleviating related tensions.

articles.title: Dynamic Democratic Consent: A System Dynamics Framework for Public Trust, Political Communication, and Policy Feedback
articles.authors: Muhammad Sukri Bin Ramli
articles.abstract: Political communication is often analyzed through event-based models that give lim ited attention to feedback, delay, saturation, and changing public trust. This conceptual paper proposes the Dynamic Democratic Consent framework, integrating selected princi ples from Edward Bernays’ account of public relations with the S-E-E-D behavior modes of Snowball growth, Equilibrium seeking, Elastic adjustment, and feedback-loop Dominance. The framework extends the conventional resource categories of manpower, mindpower, and money by treating algorithmic media infrastructure as a conditional fourth dimension. It maps an eight-stage communication-planning process onto reinforcing and balancing feed back structures, perception delays, demographic capacity, and institutional trust. Simulated reference modes illustrate how political-support momentum may encounter electoral satura tion, how delayed perception and corrective response may produce oscillatory adjustment, and how divergence between communication and policy delivery may weaken institutional trust and contract effective support capacity. A four-stage diagnostic process is proposed for describing trajectories, identifying feedback structures, designing policy interventions, and examining potential behavioral shifts. The framework is exploratory rather than predictive. Empirical estimation, comparative case testing, sensitivity analysis, and ethical evaluation are required before it can support applied political analysis.

articles_hidden.title: Faith in Action: Does Ramadan Reduce Crime?
articles_hidden.authors: Sk Niyaj Mohammed; Ashokankur Datta
articles_hidden.abstract: As a social institution, religion creates incentives or disincentives for ‘appropriate’ and ‘inappropriate’ social behaviour, including attitudes towards participation in criminal activities. The size of such an effect depends on the intensity of socio-religious norms regarding specific forms of crime. Ramadan, a period of heightened religiosity among Muslims, involves expectations regarding socially desirable behaviour among individuals. Ramadan also involves mandated fasting, which affects local economic activity. How do such expectations and religious restructuring of daily life affect the incidence of crime among believers directly and/or indirectly? Using a difference-in-differences methodology and information from a unique dataset of criminal offences, we estimate the impact of Ramadan on criminal offences committed by those affected by it. Our identification strategy leverages the shifting timing of Ramadan through the Gregorian calendar to isolate the causal effect from confounding seasonality. We find that Ramadan leads to economically and statistically significant reductions in both violent and non-violent crimes, with estimated effect sizes ranging from 8 to 23 percent. We find suggestive evidence of these results being mediated by changes in religiosity and associated behavioural norms rather than by labour market channels. Our results provide suggestive evidence that informal institutions, such as religion, may complement formal state institutions in efforts to reduce crime.

articles_hidden.title: A Research Note on the pitfalls of sample selection and what (not) to control for in gender wage gap estimations
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Collischon
articles_hidden.abstract: Estimating discriminatory gaps is one of the core topics of Sociology. A large number of studies use observational data to estimate these gaps, typically by controlling for potentially confounding factors and interpreting the coefficient of the group variable (e.g. female) as the degree of discrimination. However, estimations in this manner require choices both with regards to sample selection as well as the selection of variables to control for the stages where researchers assume discrimination to occur. Against the backdrop of the literature on gender wage gaps, this research note discusses these choices, their impact on the interpretation of the results and provides recommendations for applied researchers on how to deal with these choices in practice.

articles_hidden.title: Value Orientations Emerging from Medical Isolation Following a Life-Threatening Illness: A Phenomenological Study
articles_hidden.authors: Great I Am W. Carranza Gismundo; Krisha Mae M. Quinto
articles_hidden.abstract: Serious illness and medical isolation can disrupt individuals’ relationships, responsibilities, routines, and expectations for the future, bringing particular priorities and sources of meaning into greater awareness. This study explored the value orientations reflected in the recurring thoughts, concerns, and anticipated situations of individuals who experienced medical isolation following a life-threatening illness. A descriptive phenomenological approach within an interpretivist paradigm was employed. Criterion purposive sampling was used to recruit 13 Filipino adults who had recovered from COVID-19 and experienced medical isolation. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted through phone calls or Facebook Messenger and documented through written interview records. Data collection and analysis proceeded concurrently, with data adequacy guided by inductive thematic saturation. The primary researcher independently analyzed the interview records using Colaizzi’s phenomenological method, while credibility was supported through member checking and independent review of the emergent themes by an experienced hospital-based social worker and a social work educator. Five major themes emerged: Relational Embeddedness and Social Vulnerability; Economic and Occupational Precarity; Meaning-Making, Learning, and Future Orientation; Experiential Reframing and Emotional Restoration; and Transcendence Beyond the Self. The findings indicate that medical isolation was experienced not only as a disruption to physical health but also as a period in which relationships, responsibilities, occupational and economic roles, future aspirations, everyday experiences, spirituality, and concerns for others became particularly salient. Rather than demonstrating permanent value transformation, the findings show how serious illness and enforced isolation can bring existing priorities and sources of meaning into greater awareness. The study highlights the importance of attending to the relational, occupational, economic, existential, and everyday dimensions of illness in health and helping practice.

articles_hidden.title: A Blended Distribution
articles_hidden.authors: George Y. Nie
articles_hidden.abstract: We use an example to show that a distribution is asymmetric generally, suggesting that extant statistic methodologies are problematic. Treating the force behind asymmetry as momentum, we define a distribution with momentum as a blended distribution—as if a normal distribution is disfigured by, or blended with, momentum. We propose that a variable’s movement over a period follows a distribution longitudinally while the literature is usually limited to a variable’s population that follows a distribution cross-sectionally. We introduce a methodology of mean expected number (MEN) of observations to measure the invisible observations of a distribution, thereby obtaining the probability density curve. We show that the probabilities predicted by a normal distribution are largely incorrect.

articles_hidden.title: Same Sullivan, different worlds: When prevalence is not health, and lifetables are not mortality
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Riffe; Rustam Tursun-zade; Octavio Bramajo
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: A lifetable combined with the prevalence of a health condition is sufficient to estimate health expectancy (HLE) using the Sullivan method. Different approaches exist for decomposing differences in HLE calculated this way. It has been suggested that such results cannot be interpreted directly, as they do not adequately disentangle health and mortality effects, with each estimated component potentially reflecting unobserved contributions from both processes. Objectives: Inspired by Anscombe’s quartet, we introduce a Sullivan analog to show that multistate systems with fundamentally different dynamics can yield identical Sullivan-based summary measures. Methods: We generate 32 multistate scenarios, 16 allowing for recovery (returns) and 16 without recovery, all of which exactly match the same values for prevalence, mortality, and by extension healthy life expectancy. We then perform all 240 valid pairwise multistate decompositions to assess whether differences across scenarios are detectable. Results: As expected, the multistate decompositions yield varied and meaningful effects from individual health and mortality hazards on health expectancy, all of which sum to zero at the margin. The analogous Sullivan decompositions all imply that prevalence and lifetable effects are both zero. Conclusions: These findings suggest that results derived from Sullivan-based decompositions are inherently ambiguous. Such results can be interpreted as prevalence and lifetable effects, but not as health and mortality effects, and interpretation must therefore be approached with caution.
