Its contribution is to connect property theory, commons governance, local-government law, and democratic accountability without treating either privatization or municipal control as categorically superior.

articles_hidden.title: Natural Hazards Threat and Early Marriage for Women and Girls in Latin America and the Caribbean
articles_hidden.authors: Boyoon Lee; Guilherme Natan Fasolin; Ted Hsuan Yun Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Natural hazards threat can shift marriage practices in ways that systematically harm young women and girls, as post-disaster conditions incentivize families to marry off daughters as an adaptation response against economic and physical insecurity. We study this link using geolocated representative samples from 15 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean, a region with one of the highest early marriage rates in the world. We show that exposure to natural hazards is associated with higher prevalence of marriage among women under 18 and increased acceptance of these marriage practices among the general population. This relationship is mitigated by strong government institutions, which was previously unobserved in other regions. Our study demonstrates that rational climate adaptation behaviors at the household level can exacerbate within-household distributional inequalities, emphasizing the need for stronger institutional support structures that provide equitable means of adaptation.

articles_hidden.title: Electricity Patronage and the Energy Transition: Indonesia in Comparative Perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments across the Global South are choosing between clean electricity or fossil fuels. Electricity procurement regimes—the practices governing how governments and utilities allocate generation contracts and associated rents—are a critical and overlooked determinant of this choice. Using Indonesia as a theory-building case, I argue that the programmatic character of electricity procurement shapes whether governments can credibly commit to renewable energy producers, select least-cost projects, and provide the collective goods renewables require to scale. Patronage-based procurement regimes, in contrast, systematically favor fossil fuels. I trace Indonesia’s coal entrenchment to its patronage-based procurement regime, in which clientelist party competition, weak executive constraints, and failed reforms concentrated discretion in the state-owned utility PLN, which operated as a broker for the ruling coalition. Comparative cases in India and South Africa show how programmatic reforms enabled renewable scale-up despite similarly powerful fossil fuel incumbents. The findings advance a meso-level account that bridges the comparative politics literature on patronage and the study of global energy transitions.

articles_hidden.title: When voters take a stance: How voting on issues influences support for parties
articles_hidden.authors: Davide Morisi
articles_hidden.abstract: What are the consequences of referendums for voting for parties? Despite increased use of direct democratic instruments around the world, this question has been essentially ignored. I argue that referendums lead to a realignment between voters and parties that is consistent with a bidimensional model of proximity voting. The analysis of nine referendums that took place in seven countries between 2015 and 2025 confirm the predictions showing that, after each consulta-tion, a sizeable share of cross-pressured voters who cast a referendum vote against party recom-mendations “follow the issue”, switching to a party that is in line with their issue positions. Ideological proximity with parties, however, moderates vote switching. In highly salient consultations, this pattern persists over time. Further experimental evidence confirms the causal link between issue-based considerations and voting. These findings have relevant implications for how direct democracy impacts a fundamental aspect of democratic representation, namely voting for parties.

articles_hidden.title: Transphobia Disguised as "Academic Freedom"
articles_hidden.authors: John Michael Herbert
articles_hidden.abstract: A pattern of attacks on the transgender community, promulgated by academics and in some cases platformed by scientific journals, has become a rallying point for libertarian hardliners who conflate free speech with academic freedom, and who believe that any restrictions on university professors necessarily violate the latter. These academic transphobes provide a pseudo-scholarly veneer that emboldens legislators to pursue anti-transgender policies that  have documented consequences, including increased suicidality among transgender adolescents.  Despite a clear consensus among healthcare professionals specializing in gender dysphoria, a growing body of misinformation has been cited in court decisions as evidence of "scientific uncertainty", providing rationale to defer to legislatures that would ban gender-affirming care. The present work focuses on academic enablers, who are part of a larger ruse to launder a political agenda that is hostile to diversity, equity, and inclusion considerations. Much of that agenda is funded by, or closely affiliated with, political groups that are broadly hostile toward higher education and whose real goal is to foment censorship rather than to encourage open debate, in part by dismantling the academic tenure system. Detailed examination of scholars involved in anti-transgender crusades, especially those advocating for a clinical diagnosis of "rapid-onset gender dysphoria", reveals longstanding antipathy towards the LGBTQ+ community. Well-meaning scholars are advised to see through this bad-faith patina, to avoid inadvertently amplifying harmful attacks that also provide faux-intellectual camouflage for genuine enemies of academic freedom.

articles_hidden.title: ICT, Sustainable Development and Job Polarization: Evidence from ECOWAS
articles_hidden.authors: Dennis Nchor
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper assesses the contribution of information and communication technology (ICT) to sustainable development and job polarization in the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Panel pooled mean group models are used to assess the role of ICT in sustainable development whereas changes in employment shares of the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO08) occupations are used to investigate the changing employment distribution in the labor markets in the region. The results show that all measures of ICT had a positive and significant impact on sustainable development. The paper also finds that the West African countries are lagging in terms of ICT adoption and ICT infrastructure. The pace of adoption is slower compared to developed countries thus minimizing the pace of job polarization. The results obtained found no u-shaped employment distribution in the countries to indicate job polarization. Significantly however, there is a decline in the share of employment of the agriculture, forestry and fishery sectors. The decline in the share of employment is however offset by rising employment shares of most middle-skilled occupations in the region.

articles_hidden.title: Juicio didáctico-matemático sobre el output de la IA generativa: revisión integrativa crítica de la evidencia empírica en educación matemática
articles_hidden.authors: Hector Enrique Banquez Buendia
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objetivo. Sintetizar críticamente la evidencia sobre cómo docentes, futuros docentes y estudiantes juzgan outputs matemáticos y didácticos de IA generativa, y formular un constructo de competencia profesional con anclaje disciplinar.

Método. Revisión integrativa crítica de literatura empírica publicada entre noviembre de 2022 y agosto de 2026, desarrollada mediante procedimientos sistemáticos de búsqueda, cribado, apreciación y codificación, con reporte orientado por PRISMA 2020. El corpus se constituyó en dos fases: una búsqueda inicial en ocho fuentes, de la que se retuvieron 13 estudios tras aplicar los criterios definitivos, y una actualización en ERIC, SciELO y Dialnet que incorporó 19 estudios. El corpus final reunió 32 estudios únicos: 18 con participantes humanos y 14 de evaluación sistemática de outputs. Se distinguieron las unidades de análisis, los roles del evaluador y las unidades de evidencia independiente, controlando posibles solapamientos entre publicaciones.

Resultados. Se identificaron diez convergencias transversales, seis de grado alto y cuatro moderado. El hallazgo central muestra que el juicio tiende a concentrarse en la dimensión que la tarea hace visible y deja la otra menos examinada. La dirección observada de esta asimetría varía según el rol y la experiencia: en tareas de diseño predomina la atención didáctica, mientras en algunos escenarios de tutoría predomina la corrección matemática. Una segunda convergencia indica que la exposición a un error no garantiza su reconocimiento y que la calibración de la confianza condiciona el ejercicio del juicio.

Conclusiones. Se propone el Juicio Didáctico-Matemático sobre el Output de IA (JDMO), compuesto por cinco operaciones con indicadores observables: lectura analítica, verificación matemática, valoración de la pertinencia didáctica, curaduría del prompting y transformación y decisión. La calibración actúa como condición transversal. El constructo formaliza la mediación profesional necesaria entre el output generado y su incorporación educativa.

articles_hidden.title: Position: A Score Should Travel With Its Repair History
articles_hidden.authors: Louis Yiven Zhu
articles_hidden.abstract: In machine learning a capability claim becomes established when a model outperforms its predecessors on benchmarks the community already accepts, and peer review confines itself to checking that those scores are reported and compared correctly. We argue that benchmarks consequently perform the adjudicating role that peer review performs in other sciences, and that the field has organised no stewardship to match, since a benchmark is reviewed once, when the paper introducing it is accepted, and never again during the years in which it serves as evidence. Our position is that this arrangement, which we call review once and use forever, is the first bottleneck a meta-science of AI research should address. We support the position with the public lifecycle of MMLU, the benchmark its successors describe as the de facto standard for general capability. Between 2024 and 2025 five independent projects repaired four distinct defects in MMLU, none of them by the original authors and none as part of any joint programme. A count across the benchmark paper, model reports, leaderboards and governance syntheses then shows the qualifications attached to an MMLU score falling from 2.4 per reporting event in the repair papers to 1.0 in frontier model reports, three in ten of which carry none. On this basis we propose three norms for venues, funders and governance bodies, and we answer the objection that unstewarded benchmarks have served the field well.

articles_hidden.title: Donor Responses to Civil Society Repression
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Heiss; Suparna Chaudhry
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter examines donor responses to the global crackdown on civil society, where governments use legal measures to repress NGOs. Donors, including bilateral and multilateral agencies, respond variably; bilateral aid often decreases following anti-NGO laws, while multilateral aid remains stable. Private donors' responses depend on factors like social trust and NGO transparency. NGOs adapt by diversifying funding, forming affiliates, or shifting to community-based support. As the space for civil society continues to shrink, coordinated international efforts are essential to counteract these repressive trends and uphold civil society's role in democratic governance.

articles_hidden.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VI): The Social Foundations, Core Demands, and Future Trajectory of Han Nationalism
articles_hidden.authors: ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract:
After 2020, discussions related to Han nationalism in Chinese online space have increased markedly and have gradually become an important topic for understanding contemporary Chinese ethnic identification, historical narratives, and social contradictions. As the final article in this series of studies, the present paper attempts, from the angles of demographic change, resource allocation, ethnic policy, and national identification, to analyze the social background of the emergence and development of Han nationalism. The article argues that Han nationalism does not simply originate from historical sentiment, but is a form of identity-political expression formed in the process of change in Chinese social structure. With the decline in birth rates, adjustments in the mode of economic growth, and increases in social competitive pressure, some groups have begun to reopen discussion of the fairness of ethnic policy, the boundaries of the national community, and the relations of responsibility and interest among different groups. The article further organizes the principal demands advanced by some Han nationalists, including the abolition of preferential policies based on ethnic identity, renewed discussion of relations of autonomy and fiscal transfer in ethnic regions, and the improvement of social security for lower- and middle-strata groups. At the same time, the article analyzes the possible positive effects of Han nationalism—for example, pushing long-neglected questions into public discussion, emphasizing the principle of civic equality, and strengthening the sense of social responsibility of the majority group. Yet the article also points out that this body of thought possesses potential risks such as ethnicizing complex social problems, neglecting intra-ethnic class differences, and intensifying logics of group competition.
This article does not attempt simply to affirm or negate Han nationalism; rather, it hopes, by organizing its internal logic and social background, to provide an exploratory analytical framework for understanding changes in Chinese ethnic identification after 2020.

articles_hidden.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (V): Three Frameworks for Interpreting Qing History—Han Nationalism, New Qing History, and Chinese Nationalism
articles_hidden.authors: ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the differences that have arisen among Han nationalism, Chinese nationalism, and international New Qing History in the 2020s concerning the interpretation of Qing history. It argues that the three narratives do not revolve merely around evaluations of the Qing, but respectively focus on questions of ethnic identity, imperial structure, and the historical continuity of the modern state. Han nationalism emphasizes ethnic hierarchy and historical rupture under Qing rule; New Qing History places the Qing within a comparative framework of Eurasian empires and stresses its multi-ethnic imperial character; Chinese nationalism emphasizes the Qing’s important role in the formation of modern China’s territory and national community. The article further points out that controversies surrounding the Qing in fact reflect different understandings within contemporary Chinese society of national identification, ethnic relations, and the allocation of resources.

articles_hidden.title: Defaulting to Decarbonization?  Financial Insolvency and the Energy Transition in India’s States
articles_hidden.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles_hidden.abstract:
How do financial constraints shape the energy transition in developing countries? I study this question in India, where electricity procurement is governed at the subnational level. Electoral politics motivates state governments to subsidize electricity consumption, resulting in financial stress for electricity distribution utilities (DISCOMs). Using multiple sources of original data on utility and plant operations, I investigate the relationship between financial distress and decarbonization. I theorize that the effect of utility insolvency depends on the margin considered—dispatch vs. capacity investment—and on institutions. Counterintuitively, but consistent with my theory, I find that financial stress is associated in the short run with greater relative procurement of renewable energy and less procurement of fossil fuels. Mechanism tests suggest that coal dispatch is more sensitive to liquidity constraints, as distressed DISCOMs cut back on coal deliveries while renewable energy remains protected by “must-run” dispatch regulations. In contrast, I find at most weak evidence that insolvency raises challenges for decarbonizing electricity in the long run: insolvency shows no relationship with renewable-energy tendering, only suggestive evidence that it slows renewable capacity investment, and similarly weak evidence that it curtails expansion of transmission lines that renewables need to scale. The results qualify the conventional wisdom that electricity utility
insolvency is a binding constraint on the energy transition.

articles_hidden.title: When Are Asymmetric Fixed-Effects Models Within-Person Tests of Reversibility? Heterogeneous Responses and Bidirectional Support
articles_hidden.authors: Jiwon Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: Asymmetric fixed-effects models are increasingly used in sociological research to test whether an effect reverses when a time-varying predictor changes direction. Because these models rely on within-person change, directional asymmetry is often interpreted as evidence of within-person irreversibility. This study shows that this interpretation requires an additional cross-person homogeneity assumption. I reparameterize Allison’s (2019) cumulative asymmetric fixed-effects model exactly as a model of current state and total movement, revealing that the specification pools current-state responses across individuals. When those responses are heterogeneous and systematically related to who moves upward versus downward, pooled asymmetry can arise even when every individual’s response is perfectly reversible. I derive this mover-composition result and characterize what remains identifiable when individual state responses are unrestricted. A common path response—the additional response associated with accumulated movement conditional on current state—can then be identified only from within-person bidirectional movement, provided that the resulting variation is not absorbed by period effects. Monte Carlo simulations and a reanalysis of Allison’s wage example illustrate the resulting assumption–support–precision trade-off and show that relevant support depends on the structure of observed trajectories, not simply on the number of directional transitions.

articles_hidden.title: An Approach to the Design of Housing for Kathmandu, Nepal
articles_hidden.authors: Ambika P. Adhikari
articles_hidden.abstract: Totally modern design of housing in Nepal causes problems both in its use and construction. The modern designs have arbitrary spatial layouts that are incompatible with the cultural needs of the users. They require many foreign building materials and skills, making construction problematic. Whereas modern design can improve the performance of buildings in areas of damp-proofing and thermal control, traditional design provides culturally useful spaces. Traditional housing is easy to build but fails in some technical aspects of building. A synthesis of modern and traditional designs is the most suitable approach to housing design in Nepal, and government policy should facilitate it by redirecting education in building technology, by encouraging the production of indigenous materials, by suitable regulatory controls, and by incorporating an optimal design in its own housing projects.

articles_hidden.title: The alchemy linking “gender ideology,” left-wing authoritarianism, and political violence: Comment on Fedida et al.
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander C Tsai
articles_hidden.abstract: In a report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Fedida et al. (2026) analyze data from an opt-in nonprobability sample to describe associations among a newly developed five-item Clinical Gender Affirmation Scale (CGAS), scores on the Brief Left-Wing Authoritarianism Scale, and respondents’ justification of politically charged violent acts. Their interpretation, however, is that “gender ideology,” embedded in clinical guidance, supplies authoritarian psychology with enemies, moral urgency, and rationales for coercion. This commentary argues that the data and analyses do not support this conclusion. First, CGAS measures a narrow cluster of attitudes toward social affirmation and support, not the clinical-institutional ideology attributed to it. Second, Fedida et al. (2026) invoke selection, mediation, and effect-modification theories without specifying or testing them. In particular, an “ideological accelerant” hypothesis requires an interaction between CGAS and authoritarianism, but no such interaction is estimated. Third, the estimated associations are difficult to interpret because the measures contain overlapping ideological and aggression-related content, while the violence items assess reactions to a politically selective set of hypothetical targets rather than a generalized disposition to tolerate political violence. Moreover, modeling CGAS and left-wing authoritarianism in separate regressions adjusted only for political identity does not show that either is associated with justification of violence independently of the other. In summary, Fedida et al. (2026) describe potentially interesting covariances but provide little evidence that “gender ideology” radicalizes people.

articles_hidden.title: Social Cohesion in Iraq: Leveraging Religious, Political, and Tribal Authorities for Conflict Transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Mae Anna Chokr; Ali Al-Ahmad; Abbas Aroua
articles_hidden.abstract: How can we foster social cohesion by engaging with informal religious and political authorities in conflict contexts, such as present-day Iraq? This report answers this question by outlining a conflict transformation approach developed by Cordoba Peace Institute – Geneva (CPI), and in Samarra, Talafar, and Iraq as a whole, between 2018 and 2023. The methodology used was a combination of: 1) a ‘safe mediation space’ approach and diapraxis, 2) collaboration between insider and outsider mediators, and 3) leveraging formal and informal sources of influence, including religious, political, and tribal. The report aims to learn from the experiences of case studies to guide practitioners applying such methods in other similar contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Vanishing Vanguard:  Decline of Leadership in Revolutionary Mass Mobilization  since the 19th Century
articles_hidden.authors: Vadim Ustyuzhanin; Julia Zinkina; Andrey Korotayev
articles_hidden.abstract: “Leaderlessness” is widely held to be a defining feature of contemporary mass mobilization, yet the claim rests on a handful of recent cases. We offer the first systematic cross-national analysis of this phenomenon from 1791 to 2019. We show that the absence of leadership is real but older and more modest than claimed: the share of campaigns / revolutions lacking discernible leadership has been rising for two centuries, yet in the 21st century only about a half are leaderless. Testing six explanations drawn from the literature, we find that two factors robustly predict the absence of leadership: student participation and democracy & human-rights goals, that is, “thin” ideology in contrast to “thick” ideologies of the past. We detect no significant effect of coalition breadth, nonviolent tactic, and internet use on leadership. Thus, leaderless mobilization is rooted in who mobilizes and what they demand, but not in scale, tactics, or technology.

articles_hidden.title: La deuda que no murió: el convenio de pago que no nova, la fuerza de sentencia del mandamiento y el incidente que no puede matar al juicio ejecutivo (comentario a la sentencia de la Corte Suprema de 2 de junio de 2025, rol N° 38.560-2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles_hidden.abstract:
La Corte Suprema, conociendo de un recurso de casación en el fondo, invalidó de oficio —en
ejercicio de las facultades correctoras del artículo 84 del Código de Procedimiento Civil— la resolución
que, acogiendo un incidente de alzamiento de embargo, había puesto término a un juicio ejecutivo bancario
fundándose en un convenio de pago celebrado tres años después de trabada la ejecución (Primera Sala, 2 de
junio de 2025, rol N° 38.560-2024, redacción de la ministra señora Repetto). La doctrina del fallo es de
manual y de trinchera a la vez: si el ejecutado no opuso excepciones, el mandamiento de ejecución y
embargo adquiere, por el artículo 472, la virtud procesal de una sentencia firme; y el convenio posterior —
que en su propio texto declaraba no producir novación, constituir una mera modalidad o facilidad de pago y
extinguir las obligaciones solo con el pago íntegro— no altera la exigibilidad del título ni autoriza a matar el
procedimiento por vía incidental. El comentario reconstruye el caso —un pagaré de $5,6 millones
convertido, por obra del interés, en un convenio de $27,7 millones—, sistematiza la ratio sobre los artículos
472 y 437 del Código de Procedimiento Civil y 1628, 1634 y 1649 del Código Civil, examina el flanco
olvidado de las cauciones de terceros ante las esperas, destila las cláusulas de blindaje que salvaron el juicio
del banco y cierra con un decálogo del ejecutante prudente. La tesis: el juicio ejecutivo solo muere por pago,
por sentencia o por acto conclusivo expreso — quien calló las excepciones no puede, años después, gritar
convenios.

articles_hidden.title: A cautionary tale of industrial decline, economic grievances, and far-right voting
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Kerler; Valentina Petrović
articles_hidden.abstract: Economic grievances are central in explaining the rise of right-wing illiberalism. Grievances allow challenger parties to rally around scapegoating outsider groups, such as ethnic minorities, immigrants, or foreigners. Some research argues that continuing decline allows illiberal parties to consolidate power by entrenching and polarizing around such cleavages. However, when illiberal parties are in power and economic decline continues, we argue that, absent cultural cleavages, retrospective economic voting prevails. Zooming in on the case of Trstenik, a Serbian town with a significant industrial legacy, strongly affected by deindustrialization, we leverage data from a novel survey and semi-structured interviews in a mixed-methods approach. We document clear patterns of existing grievances and blame on the government. However, positive, hopeful interpretations also exist among affected individuals. We show that support for the illiberal right-wing incumbent Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is positively associated with positive interpretations and negatively associated with grievances. Our study contributes an important qualifying account to current debates about the economic roots of right-wing illiberalism by highlighting the importance of scope conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (IV): Why Chinese Scholars Rarely Discuss Han Nationalism
articles_hidden.authors: ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: This article is one of a series of papers examining Han nationalist ideology in China in the 2020s. It seeks to explore the phenomenon whereby discourse related to Han nationalism has increased in Chinese online space in recent years, yet has rarely been treated as an independent object of inquiry within China’s mainstream social-science research system. The article argues that this phenomenon does not simply stem from a lack of scholarly attention, but is related to the operating environment of Chinese social science. Analyzing academic tradition, research frameworks, academic norms, the functions of think tanks, and the situation of scholars, the article points out that Chinese social-science research has long been shaped by existing theoretical systems, modes of resource allocation, and traditions of policy research, making it relatively difficult for certain issues involving ethnic identity, historical memory, and identity competition to form independent research paths. The article further discusses the distance between theoretical systems and public discourse, and how this structure affects the explanatory capacity of Chinese social science with respect to social currents such as Han nationalism. The article does not attempt to provide statistical estimates of the scale or social support for Han nationalism in China; rather, it seeks to pose a question: when a social idea enters the space of public discussion, why does the existing academic system find it difficult to explain the phenomenon adequately?

articles_hidden.title: Making the Case for an Experiential Approach to Test Validation
articles_hidden.authors: Sergio Araneda; Stephen Sireci
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper introduces the Experiential Approach to test validation (Araneda, 2023; Araneda & Sireci, 2021), a framework grounded in phenomenology, rhetorical argumentation, and participatory epistemologies. Departing from traditional validation models centered on psychometric inference and technical justification, the Experiential Approach treats the lived experiences of test-takers and stakeholders as primary sources of validity inquiry. Drawing on standpoint theory, situated knowledges, and participatory action research, it reconceptualizes assessment as a system of interrelated devices whose validity depends on how they function in context. The paper contrasts this framework with Kane's argument-based approach, emphasizing its recursive, device-centered structure and its use of normative, functional, comparative, and critical lenses for generating validity claims. It also examines unresolved challenges concerning stakeholder negotiation, face validity, and the political limits of experiential critique. The paper contributes to emerging efforts toward more context-sensitive, pluralistic, and ethically reflexive approaches to validation.

articles_hidden.title: Climate Barriers to Democratic Participation
articles_hidden.authors: Vítor Calafate; Francisco J M Costa; João Paulo Pessoa
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate change can reshape political representation not only by changing voters' preferences, but also by changing who can vote. Using georeferenced polling-station records from eight Brazilian elections (2010-2024) matched to daily river discharge, we show that historically low river discharge on election day increases voter abstention in communities that depend on river transportation. Effects are absent in comparable communities without river transport, consistent with disruption to fluvial access rather than a general drought effect on participation. Losses are larger among married voters and in sections with higher illiteracy rates, thereby shifting the electorate's composition. These shocks reduce votes for parties whose bases overlap with affected populations, redistributing political power along the lines of climate exposure.
